What was still missing was the arrangement of the charges inside the atom — its structure. In 1897, experiments on electric discharge through gases by J. J. Thomson showed that atoms of different elements contain negatively charged constituents — electrons — identical for all atoms. Atoms as a whole are electrically neutral, so an atom must also contain positive charge to neutralise the electrons. The open question was: how are the positive charge and the electrons arranged inside the atom? The positive charge of the atom is uniformly distributed throughout the volume of the atom and the negatively charged electrons are embedded in it like seeds in a watermelon. This model was picturesquely called plum pudding model of the atom. Subsequent studies on atoms showed that the distribution of the electrons and positive charges is very different from this model. The atom is not a continuous smear of positive charge with electrons planted in it. Two experimental facts about radiation carry the clue to atomic structure. Condensed matter (solids and liquids) and dense gases at all temperatures emit electromagnetic radiation in which a continuous distribution of several wavelengths is present, though with different intensities. That radiation is due to oscillations of atoms and molecules, governed by the interaction of each atom or molecule with its neighbours. In contrast, light emitted from rarefied gases heated in a flame, or excited electrically in a glow tube such as the familiar neon sign or mercury vapour light, has only certain discrete wavelengths. The spectrum of such a gas appears as a series of bright lines. In rarefied gases the average spacing between atoms is large, so the radiation can be considered due to individual atoms rather than to interactions between atoms or molecules. In the early nineteenth century it was also established that each element is associated with a characteristic spectrum of radiation: hydrogen always gives a set of lines with fixed relative position between the lines. This fact suggested an intimate relationship between the internal structure of an atom and the spectrum of radiation emitted by it. In 1885, Johann Jakob Balmer obtained a simple empirical formula which gave the wavelengths of a group of lines emitted by atomic hydrogen. Hydrogen is the simplest element known, so its spectrum is taken up in detail in this chapter. Ernst Rutherford, a former research student of J. J. Thomson, was engaged in experiments on α-particles emitted by some radioactive elements. In 1906 he proposed a classic experiment of scattering of these α-particles by atoms to investigate the atomic structure. The experiment was later performed around 1911 by Hans Geiger and Ernst Marsden — Marsden was a 20-year-old student who had not yet earned his bachelor's degree. The explanation of the results led to the birth of Rutherford's planetary model of the atom. The entire positive charge and most of the mass of the atom is concentrated in a small volume called the nucleus , with electrons revolving around the nucleus just as planets revolve around the sun. Rutherford's nuclear model was a major step towards how we see the atom today. However, it could not explain why atoms emit light of only discrete wavelengths. How could an atom as simple as hydrogen, with a single electron and a single proton, emit a complex spectrum of specific wavelengths? In the classical picture the electron revolves round the nucleus much like a planet round the sun — and that picture runs into serious difficulties, as Section 12.4 shows. 12.2 Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford's Nuclear Model of Atom At the suggestion of Ernst Rutherford, in 1911, H. Geiger and E. Marsden performed some experiments. In one of them (Fig. 12.1) they directed a beam of α-particles at a thin metal foil made of gold. A beam of 5.5 MeV α-particles, emitted from a ^ _ \text `} radioactive source, was collimated into a narrow beam by passage through lead bricks. The beam fell on a thin foil of gold of thickness \ \text `} . The scattered α-particles were observed through a rotatable detector consisting of a zinc sulphide screen and a microscope. Scattered α-particles striking the screen produced brief light flashes, or scintillations , viewed through the microscope. The distribution of the number of scattered particles was studied as a function of the angle of scattering. To deflect the α-particle backwards, it must experience a large repulsive force. This force could be provided if the greater part of the mass of the atom and its positive charge were concentrated tightly at its centre. Then the incoming α-particle could get very close to the positive charge without penetrating it, and such a close encounter would result in a large deflection. This agreement supported the hypothesis of the nuclear atom — which is why Rutherford is credited with the discovery of the nucleus. In the nuclear model the entire positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in the nucleus, with the electrons some distance away, moving in orbits about the nucleus just as the planets do around the sun. Rutherford's experiments suggested the size of the nucleus to be about \ \text `} to \ \text `} , while from kinetic theory the size of an atom was known to be about \ \text `} . So the nucleus is 10,000 to 100,000 times smaller than the atom, and the electrons sit at that many nuclear radii from it. Most of an atom is empty space — which is why most α-particles go right through a thin metal foil. When an α-particle happens to come near a nucleus, the intense electric field there scatters it through a large angle. The atomic electrons, being so light, do not appreciably affect the α-particles. The scattering data can be analysed using the nuclear model, under a short list of assumptions. The gold foil is very thin, so an α-particle suffers not more than one scattering during its passage; computing the trajectory for a single nucleus is enough. α-particles are nuclei of helium atoms: charge 2e and the mass of the helium atom. The charge of the gold nucleus is Ze, where Z is the atomic number; for gold, Z = 79. The gold nucleus is about 50 times heavier than an α-particle, so it is reasonable to assume it remains stationary throughout the scattering. The trajectory then follows from Newton's second law together with Coulomb's law for the electrostatic force of repulsion. is the distance between the α-particle and the nucleus, and the force acts along the line joining them. The magnitude and direction of the force continuously change as the α-particle approaches the nucleus and recedes away from it. 12.2.1 Alpha-particle trajectory The trajectory traced by an α-particle depends on the impact parameter , b, of the collision. The impact parameter is the perpendicular distance of the initial velocity vector of the α-particle from the centre of the nucleus. A given beam of α-particles has a distribution of impact parameters b, so the beam is scattered in various directions with different probabilities. In a beam, all particles have nearly the same kinetic energy. An α-particle close to the nucleus (small impact parameter) suffers large scattering. For a head-on collision the impact parameter is minimum and the α-particle rebounds back, . For a large impact parameter the α-particle goes nearly undeviated and has a small deflection, . Only a small fraction of the incident particles rebound back, so the number of α-particles undergoing head-on collision is small — which implies that the mass and positive charge of the atom are concentrated in a small volume. Rutherford scattering is a powerful way to determine an upper limit to the size of the nucleus — how close an α-particle can get before it is turned back bounds how far the nuclear charge can extend. When an atomic gas or vapour is excited at low pressure, usually by passing an electric current through it, the emitted radiation has a spectrum which contains certain specific wavelengths only. A spectrum of this kind is termed as emission line spectrum and it consists of bright lines on a dark background. Study of emission line spectra of a material can therefore serve as a type of “fingerprint” for identification of the gas. When white light passes through a gas and we analyse the transmitted light using a spectrometer, we find some dark lines in the spectrum. These dark lines correspond precisely to those wavelengths which were found in the emission line spectrum of the gas. The spectrum with these dark lines is called the absorption spectrum of the material of the gas. Lightning is a natural current: charges flow from the clouds to the earth through the atmosphere, sometimes with disastrous results. The flow of charges in lightning is not steady. A torch and a cell-driven clock carry charges in a steady manner, like water flowing smoothly in a river. Towards the same period at the end of the nineteenth century, experiments on the conduction of electricity (electric discharge) through gases at low pressure in a discharge tube led to discoveries no less historic. At a sufficiently low pressure of about 0.001 mm of mercury column, a discharge takes place between the two electrodes when an electric field is applied to the gas in the tube. A fluorescent glow appears on the glass opposite the cathode. The colour of the glow depends on the type of glass — yellowish-green for soda glass. The cause of this fluorescence was attributed to radiation which appeared to be coming from the cathode. The British physicist J. J. Thomson confirmed this hypothesis. By applying mutually perpendicular electric and magnetic fields across the discharge tube, Thomson was the first to determine experimentally the speed and the specific charge (charge-to-mass ratio e/m) of the cathode-ray particles. The particles were found to travel with speeds ranging from about 0.1 to 0.2 times the speed of light. The presently accepted value of e/m is 1.76 × 10¹¹ C/kg. The value of e/m was independent of the nature of the metal used as the cathode, and of the gas introduced in the discharge tube. That independence suggested the universality of the cathode-ray particles. Around the same time, in 1887, it was found that certain metals, when irradiated by ultraviolet light, emitted negatively charged particles having small speeds. Certain metals heated to a high temperature were also found to emit negatively charged particles. The value of e/m of these particles was found to be the same as that of the cathode-ray particles. All these particles, although produced under different conditions, were therefore identical in nature. J. J. Thomson, in 1897, named these particles electrons , and suggested that they were fundamental, universal constituents of matter. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906 for the discovery of the electron. In 1913, the American physicist R. A. Millikan performed the pioneering oil-drop experiment for the precise measurement of the charge on an electron. He found that the charge on an oil droplet was always an integral multiple of an elementary charge, 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Millikan's experiment therefore established that electric charge is quantised . From the values of the charge e and the specific charge e/m, the mass m of the electron could be determined. div]:my-0"> The same electron that Thomson pulled out of a discharge tube turns out to be the particle knocked out of a metal by light — and the light itself behaves like a stream of particles. At the far end, matter borrows the wave behaviour back from radiation. 11.2 Electron Emission Metals have free electrons — the negatively charged particles responsible for their conductivity. These electrons cannot normally escape out of the metal surface. If an electron attempts to come out of the metal, the metal surface acquires a positive charge and pulls the electron back. The free electron is held inside the metal surface by the attractive forces of the ions. It can come out only if it has sufficient energy to overcome the attractive pull. A certain minimum amount of energy is required to be given to an electron to pull it out from the surface of the metal. This minimum energy required by an electron to escape from the metal surface is called the work function of the metal. It is generally denoted by and measured in eV (electron volt). The work function depends on the properties of the metal and the nature of its surface. The minimum energy required for electron emission from the metal surface can be supplied to the free electrons by any one of three physical processes. Energy comes from heat . The metal is raised to a high temperature. Emission is a continuous function of temperature, not of any frequency. No threshold frequency is involved. ), }, { title: "Photoelectric emission", children: ( Energy comes from light . The metal stays cold; only its surface is illuminated. Emission needs a minimum frequency, the threshold frequency. Emission starts within about 10⁻⁹ s of illumination. ), }, ]} /> 11.3 The Photoelectric Effect 11.3.1 Hertz's observations The phenomenon of photoelectric emission was discovered in 1887 by Heinrich Hertz, during his electromagnetic wave experiments. In his investigation on the production of electromagnetic waves by means of a spark discharge, Hertz observed that high-voltage sparks across the detector loop were enhanced when the emitter plate was illuminated by ultraviolet light from an arc lamp. Light shining on the metal surface somehow facilitated the escape of free charged particles — electrons. When light falls on a metal surface, some electrons near the surface absorb enough energy from the incident radiation to overcome the attraction of the positive ions in the surface material. After gaining sufficient energy, those electrons escape from the surface into the surrounding space. 11.3.2 Hallwachs' and Lenard's observations Wilhelm Hallwachs and Philipp Lenard investigated the phenomenon of photoelectric emission in detail during 1886–1902. Lenard observed that when ultraviolet radiations were allowed to fall on the emitter plate of an evacuated glass tube enclosing two electrodes, current flows in the circuit. As soon as the ultraviolet radiations were stopped, the current flow also stopped. Electrons are ejected from the emitter plate C and are attracted towards the positive collector plate A by the electric field. The electrons flow through the evacuated glass tube, producing the current — light falling on the surface of the emitter causes current in the external circuit. Hallwachs, in 1888, undertook the study further and connected a negatively charged zinc plate to an electroscope. The zinc plate lost its charge when it was illuminated by ultraviolet light. An uncharged zinc plate became positively charged when irradiated by ultraviolet light. The positive charge on a positively charged zinc plate was further enhanced under ultraviolet light. He concluded that negatively charged particles were emitted from the zinc plate under the action of ultraviolet light. When ultraviolet light fell on the emitter plate, no electrons were emitted at all when the frequency of the incident light was smaller than a certain minimum value , called the threshold frequency . This minimum frequency depends on the nature of the material of the emitter plate. Different photosensitive materials respond to completely different regions of the spectrum. Certain metals like zinc, cadmium and magnesium responded only to ultraviolet light, having short wavelength. Some alkali metals — lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium and rubidium — were sensitive even to visible light. If light were a wave, a brighter beam should always work and a dim one should merely take longer. The threshold frequency says otherwise — which is why this chapter had to be written. 11.4 Experimental Study of the Photoelectric Effect Fig. 11.1 depicts a schematic view of the arrangement used for the experimental study of the photoelectric effect. An evacuated glass or quartz tube holds a thin photosensitive plate C and another metal plate A. Monochromatic light from the source S of sufficiently short wavelength passes through the window W and falls on the photosensitive plate C (emitter). A transparent quartz window is sealed onto the glass tube; it permits ultraviolet radiation to pass through and irradiate plate C. Electrons emitted by plate C are collected by the plate A (collector), by the electric field created by the battery. The battery maintains the potential difference between C and A, which can be varied. The polarity of the plates can be reversed by a commutator , so A can be kept at any desired positive or negative potential with respect to C. The potential difference is measured by a voltmeter and the resulting photocurrent by a microammeter. Light of different frequencies is obtained by putting an appropriate coloured filter in the path of the light; the intensity is varied by changing the distance of the source from the emitter. The same arrangement is used to study the variation of photocurrent with (a) the intensity of radiation, (b) the frequency of incident radiation, (c) the potential difference between A and C, and (d) the nature of the material of plate C. 11.4.1 Effect of intensity of light on photocurrent The collector A is kept at a positive potential with respect to emitter C, so the ejected electrons are attracted towards A. With the frequency and the potential kept fixed, the intensity of light is varied and the photocurrent measured each time. The photocurrent increases linearly with the intensity of incident light. The photocurrent is directly proportional to the number of photoelectrons emitted per second. Hence the number of photoelectrons emitted per second is directly proportional to the intensity of the incident radiation. 11.4.2 Effect of potential on photoelectric current Plate A is first kept at a positive potential with respect to C, with light of fixed frequency ν and fixed intensity I₁. The photocurrent increases with an increase in the positive (accelerating) potential. At a certain positive potential of A, all the emitted electrons are collected and the current becomes maximum. Increasing the accelerating potential further does not increase the photocurrent. This maximum value of the photoelectric current is called the saturation current . Saturation current corresponds to the case when all the photoelectrons emitted by the emitter plate C reach the collector plate A. A negative (retarding) potential is now applied to plate A and made increasingly negative. Electrons are repelled, and only the sufficiently energetic ones reach the collector. The photocurrent decreases rapidly until it drops to zero at a certain sharply defined, critical value of the negative potential V₀. For a particular frequency of incident radiation, the minimum negative (retarding) potential V₀ given to plate A for which the photocurrent stops or becomes zero is called the cut-off or stopping potential . All the photoelectrons emitted from the metal do not have the same energy. The photocurrent is zero when the stopping potential is sufficient to repel even the most energetic photoelectrons, with the maximum kinetic energy `} , so that The experiment is repeated with radiation of the same frequency but of higher intensities I₂ and I₃, with I₃ > I₂ > I₁. The saturation currents are now found to be at higher values. More electrons are emitted per second, in proportion to the intensity of the incident radiation. The stopping potential, however, remains the same as it was for intensity I₁. Thus, for a given frequency of the incident radiation, the stopping potential is independent of its intensity . In other words, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons depends on the light source and the emitter plate material, but is independent of the intensity of the incident radiation. 11.4.3 Effect of frequency on stopping potential The same intensity of light is adjusted at various frequencies, and the variation of photocurrent with collector plate potential is studied again. Different values of stopping potential are obtained, but the same value of saturation current, for incident radiation of different frequencies. The energy of the emitted electrons depends on the frequency of the incident radiations. The stopping potential is more negative for higher frequencies of incident radiation. The stopping potentials are in the order V₀₃ > V₀₂ > V₀₁ when the frequencies are in the order ν₃ > ν₂ > ν₁. The greater the frequency of incident light, the greater is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, and the greater the retarding potential needed to stop them completely. A graph between the frequency of incident radiation and the corresponding stopping potential, for different metals, gives a straight line. The graph shows that the stopping potential V₀ varies linearly with the frequency of incident radiation for a given photosensitive material; there exists a certain minimum cut-off frequency ν₀ for which the stopping potential is zero. These observations have two implications. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons varies linearly with the frequency of incident radiation, but is independent of its intensity. For a frequency ν of incident radiation lower than the cut-off frequency ν₀, no photoelectric emission is possible even if the intensity is large. This minimum cut-off frequency ν₀ is called the threshold frequency , and it is different for different metals. Different photosensitive materials respond differently to light: selenium is more sensitive than zinc or copper. The same substance gives a different response to light of different wavelengths — ultraviolet gives rise to photoelectric effect in copper, while green or red light does not. If the frequency of the incident radiation exceeds the threshold frequency, the photoelectric emission starts instantaneously , without any apparent time lag, even if the incident radiation is very dim. Emission starts in a time of the order of 10⁻⁹ s or less. 11.5 Photoelectric Effect and Wave Theory of Light The wave nature of light was well established by the end of the nineteenth century. Interference, diffraction and polarisation were explained in a natural and satisfactory way by the wave picture, in which light is an electromagnetic wave with a continuous distribution of energy over the region of space in which the wave is extended. Compare what that continuous picture predicts with what the experiment shows. The free electrons at the surface absorb the radiant energy continuously

Conductivity can be controlled (basis of modern electronics). 1.4 Basic Properties of Electric Charges Electric charge has three fundamental properties that govern all electrostatic behaviour. Total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of individual charges. Charges are scalars — they add like real numbers, not vectors. Sign matters: +ve for positive charge, −ve for negative. Formula: q total = q₁ + q₂ + ... + qₙ Five charges in a system: +1, +2, −3, +4, −5 (in some unit). Net charge of an isolated system remains constant, regardless of internal redistribution. Charging by rubbing transfers electrons — no charge is created or destroyed. Conservation of charge has been established experimentally. Conservation of charge: A neutron turns into a proton and an electron. Total charge is zero before and after — equal and opposite charges created simultaneously. All observable charges are integral multiples of a fundamental unit charge e. Electron carries −e, proton carries +e. SI unit: 1 C = charge flowing at 1 A for 1 s. ~6 × 10¹⁸ electrons per coulomb. Practical units: 1 μC = 10⁻⁶ C, 1 mC = 10⁻³ C. Every charge is an integral multiple of e ), }, { title: "Additivity", children: ( Charges add algebraically with proper signs ), }, { title: "Conservation", children: ( Net charge of an isolated system never changes ), }, ]} /> 1.5 Coulomb's Law Coulomb's Law: The electrostatic force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the two charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The force acts along the line joining the two charges. 1.5.1 Scalar Form If two point charges q₁ and q₂ are separated by a distance r in vacuum, the magnitude of the force between them is: Valid for both like charges (repulsion) and unlike charges (attraction). Valid down to subatomic level (r ~ 10⁻¹⁰ m). Let the position vectors of charges q₁ and q₂ be r⃗₁ and r⃗₂. The vector from 1 to 2 is r⃗₂₁ = r⃗₂ − r⃗₁. The unit vector is r̂₂₁ = r⃗₂₁/r₂₁. If q₁ and q₂ have same sign: F⃗₂₁ is along r̂₂₁ (repulsion). If q₁ and q₂ have opposite signs: F⃗₂₁ is along −r̂₂₁ (attraction). By Newton's third law: F⃗₁₂ = −F⃗₂₁. 1.5.2 Force in a Medium When charges are placed in a medium instead of vacuum, the force between them decreases. The greatest speed with which a signal can go from one point to another is c, the speed of light. The effect of any motion of q₁ on q₂ cannot arise instantaneously. The accelerated motion of charge q₁ produces electromagnetic waves, which propagate with speed c, reach q₂ and cause a force. The notion of field elegantly accounts for the time delay. The concept was first introduced by Faraday. 1.8 Electric Field Lines An electric field line is a curve drawn so that the tangent at each point is in the direction of the net field at that point. The magnitude of the field is represented by the density of field lines — strong near the charge, weak far from it. Properties of electric field lines: (i) Start from positive charges and end at negative charges. (ii) Continuous curves without breaks in charge-free regions. (iii) Two field lines can never cross. (iv) Electrostatic field lines do not form closed loops. The picture of field lines was invented by Faraday. Faraday called them lines of force. The more appropriate term is field lines. 1.9 Electric Flux Consider flow of a liquid with velocity v⃗ through a small flat surface dS normal to the flow. The rate of flow v dS represents the flux. CO₂ and CH₄ are of this type. They develop a dipole moment when an electric field is applied. Polar molecules have a permanent electric dipole moment even without an external field, because the centres of positive and negative charges do not coincide. Gauss's Law: The total electric flux through a closed surface is zero if no charge is enclosed. The term q includes sum of all charges enclosed by the surface. Gauss's law is true for any closed surface. The electric field on the left side is due to ALL charges (inside and outside), but q on the right side represents only the total charge inside S. 1.14 Applications of Gauss's Law 1.14.1 Infinitely Long Straight Uniformly Charged Wire Consider an infinitely long thin wire with uniform linear charge density λ. The experiments of Oersted, ampere and others (early 19th century) first proved they are inter-related — moving electric charges produce magnetic fields, e.g. a current deflects a compass needle. This naturally raises the questions: Is the converse effect possible? Can moving magnets produce electric currents? Does nature permit such a relation between electricity and magnetism? The answer is a resounding yes ! The experiments of Michael Faraday (England) and Joseph Henry (USA), conducted around 1830 , demonstrated conclusively that electric currents were induced in closed coils when subjected to changing magnetic fields — the very inverse of Oersted's discovery. The phenomenon of producing an induced emf (or current) due to a changing magnetic flux is known as electromagnetic induction . 6.2 The Experiments of Faraday and Henry The discovery and understanding of electromagnetic induction are based on a long series of experiments carried out by Faraday and Henry. Experiment 6.1 A coil C₁ is connected to a galvanometer G . Experiment 6.1 — a coil C₁ connected to a galvanometer G. The key observations, in brief: The deflection appears only while the magnet is in motion — pushing the north-pole towards the coil, or pulling it away, deflects the galvanometer; holding it stationary gives no deflection. Moving the south-pole towards or away gives deflections opposite to those with the north-pole. The deflection is larger when the magnet moves faster . It is the relative motion between the magnet and the coil that is responsible for the generation (induction) of the electric current in the coil. Experiment 6.2 The bar magnet is replaced by a second coil C₂ connected to a battery — a steady current in C₂ produces a steady magnetic field. Experiment 6.2 — coil C₂ carrying a steady current, near coil C₁ connected to the galvanometer. As coil C₂ is moved towards C₁, the galvanometer shows a deflection — current is induced in C₁. Moving C₂ away gives a deflection in the opposite direction . The deflection lasts only while C₂ is in motion . When C₂ is fixed and C₁ is moved, the same effects are observed. Again, it is the relative motion between the coils that induces the electric current. Experiment 6.3 Through a third experiment, Faraday showed that this relative motion is not an absolute requirement. Both coils C₁ and C₂ are held stationary — C₁ connected to the galvanometer G, C₂ connected to a battery through a tapping key K . Experiment 6.3 — stationary coils; C₂ connected to a battery through a tapping key K. There is a momentary deflection when the tapping key K is pressed . The pointer returns to zero immediately. If the key is held pressed continuously , there is no deflection . On releasing the key, a momentary deflection appears again, but in the opposite direction . The deflection increases dramatically when an iron rod is inserted into the coils along their axis. 6.3 Magnetic Flux Faraday's great insight lay in discovering a simple mathematical relation to explain his series of experiments. Before stating his laws, we must get familiar with the notion of magnetic flux, Φ_B — defined the same way as electric flux in Chapter 1. The magnetic flux Φ_B through a surface is the number of magnetic field lines passing normally through the surface . Magnetic flux — field lines passing normally through a surface. For a plane surface of area A placed in a uniform magnetic field B : θ is the angle between B and A . The area is treated as a vector , with direction normal to the surface (as discussed in Chapter 1). This relation extends to curved surfaces and nonuniform fields. If the field varies over the surface, we sum over area elements, taking the normal component of B at each element: Equivalently, in vector form : div]:my-0"> 6.4 Faraday's Law of Induction From the experimental observations, Faraday arrived at a conclusion, and summarised it in the form of two laws : Whenever a coil is placed in a changing magnetic field , an induced emf is produced . If the circuit is closed, an induced current also flows . The magnitude of the induced emf is directly proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkages over time. The motion of the magnet (Exp. 6.1), the moving current-carrying coil (Exp. 6.2), and the changing current (Exp. 6.3) all change the magnetic flux through the coil — and it is this change that induces the emf. The induced emf lasts only as long as the flux is changing . The negative sign indicates the direction of ε (and hence the direction of current in a closed loop) — discussed in Section 6.5. Faraday's law could not, however, explain the polarity of the induced emf — that question was resolved by Lenz's law , which we take up in Section 6.5. For a closely wound coil of N turns , the flux change associated with each turn is the same, so the total induced emf is: The induced emf can be increased by increasing the number of turns N of a closed coil. (a) One or more of the following: Use a rod made of soft iron inside the coil C₂, Connect the coil to a powerful battery , Move the arrangement rapidly towards the test coil C₁. (b) Replace the galvanometer by a small bulb (of the kind used in a small torch light). The relative motion between the two coils will cause the bulb to glow. In experimental physics one must learn to innovate. Michael Faraday — ranked as one of the best experimentalists ever — was legendary for his innovative skills. The induced emf: The values of ε and I are estimated — instantaneous values differ and depend on the speed of rotation at each instant. 6.5 Lenz's Law and Conservation of Energy Lenz's law: the polarity of the induced emf is such that it tends to produce a current which opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it. The negative sign in Faraday's law represents this effect. We can understand Lenz's law by examining Experiment 6.1. First, learn to identify the polarity of a coil face from the sense (clockwise / counter-clockwise) of the induced current: Identifying the polarity of a coil face from the direction of the induced current. Now apply this to all four cases of Experiment 6.1: figure]:my-0"> North-pole — towards and away from the coil. South-pole — towards and away from the coil. Open-circuit case: even if an open circuit replaces the closed loop, an emf is induced across the open ends . The direction of the induced emf can be found using Lenz's law. Mechanically, the result is repulsion of an advancing magnet and attraction of a receding one — the induced current resists the very motion that created it. This opposing force is what you feel when pushing a magnet into a coil, and it is the hand of the conservation of energy (below). Lenz's law is a direct consequence of the law of conservation of energy . The induced current is always so directed as to oppose the change in flux ; the work done by the external agent appears as Joule heating produced by the induced current. Can very strong magnets generate current in the loop? (b) A closed loop moves normal to a constant electric field between the plates of a large capacitor. (c) A rectangular loop and a circular loop move out of a uniform field region with constant velocity v. In which is the induced emf constant? (d) Predict the polarity of the capacitor in the described situation. (a) No. However strong the magnet, current can be induced only by changing the magnetic flux through the loop — a stationary loop in a steady field experiences no flux change. (b) No current is induced in either case. Current cannot be induced by changing the electric flux. (c) Only the rectangular loop. Its rate of change of area during exit is constant. For the circular loop, the rate of change of area is not constant, so the induced emf varies. (d) Plate A will be positive with respect to plate B . 6.6 Motional Electromotive Force Consider a straight conductor moving in a uniform and time-independent magnetic field. Motional emf — a conductor moving in a uniform magnetic field. The induced emf Blv is called motional emf . We are able to produce induced emf by moving a conductor instead of varying the magnetic field — that is, by changing the flux enclosed by the circuit. A handy mnemonic for the direction of the induced current is Fleming's right-hand rule ; Forefinger → direction of the magnetic field (B) Thumb → direction of the motion of the conductor (v) Middle finger → direction of the induced current (I) ), }, { title: "Fleming's left-hand rule (motor)", children: ( Forefinger → direction of the magnetic field (B) Middle finger → direction of the current (I) Thumb → direction of the force on the conductor (F) ), }, ]} /> Which to use when? Use the right-hand rule for a generator — finding the induced current caused by motion in a field. Use the left-hand rule for a motor — finding the force on a conductor carrying current in a field. Both encode the same physics; the generator's emf is the reverse of the motor's force. Lorentz force explanation of motional emf The motional emf can also be explained by the Lorentz force acting on the free charge carriers of the conductor PQ: Any charge q in the moving rod PQ moves with speed v in field B . The Lorentz force is qvB in magnitude, directed towards Q . All charges experience the same force, in magnitude and direction, irrespective of position in the rod. Work done in moving the charge from P to Q: . Since emf is work done per unit charge: This matches the motional-emf expression derived above, helping us understand the basis of Faraday's law when the conductor moves through a uniform, time-independent field. For a stationary conductor, the force on its charges is: Since v = 0, any force on the charge must arise from the electric field term E alone . Therefore, to explain induced emf or current, we must assume that a time-varying magnetic field generates an electric field . In Chapter 4, we learnt that charges in motion (current) can exert force/torque on a stationary magnet . Conversely, a moving bar magnet (or more generally, a changing magnetic field) can exert a force on a stationary charge . All this demonstrates that electricity and magnetism are related. When an external force does work in taking a body from one point to another against a force like spring force or gravitational force, that work gets stored as potential energy of the body. When the external force is removed, the body moves, gaining kinetic energy and losing an equal amount of potential energy. The sum of kinetic and potential energies is thus conserved . Forces of this kind are called conservative forces — spring force and gravitational force are examples. The Coulomb force between two stationary charges is also a conservative force. The Coulomb force being conservative is no surprise — it has the same inverse-square dependence on distance as gravitation and differs mainly in the proportionality constant: the masses of Newton's law are replaced by charges. So, exactly as we define the potential energy of a mass in a gravitational field, we can define the electrostatic potential energy of a charge in an electrostatic field. Consider an electrostatic field `} due to a charge configuration. First, for simplicity, take the field due to a charge Q placed at the origin. Imagine bringing a test charge q from a point R to a point P against the repulsive force on it due to Q (NCERT Fig. 2.1) — this happens if Q and q are both positive, or both negative. For definiteness take Q, q > 0. The test charge q is taken so small that it does not disturb the original configuration, i.e. the charge Q stays at the origin. The external force applied, _ `} , is just enough to counter the electric force: _ = -\mathbf _ `} . There is therefore no net force on q and no acceleration — it is brought with infinitesimally slow constant speed. The work done by the external force is the negative of the work done by the electric force, and gets fully stored as potential energy of q. If the external force is removed on reaching P, the electric force takes q away from Q — the stored energy at P is used to provide kinetic energy, with kinetic plus potential energy conserved. The work done by external forces in moving q from R to P is: This work is done against the electrostatic repulsive force, and gets stored as potential energy. The work increases the potential energy by an amount equal to the potential energy difference between R and P: Electric potential energy difference between two points is the work required to be done by an external force in moving (without accelerating) charge q from one point to another for electric field of any arbitrary charge configuration . This is the fundamental characteristic of a conservative force. The concept of potential energy would not be meaningful if the work depended on the path. The crucial fact is that isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist . The word “magnet” comes from Magnesia , an island in Greece where magnetic ore was found as early as 600 BC. Some commonly known ideas regarding magnetism: The earth behaves as a magnet, with the magnetic field pointing approximately from the geographic south to north . When a bar magnet is freely suspended, it points north-south. The tip toward the geographic north is the north pole ; the other is the south pole . Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. We cannot isolate the north or south pole — cutting a bar magnet yields two weaker magnets , never an isolated pole. It is possible to make magnets out of iron and its alloys. Answer: Each part becomes a complete magnet with both a north pole and a south pole — the two poles are never separated. This is a direct consequence of the fact that isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) do not exist — however many times you cut, every piece retains a pair of opposite poles, and the pieces get progressively weaker. Answer: The Earth itself behaves as a giant magnet with a magnetic field around it, and a freely suspended magnet acts like a compass needle — it aligns with this field. The Earth's magnetic field exerts a restoring torque on the suspended magnet, turning it until the field lines through it align with the Earth's field, pointing essentially from geographic south to geographic north. The tip that points toward geographic north is called the north pole ; the opposite tip is the south pole . 5.2 The Bar Magnet Iron-filing patterns over a bar magnet suggest two poles, analogous to an electric dipole, and resemble the pattern around a current-carrying solenoid — the first hint that magnetism and moving charges are related . } function SemicircleDiagram() { return ( (a) I R P dl ∥ r on the straight parts — no contribution (b) bent the other way R P same magnitude, opposite direction ); } export default function MovingChargesAndMagnetismChapter() { return ( <> 4.1 Introduction Electricity and magnetism were studied as separate subjects for more than 2000 years. Their connection surfaced only in 1820 , when the Danish physicist Hans Christian Oersted noticed, during a lecture demonstration, that a current in a straight wire deflected a nearby compass needle. The needle sets itself tangential to an imaginary circle drawn round the wire, in a plane perpendicular to the wire. Reversing the current reverses the deflection ; the deflection grows if the current is larger or the needle is brought closer. Iron filings sprinkled round the wire settle along concentric circles — the field pattern made visible. Oersted concluded that moving charges or currents produce a magnetic field in the surrounding space . This was the first empirical evidence of a connection between electric and magnetic phenomena. In 1864 James Clerk Maxwell unified the laws of electricity and magnetism, and realised that light is an electromagnetic wave. Hertz discovered radio waves, J. C. Bose and Marconi produced them for practical use, and the twentieth century built the whole technology of generating, amplifying, transmitting and detecting electromagnetic waves on this foundation. Two questions organise the chapter: how a magnetic field pushes a moving charge or a current-carrying wire, and how a current creates a magnetic field of its own. Along the way come the cyclotron, which exploits the fact that the circulation frequency of a charge in a field does not depend on its speed, and the galvanometer, which converts a current into a readable deflection. A current or field emerging out of the page is drawn as a dot (·) — the tip of an arrow aimed at you. One going into the page is drawn as a cross (×) — the feathered tail of an arrow moving away. 4.2 Magnetic Force 4.2.1 Sources and fields Charge–charge interaction is described in two stages. A source charge Q creates a field E everywhere in space, and a test charge q placed in that field feels the force The field is not a bookkeeping device: it carries energy and momentum , and it is not established instantaneously — it takes a finite time to propagate. Faraday stressed the concept of the field and Maxwell built it into his unification. A field may also vary with time; throughout this chapter the fields are assumed steady. With several sources the fields add vectorially — the principle of superposition . Currents and moving charges produce, in addition, a magnetic field B ( r ), another vector field with the same basic properties: defined at each point of space, possibly time-dependent, and obeying the same superposition principle. 4.2.2 Magnetic field, Lorentz force A charge q moving with velocity v in the simultaneous presence of an electric field E and a magnetic field B feels two forces at once, added vectorially: The total force on a charge q moving with velocity v in the presence of an electric field E and a magnetic field B is F = q [ E + v × B ], the sum of an electric part and a magnetic part. It is called the Lorentz force , after H. A. Lorentz, who gave it on the basis of the extensive experiments of Ampere and others. Three features of the magnetic part are worth memorising. It depends on the charge, the velocity and the field. A negative charge feels the force opposite to a positive one with the same velocity. Because it contains the cross product v × B , it vanishes when v is parallel or antiparallel to B , and acts sideways — perpendicular to both v and B . Its magnitude is F = qvB sin θ . It is zero if the charge is at rest : only a moving charge feels a magnetic force. The magnitude of the magnetic field is 1 SI unit when the force acting on a unit charge (1 C), moving perpendicular to B with a speed of 1 m s⁻¹, is one newton. This unit is the tesla (T), named after Nikola Tesla. Dimensionally [ B ] = [ F / qv ], so 1 T = 1 N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹. div]:my-0"> The force direction follows from the screw rule or the right-hand rule for the cross product: rotate v towards B through the smaller angle, and the direction in which a right-handed screw advances is the direction of v × B . 4.2.3 Force on a current-carrying conductor A current-carrying rod is a crowd of drifting charges, so the Lorentz force on each carrier adds up to a force on the rod. Take a rod of cross-section A , length l , carrying a steady current I , with n mobile carriers per unit volume drifting at v d . A rod of length l holds nlA mobile carriers, each with charge q . }, { label: "Add the forces", description: <>The total force on the rod is F = ( nlA ) q v d × B . }, { label: "Recognise the current", description: <>The current density is j = nq v d , so its flux through the rod is the current I . }, { label: "Move the vector to the length", description: <>Write F = [( nq v d ) lA ] × B = I l × B , taking the vector sign over to the length. }, ]} /> Here l is a vector of magnitude equal to the rod's length and direction equal to that of the current. The current I itself is not a vector, and B in Eq. 4.4 is the external field, not the field produced by the rod itself. A bent wire is treated as a chain of straight strips: F = Σ I d l × B , which becomes an integral in most cases. For a uniform field only the end-to-end vector matters, so a curved wire feels the same force as the straight wire joining its ends. A straight wire of mass 200 g and length 1.5 m carries a current of 2 A. It is suspended in mid-air by a uniform horizontal magnetic field B . What is the magnitude of the magnetic field? The field gives an upward force IlB . For mid-air suspension it must balance gravity: Only the mass per unit length of the wire mattered, so specifying m/l alone would have been enough. The earth's field here is about 4 × 10⁻⁵ T and has been ignored. The magnetic field is parallel to the positive y -axis and a charged particle moves along the positive x -axis. Which way does the Lorentz force act for (a) an electron, (b) a proton? With v along +x and B along +y, the cross product v × B points along +z, by the screw rule. The force q ( v × B ) then follows the sign of the charge: (a) Electron — negative, so the force is along −z . (b) Proton — positive, so the force is along +z . 4.3 Motion in a Magnetic Field A force does work on a particle only if it has a component along the motion. The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and leaves the speed unchanged — only the direction of the momentum turns. This is quite unlike the electric force qE , which can have a component along the motion and therefore transfers energy as well as momentum. Take first the case v perpendicular to B . The force qvB is perpendicular to the velocity, so it acts as a centripetal force and the charge runs round a circle in the plane normal to B . If the velocity has a component along B , that component is untouched by the field while the perpendicular component still circles, and the path becomes a helix . The frequency ν = qB /2π m is independent of the speed and of the radius . A charge spiralling outward in a fixed field therefore completes every turn in exactly the same time — so one fixed-frequency oscillator can keep pushing it, lap after lap. The cyclotron The constancy of ν is the working principle of the cyclotron , a machine that accelerates charged particles to high energies. Two hollow D-shaped metal boxes ( dees ) sit inside a uniform magnetic field, with a narrow gap between them across which an alternating voltage is applied. The oscillator is tuned to the cyclotron frequency ν c = qB /2π m , so the voltage reverses exactly when the particle reaches the gap. The particle crosses the gap twice per revolution and gains energy qV each time; its radius grows, but its period does not. The kinetic energy is largest at the outer edge, where the radius equals the dee radius R : At high speeds the relativistic increase of mass changes ν , the particle drifts out of step with the oscillator and acceleration stalls. Electrons become relativistic at quite low energies, so a classical cyclotron is used for heavier particles and for modest energies; synchrocyclotrons and synchrotrons handle the rest. The velocity selector Cross an electric field and a magnetic field at right angles, with the beam entering normal to both. The electric force qE and the magnetic force qvB then point in opposite directions along the same line, and a charge passes undeviated only if the two balance: Only charges with this speed leave the region — whatever their mass or the sign of their charge, since q cancels. A velocity selector therefore puts a single speed into the next stage of an instrument such as a mass spectrometer. What is the radius of the path of an electron (mass 9 × 10⁻³¹ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moving at 3 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ in a magnetic field of 6 × 10⁻⁴ T perpendicular to it? What is its frequency, and its energy in keV? (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) Radius. From r = mv / qB , Frequency. Using ν = v /2π r , Energy. From E = ½ mv ², 4.4 Magnetic Field due to a Current Element — Biot–Savart Law Every magnetic field we know is produced either by currents (moving charges) or by the intrinsic magnetic moments of particles. The relation between a current and the field it produces is the Biot–Savart law . Take a finite conductor carrying a current I and an infinitesimal element d l of it. The field d B that this element produces at a point P , a distance r away, is proportional to the current, to |d l |, and to sin θ , where θ is the angle between d l and the displacement r ; it falls off as 1/ r ². The magnetic field d B due to an element d l carrying a steady current I , at a point P at a distance r from the element, is proportional to I d l × r̂ / r ² and its direction is perpendicular to the plane containing d l and r . The constant of proportionality is μ₀/4π, and the expression holds in vacuum. The constant has the exact SI value and μ₀ is called the permeability of free space . The sense of d l × r is given by the right-hand screw rule: look at the plane of the two vectors, move from the first to the second, and take the direction in which a right-handed screw would advance. There is a striking numerical link between the two constants: the product μ₀ε₀ is fixed by the speed of light in vacuum, Choosing either ε₀ or μ₀ fixes the other; in SI units μ₀ is fixed at 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹. The full significance of this relation appears in the chapter on electromagnetic waves. An element d l = Δ x î , with Δ x = 1 cm, is placed at the origin and carries a large current I = 10 A. What is the magnetic field on the y -axis at a distance of 0.5 m? With d l along î and r along ĵ , the angle is θ = 90°, so sin θ = 1. Using Eq. 4.7(b) with r = 0.5 m, The direction is +z , since d l × r = (Δ x î ) × ( y ĵ ) = Δ x y k̂ . Recall the cyclic property of the unit vectors: î × ĵ = k̂ , ĵ × k̂ = î , k̂ × î = ĵ . The field is small because a single element is a very weak source. 4.5 Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Current Loop A circular loop of radius R carrying a steady current I lies in a plane with its centre at O ; the axis of the loop is the x -axis. We want the field at a point P on that axis, a distance x from the centre, in free space. The sum of d l round the loop is just the circumference 2π R , which is how the factor R ² appears in the numerator. The field points along the axis, in the sense given by the right-hand thumb rule. Curl the palm of your right hand round the circular wire with the fingers pointing in the direction of the current. The right-hand thumb then gives the direction of the magnetic field on the axis. The field lines of the loop are closed loops of their own, threading through the loop and returning outside it — the upper face behaves like a north pole and the lower face like a south pole. This is why a current loop is a magnet in miniature. A straight wire carrying 12 A is bent into a semicircular arc of radius 2.0 cm. Consider the field at the centre of the arc. Experiments on the scattering of α-particles showed that the radius of a nucleus is smaller than the radius of an atom by a factor of about `} , so the volume of a nucleus is about `} times the volume of the atom. An atom is almost empty — enlarged to the size of a classroom, its nucleus would be the size of a pinhead — yet the nucleus carries more than 99.9% of the mass of the atom. The chapter asks what the nucleus is made of, how its parts are held together, and what its size, mass and stability are. It then takes up the nuclear phenomena that follow from these properties: radioactivity , fission and fusion . 13.2 Atomic Masses and Composition of the Nucleus The mass of an atom is very small compared with a kilogram — the mass of a carbon atom, ^ \text `} , is \ \text `} . Atomic masses in u are close to integral multiples of the mass of a hydrogen atom. There are striking exceptions: the atomic mass of a chlorine atom is 35.46 u, not an integer. Accurate atomic masses are measured with a mass spectrometer . Such measurements revealed atoms of the same element with identical chemical properties but different masses. Atomic species of the same element differing in mass are called isotopes . (In Greek, isotope means the same place — they occur in the same place in the periodic table of elements.) Practically every element is a mixture of several isotopes, and the relative abundance differs from element to element. Chlorine has two isotopes of masses 34.98 u and 36.98 u, with relative abundances of 75.4 and 24.6 per cent. The atomic mass of chlorine is the weighted average: which agrees with the measured atomic mass of chlorine. Even the lightest element has three isotopes. Since the positive charge is confined to the nucleus, the actual size of the nucleus must be less than \ \text `} . With α-particles of higher energy the distance of closest approach is smaller; at some point the short-range nuclear force begins to affect the scattering and the result departs from the pure-Coulomb prediction. We cannot actually tear a nucleus apart in this way, but the binding energy is still a convenient measure of how well a nucleus is held together. Binding energy per nucleon is the average energy per nucleon needed to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons. 13.4.3 Binding Energy per Nucleon and the Mass Number Figure 13.1 plots `} against the mass number for a large number of nuclei. Many features of the nuclear binding force, obtained from experiments between 1930 and 1950: The nuclear force is much stronger than the Coulomb force acting between charges or the gravitational force between masses. Before the discovery of the transistor in 1948, such devices were mostly vacuum tubes , also called valves . A vacuum diode has two electrodes — anode (often called the plate) and cathode; a triode has three (cathode, plate, grid); tetrodes and pentodes carry four and five. In a vacuum tube, electrons are supplied by a heated cathode. The controlled flow of these electrons in vacuum is obtained by varying the voltage between the electrodes. Vacuum is required in the inter-electrode space; otherwise the moving electrons lose energy in collisions with air molecules. Electrons can flow only from the cathode to the anode — one direction only; hence the name valve. Bulky, consumes high power Operates at high voltages (~100 V) Limited life, low reliability Needs a heated cathode and an evacuated space ), }, { title: "Semiconductor device", children: ( Small in size, consumes low power Operates at low voltages Long life, high reliability Supply and flow of carriers are inside the solid itself ), }, ]} /> The seed of modern solid-state semiconductor electronics goes back to the 1930s, when it was realised that some solid-state semiconductors and their junctions offer the possibility of controlling the number and the direction of flow of charge carriers through them. Simple excitations like light, heat or a small applied voltage can change the number of mobile charges in a semiconductor. No external heating and no large evacuated space are required. CRT monitors, which work on the principle of vacuum tubes, are being replaced by LCD monitors with solid-state electronics. Much before the full implications of semiconductor devices were formally understood, a naturally occurring crystal of galena (lead sulphide, PbS) with a metal point contact attached to it was used as a detector of radio waves. The basic concepts of semiconductor physics, the junction diode (a two-electrode device) and the bipolar junction transistor (a three-electrode device), with circuits illustrating their applications. 14.2 Classification of Metals, Conductors and Semiconductors Solids are classified in two independent ways: by their conductivity, and by their energy-band structure. 14.2.1 On the Basis of Conductivity On the basis of the relative values of electrical conductivity (σ) or resistivity (ρ = 1/σ), the solids are broadly classified as: (i) Metals — they possess very low resistivity (or high conductivity); (ii) Semiconductors — they have resistivity or conductivity intermediate to metals and insulators; (iii) Insulators — they have high resistivity (or low conductivity). 14.2.2 Types of Semiconductors After 1990, devices using organic semiconductors and semiconducting polymers appeared, signalling the birth of polymer electronics and molecular electronics . This chapter restricts itself to inorganic semiconductors, particularly the elemental semiconductors Si and Ge. The concepts introduced here apply by and large to most compound semiconductors as well. 14.2.3 On the Basis of Energy Bands According to the Bohr atomic model, in an isolated atom the energy of an electron is decided by the orbit in which it revolves. In a solid, atoms sit close together, so the outer orbits of electrons from neighbouring atoms come very close or even overlap. Inside the crystal each electron has a unique position, and no two electrons see exactly the same pattern of surrounding charges. Because of this, each electron has a different energy level. These levels, with continuous energy variation, form what are called energy bands . With no external energy, all the valence electrons reside in the valence band. Normally the conduction band is empty; when it overlaps the valence band, electrons can move freely into it. The energy band which includes the energy levels of the valence electrons is called the valence band . The energy band above the valence band is called the conduction band . The gap between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band is called the energy band gap (energy gap E g ). It may be large, small, or zero, depending upon the material. Consider a Si or Ge crystal of N atoms. For Si the outermost orbit is the third (n = 3), for Ge the fourth (n = 4), and both have four outer electrons. The total number of outer electrons in the crystal is therefore 4N. The maximum possible number of electrons in the outer orbit is 8, so 8N energy states are available. At the lattice spacing of Si and Ge, these 8N states split into two bands separated by an energy gap E g . The lower band, completely occupied by the 4N valence electrons at absolute zero, is the valence band. The band of 4N states above it, completely empty at absolute zero, is the conduction band. The lowest level of the conduction band is E C ; the highest level of the valence band is E V ; above E C and below E V lie many closely spaced levels. The size of the gap produces three possible band pictures. 3 eV", "no electrons in the conduction band — no conduction"] }, { cells: ["Semiconductor", "conduction band nearly empty, valence band full", "E_g In a metal, electrons move easily into the conduction band, and when the valence band is partly empty electrons within it can also move to higher levels — so the resistance is low. In an insulator the gap is so large that electrons cannot be excited across it by thermal excitation. In a semiconductor some electrons acquire enough thermal energy to cross the small gap, so its resistance is not as high as that of an insulator. A valence electron that crosses the gap leaves a vacancy behind — so conduction becomes possible both by electrons in the conduction band and by vacancies in the valence band. 14.3 Intrinsic Semiconductor Ge and Si crystallise in what are called diamond-like structures , with each atom surrounded by four nearest neighbours. Every Si or Ge atom shares one of its four valence electrons with each of its four neighbours, and takes a share of one electron from each. These shared electron pairs form a covalent bond , also called a valence bond . The two shared electrons shuttle back and forth between the associated atoms, holding them together strongly. A pure semiconductor of this kind is called an intrinsic semiconductor . At low temperatures all bonds are intact. As the temperature increases, thermal energy becomes available and some electrons break away, becoming free electrons that contribute to conduction. The neighbourhood from which the free electron (with charge −q) has come out leaves a vacancy with an effective charge (+q). This vacancy with the effective positive electronic charge is called a hole . The hole behaves as an apparent free particle with effective positive charge. In an intrinsic semiconductor the number of free electrons equals the number of holes: where is called the intrinsic carrier concentration . How a hole moves Semiconductors possess the unique property that, apart from electrons, the holes also move. Suppose there is a hole at site 1. An electron from the covalent bond at site 2 jumps to the vacant site 1. }, { label: "The hole appears to have moved", description: <>After the jump the hole is at site 2 and site 1 now has an electron. Apparently the hole has moved from site 1 to site 2. }, { label: "The original free electron is not involved", description: <>The electron set free earlier moves independently as a conduction electron and gives an electron current under an applied field. }, { label: "Holes drift the other way", description: <>Under the action of an electric field the holes move towards the negative potential, giving the hole current . }, ]} /> Motion of a hole is only a convenient way of describing the actual motion of bound electrons whenever there is an empty bond anywhere in the crystal. The total current is the sum of the electron and hole currents: Apart from the generation of conduction electrons and holes, a simultaneous process of recombination occurs, in which electrons recombine with holes. At equilibrium the rate of generation equals the rate of recombination of charge carriers. Recombination occurs due to an electron colliding with a hole. Pure material; carriers created only by thermal excitation; equal numbers of electrons and holes; conductivity rises with temperature but is very low at room temperature. C, Si and Ge have the same lattice structure. Why is C an insulator while Si and Ge are intrinsic semiconductors? The 4 bonding electrons of C, Si or Ge lie respectively in the second, third and fourth orbit. Hence the energy required to take an electron out of these atoms (the ionisation energy E g ) is least for Ge, followed by Si, and highest for C. The number of free electrons available for conduction is significant in Ge and Si but negligibly small in C , which makes diamond an insulator. 14.4 Extrinsic Semiconductor The conductivity of an intrinsic semiconductor depends on temperature, but at room temperature it is very low, so no important electronic devices can be built from it. Its conductivity must be improved by adding impurities. When a small amount, say a few parts per million (ppm), of a suitable impurity is added to the pure semiconductor, the conductivity increases manifold. Such materials are known as extrinsic semiconductors or impurity semiconductors . The deliberate addition of a desirable impurity is called doping and the impurity atoms are called dopants . Such a material is also called a doped semiconductor. The dopant must not distort the original pure semiconductor lattice. It occupies only a very few of the original semiconductor atom sites in the crystal. For this, the sizes of the dopant and semiconductor atoms should be nearly the same. Si and Ge belong to the fourth group, so the dopant is chosen from the neighbouring fifth or third group. Two types are used: pentavalent (As, Sb, P) and trivalent (In, B, Al). 14.4.1 n-type Semiconductor Dope Si or Ge with a pentavalent element. When an atom of +5 valency occupies the position of a Si atom, four of its electrons bond with the four silicon neighbours. The fifth electron remains very weakly bound to its parent atom. The four bonding electrons screen the nucleus, so the ionisation energy needed to set the fifth electron free is very small. Even at room temperature that electron is free to move in the lattice. About 0.01 eV frees it in germanium and 0.05 eV in silicon — against about 0.72 eV (Ge) and 1.1 eV (Si) to jump the forbidden gap in the intrinsic material. The pentavalent dopant therefore donates one extra electron for conduction: it is a donor impurity . The number of electrons made available by dopant atoms depends strongly on the doping level and is independent of any increase in ambient temperature, whereas the intrinsic electrons (with an equal number of holes) increase only weakly with temperature. Total conduction electrons = electrons contributed by donors + those generated intrinsically. Total holes come only from the intrinsic source. The increased number of electrons raises the recombination rate, so the number of holes is reduced further. With proper doping, electrons far outnumber holes. In an extrinsic semiconductor doped with pentavalent impurity, electrons become the majority carriers and holes the minority carriers . Such semiconductors are known as n-type semiconductors. 14.4.2 p-type Semiconductor Dope Si or Ge with a trivalent impurity such as Al, B or In. The dopant has one valence electron less, so it forms covalent bonds with only three neighbouring Si atoms. It has no electron to offer to the fourth Si atom, so that bond has a vacancy — a hole. An electron from a neighbouring atom may jump to fill the vacancy, leaving a hole at its own site; thus the hole is available for conduction. The trivalent foreign atom becomes effectively negatively charged when it shares the fourth electron, so it is a core of one negative charge along with its associated hole. Predicts that if the ray bends towards the normal, light is slower in the second medium: {String.raw`v_2 . ), }, ]} /> The two models made opposite predictions about the speed of light in water, so one experiment could decide between them. Foucault's measurement of 1850 showed that the speed of light in water is less than the speed in air — the prediction of the wave model. The wavelength of visible light turned out to be extremely small — about `} for yellow light. Compared with the dimensions of ordinary mirrors and lenses, that is nearly nothing, which is why light appears to travel in straight lines. The branch of optics in which one completely neglects the finiteness of the wavelength is called geometrical optics , and a ray is defined as the path of energy propagation in the limit of wavelength tending to zero. Maxwell derived the wave equation from his equations of electricity and magnetism and predicted the existence of electromagnetic waves around 1855. The theoretical speed in free space came out very close to the measured speed of light, so he propounded that light must be an electromagnetic wave. Radio waves were produced in the laboratory much later, around 1890, by Heinrich Hertz; J. C. Bose and G. Marconi made the practical applications of the Hertzian waves. Huygens' principle → the laws of reflection and refraction (§10.3). Superposition of waves → coherent and incoherent addition, and interference in Young's double slit (§10.4, §10.5). Huygens–Fresnel principle → diffraction at a single slit (§10.6). The transverse nature of the electromagnetic wave → polarisation (§10.7). 10.2 Huygens Principle Drop a small stone on a calm pool of water and waves spread out from the point of impact. Every point on the surface starts oscillating with time, and at any instant a photograph of the surface would show circular rings on which the disturbance is maximum. A wavefront is defined as a surface of constant phase . All points on such a circle are oscillating in phase because they are at the same distance from the source; the locus of points which oscillate in phase is called a wavefront. The speed with which the wavefront moves outwards from the source is called the speed of the wave . The energy of the wave travels in a direction perpendicular to the wavefront . A line drawn perpendicular to the wavefront, showing the direction of energy flow, is a ray . According to Huygens principle, each point of the wavefront is the source of a secondary disturbance and the wavelets emanating from these points spread out in all directions with the speed of the wave. These wavelets are referred to as secondary wavelets , and if we draw a common tangent to all these spheres we obtain the new position of the wavefront at a later time. Huygens principle is essentially a geometrical construction: given the shape of the wavefront at any time, it allows us to determine the shape of the wavefront at a later time. Take the surface F₁F₂ as the wavefront at t = 0, as in Fig. 10.2. , }, { label: "Treat every point of it as a source", description: ( <> Each point of F₁F₂ emits a secondary wavelet that travels with the wave speed . ), }, { label: "Draw spheres of radius vτ", description: ( <> After a time τ each wavelet has become a sphere of radius around its point of origin. ), }, { label: "Take the common tangent", description: <>The forward tangent plane or surface — the envelope G₁G₂ — is the new wavefront at t = τ. , }, { label: "Draw the rays", description: <>Rays are drawn perpendicular to both wavefronts; the wavefront travels along the rays. , }, ]} /> The construction above also produces a wavefront travelling backwards, shown as D₁D₂ in Fig. 10.2. Huygens argued that the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction. By making this ad hoc assumption, Huygens could explain the absence of the backwave — but the assumption itself is not satisfactory. The absence of the backwave is really justified only by more rigorous wave theory. In exactly the same manner the principle gives the shape of the wavefront of a plane wave propagating through a medium: the secondary spheres are drawn from every point of the plane wavefront, and their envelope is again a plane, parallel to the first. 10.3 Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves Using Huygens Principle We now use Huygens principle to derive the laws of refraction and reflection — the same laws that Chapter 9 used, but now obtained from the wave picture instead of being assumed. 10.3.1 Refraction of a Plane Wave Let PP′ represent the surface separating medium 1 and medium 2, with light speeds and respectively.
