blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/Formula"; import from "@/components/content/Stepper"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/chemistry/MoleculeStructure"; import from "./structures.generated"; export default function AlcoholsPhenolsEthersChapter() { return ( <> Alcohols, phenols and ethers are the basic compounds for the formation of detergents, antiseptics and fragrances respectively. The spirit used for polishing wooden furniture is chiefly ethanol — a compound containing a hydroxyl group. An alcohol contains one or more hydroxyl (—OH) groups directly attached to carbon atom(s) of an aliphatic system (CH 3 OH). A phenol contains —OH group(s) directly attached to carbon atom(s) of an aromatic system (C 6 H 5 OH). Replacing a hydrogen atom of a hydrocarbon by an alkoxy or aryloxy group (R—O/Ar—O) gives an ether , for example CH 3 OCH 3 . Ethers can also be seen as compounds formed by replacing the hydrogen of the hydroxyl group of an alcohol or phenol by an alkyl or aryl group. 7.1 Classification 7.1.1 Alcohols — Mono, Di, Tri or Polyhydric Alcohols and phenols are classified as mono-, di-, tri- or polyhydric depending on whether they contain one, two, three or many hydroxyl groups. Monohydric alcohols are further classified according to the hybridisation of the carbon carrying the —OH group. (i) Compounds containing an sp³ C—OH bond. The —OH group is attached to an sp 3 hybridised carbon of an alkyl group. These are further divided into: Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols — the —OH group is attached to a primary, secondary or tertiary carbon respectively. Allylic alcohols — the —OH group is attached to an sp 3 carbon adjacent to a C=C bond, i.e. to an allylic carbon. Benzylic alcohols — the —OH group is attached to an sp 3 carbon next to an aromatic ring. Allylic and benzylic alcohols may themselves be primary, secondary or tertiary. (ii) Compounds containing an sp² C—OH bond. These alcohols contain —OH bonded to a carbon–carbon double bond (a vinylic carbon) or to an aryl carbon; they are also called vinylic alcohols . Example: CH 2 =CH—OH. 7.1.2 Phenols — Mono, Di and Trihydric Phenols Phenols containing one, two or three hydroxyl groups attached to an aromatic ring are called monohydric, dihydric and trihydric phenols respectively. 7.1.3 Ethers Ethers are simple or symmetrical when the two alkyl or aryl groups attached to oxygen are the same, and mixed or unsymmetrical when they differ. Diethyl ether, C 2 H 5 OC 2 H 5 , is symmetrical, whereas C 2 H 5 OCH 3 and C 2 H 5 OC 6 H 5 are unsymmetrical. 7.2 Nomenclature (a) Alcohols The common name of an alcohol is derived from the common name of the alkyl group plus the word alcohol (CH 3 OH is methyl alcohol). In the IUPAC system the name of the alkane is modified by substituting the final 'e' with the suffix 'ol'; the longest chain is numbered from the end nearest the hydroxyl group. For polyhydric alcohols the 'e' of the alkane is retained and the multiplicative prefix di, tri, etc. is added before 'ol' — HOCH 2 CH 2 OH is ethane-1,2-diol. Cyclic alcohols use the prefix cyclo with —OH attached to C-1. (b) Phenols The simplest hydroxy derivative of benzene is phenol — both its common and accepted IUPAC name. Because the structure involves a benzene ring, the terms ortho (1,2-), meta (1,3-) and para (1,4-disubstituted) are often used in common names. (c) Ethers Common names are derived from the alkyl/aryl groups written as separate words in alphabetical order, followed by 'ether' (CH 3 OC 2 H 5 is ethylmethyl ether). If both groups are the same the prefix 'di' is used. In the IUPAC system ethers are regarded as hydrocarbon derivatives in which a hydrogen atom is replaced by an —OR or —OAr group; the larger group is chosen as the parent hydrocarbon. Give IUPAC names of the following compounds: (i) 4-chloro-2,3-dimethylpentan-1-ol (ii) 2-ethoxypropane (iii) 2,6-dimethylphenol (iv) 1-ethoxy-2-nitrocyclohexane. Solution 7.3 Structures of Functional Groups In alcohols the oxygen of the —OH group is attached to carbon by a σ bond formed by overlap of an sp 3 orbital of carbon with an sp 3 orbital of oxygen. The bond angle in alcohols is slightly less than the tetrahedral angle (109°28′) because of repulsion between the unshared electron pairs of oxygen. In phenols the —OH group is attached to an sp 2 hybridised carbon of an aromatic ring. The C—O bond length in phenol (136 pm) is slightly less than in methanol, because of (i) partial double bond character arising from conjugation of the oxygen lone pair with the ring and (ii) the sp 2 hybridised state of the carbon bearing oxygen. In ethers the two bond pairs and two lone pairs on oxygen are arranged approximately tetrahedrally. The bond angle is slightly greater than tetrahedral because of repulsion between the two bulky —R groups, and the C—O bond length (141 pm) is almost the same as in alcohols. 7.4 Alcohols and Phenols 7.4.1 Preparation of Alcohols 1. From alkenes (i) By acid catalysed hydration. Alkenes react with water in the presence of acid to form alcohols; with unsymmetrical alkenes the addition follows Markovnikov's rule. Electrophilic attack of H 3 O + on the double bond gives a carbocation. ), }, { label: "Step 2: Nucleophilic attack of water", description: "Water attacks the carbocation, giving a protonated alcohol.", }, { label: "Step 3: Deprotonation", description: "Loss of a proton gives the alcohol and regenerates the acid catalyst.", }, ]} /> (ii) By hydroboration–oxidation. Diborane (BH 3 ) 2 adds to alkenes giving trialkyl boranes, which are oxidised to alcohols by hydrogen peroxide in aqueous sodium hydroxide. Boron attaches to the sp 2 carbon carrying the greater number of hydrogen atoms, so the alcohol looks as if water had added against Markovnikov's rule. Yields are excellent. 2. From carbonyl compounds (i) By reduction of aldehydes and ketones. Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to alcohols by catalytic hydrogenation over finely divided platinum, palladium or nickel, or by treatment with NaBH 4 or LiAlH 4 . Aldehydes give primary alcohols; ketones give secondary alcohols. (ii) By reduction of carboxylic acids and esters. Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols in excellent yields by LiAlH 4 , a strong reducing agent. Since LiAlH 4 is expensive, it is used only for special chemicals; commercially acids are converted to esters and then hydrogenated over a catalyst. 3. From Grignard reagents Alcohols are produced by the reaction of Grignard reagents with aldehydes and ketones. The first step is nucleophilic addition of the Grignard reagent to the carbonyl group, giving an adduct; hydrolysis of the adduct gives the alcohol. Give the structures and IUPAC names of the products expected from: (a) catalytic reduction of butanal, (b) hydration of propene in dilute sulphuric acid, (c) reaction of propanone with methylmagnesium bromide followed by hydrolysis. Solution (a) Butanal is an aldehyde, so reduction gives a primary alcohol — butan-1-ol, CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 CH 2 OH. (b) Markovnikov addition of water gives propan-2-ol, CH 3 CH(OH)CH 3 . (c) A ketone with a Grignard reagent gives a tertiary alcohol — 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH 3 ) 3 COH. 7.4.2 Preparation of Phenols Phenol, also known as carbolic acid, was first isolated in the early nineteenth century from coal tar; today it is produced synthetically. In the laboratory, phenols are prepared from benzene derivatives by four routes. 7.4.3 Physical Properties Boiling points of alcohols and phenols increase with the number of carbon atoms (stronger van der Waals forces) and, within alcohols, decrease with increasing branching (smaller surface area). The —OH group is involved in intermolecular hydrogen bonding , so alcohols and phenols boil much higher than hydrocarbons, ethers, haloalkanes and haloarenes of comparable molecular mass. Ethanol and propane have comparable molecular masses but very different boiling points, with methoxymethane lying in between. Solubility in water is due to hydrogen bonding with water molecules and decreases as the hydrophobic alkyl/aryl group grows; several lower alcohols are miscible with water in all proportions. (a) Pentan-1-ol, butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, ethanol, propan-1-ol, methanol. (b) Pentan-1-ol, n-butane, pentanal, ethoxyethane. Solution (a) Methanol < ethanol < propan-1-ol < butan-2-ol < butan-1-ol < pentan-1-ol. (b) n-Butane < ethoxyethane < pentanal < pentan-1-ol. 7.4.4 Chemical Reactions Alcohols are versatile: they react both as nucleophiles and as electrophiles. The O—H bond breaks when an alcohol acts as a nucleophile; the C—O bond breaks when it acts as an electrophile (protonated alcohols react this way). On this basis the reactions fall into two groups. (a) Reactions involving cleavage of the O—H bond 1. Acidity of alcohols and phenols. Alcohols and phenols react with active metals such as sodium, potassium and aluminium to give alkoxides/phenoxides and hydrogen. Phenols also react with aqueous NaOH to form sodium phenoxide. Both classes are Brønsted acids — they donate a proton to a stronger base. The acidic character of alcohols comes from the polar O—H bond. An electron-releasing group (—CH 3 , —C 2 H 5 ) increases electron density on oxygen and reduces the polarity of O—H, so acid strength falls in the order primary > secondary > tertiary . Alcohols are weaker acids than water: This shows water to be a better proton donor (stronger acid) than an alcohol, and the alkoxide ion to be a better proton acceptor than hydroxide — sodium ethoxide is a stronger base than NaOH. Alcohols also act as Brønsted bases, because the unshared electron pairs on oxygen make them proton acceptors. Why phenols are stronger acids than alcohols and water. In phenol the —OH is attached to an sp 2 carbon of the ring, which acts as an electron-withdrawing group. The higher electronegativity of that carbon decreases electron density on oxygen, increasing the polarity of O—H and hence ionisation. Moreover, in the alkoxide ion the negative charge is localised on oxygen, while in the phenoxide ion it is delocalised over the ring — the phenoxide is therefore more stable, which favours ionisation of phenol. Phenol itself has charge separation in its resonance structures, so the molecule is less stable than the phenoxide ion. The greater the pKa, the weaker the acid. From the table, phenol is about a million times more acidic than ethanol. Electron-withdrawing groups (—NO 2 ) enhance acidity, and the effect is most pronounced at ortho and para positions because the negative charge is delocalised onto those positions; electron-releasing groups such as alkyl decrease acidity, so cresols are less acidic than phenol. Arrange in increasing order of acid strength: propan-1-ol, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, 3-nitrophenol, 3,5-dinitrophenol, phenol, 4-methylphenol. Solution Propan-1-ol < 4-methylphenol < phenol < 3-nitrophenol < 3,5-dinitrophenol < 2,4,6-trinitrophenol. 2. Esterification. Alcohols and phenols react with carboxylic acids, acid chlorides and acid anhydrides to form esters. The reaction with a carboxylic acid or anhydride is carried out with a small amount of concentrated sulphuric acid; it is reversible, so water is removed as soon as it forms. With an acid chloride a base (pyridine) is used to neutralise the HCl formed and shift the equilibrium to the right. Introducing an acetyl (CH 3 CO) group into an alcohol or phenol is called acetylation . Acetylation of salicylic acid produces aspirin , which possesses analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic properties. (b) Reactions involving cleavage of the C—O bond in alcohols These take place only in alcohols; phenols show this type of reaction only with zinc. 1. Reaction with hydrogen halides. Alcohols react with hydrogen halides to form alkyl halides. The difference in reactivity of the three classes of alcohols with HCl distinguishes them — the Lucas test . Alcohols dissolve in Lucas reagent (conc. HCl + ZnCl 2 ) while their halides are immiscible and produce turbidity. Tertiary alcohols give turbidity immediately, secondary alcohols on heating, and primary alcohols do not give turbidity at room temperature. 2. Reaction with phosphorus trihalides. Alcohols are converted to alkyl bromides by reaction with phosphorus tribromide. 3. Dehydration. Alcohols lose a molecule of water to form alkenes when treated with a protic acid such as concentrated H 2 SO 4 or H 3 PO 4 , or with catalysts such as anhydrous ZnCl 2 or alumina. Ethanol is dehydrated by heating with concentrated H 2 SO 4 at 443 K. Secondary and tertiary alcohols are dehydrated under milder conditions, so the ease of dehydration follows tertiary > secondary > primary . 4. Oxidation. Oxidation of an alcohol forms a C=O double bond with cleavage of an O—H and a C—H bond, so these are also called dehydrogenation reactions. Depending on the oxidising agent, a primary alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid. Strong oxidising agents such as acidified potassium permanganate give carboxylic acids directly from alcohols. CrO 3 in anhydrous medium is used to isolate aldehydes, and a better reagent for oxidising primary alcohols to aldehydes in good yield is pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) , a complex of CrO 3 with pyridine and HCl. Tertiary alcohols do not undergo oxidation. Under strong conditions (KMnO 4 , elevated temperature) C—C bonds cleave as well, giving a mixture of carboxylic acids with fewer carbon atoms. Passing vapours of a primary or secondary alcohol over heated copper at 573 K dehydrogenates it to an aldehyde or ketone, while tertiary alcohols undergo dehydration. Biological oxidation of methanol and ethanol in the body produces the corresponding aldehyde followed by the acid. Methanol is oxidised first to methanal and then to methanoic acid, which may cause blindness and death. A methanol-poisoned patient is treated with intravenous infusions of diluted ethanol: the enzyme that oxidises HCHO to acid is swamped, allowing time for the kidneys to excrete methanol. (c) Reactions of phenols The following reactions are shown by phenols only. 1. Electrophilic aromatic substitution. The —OH group activates the benzene ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions, which become electron-rich through the resonance effect. (i) Nitration. With dilute nitric acid at low temperature (298 K) phenol gives a mixture of ortho and para nitrophenols. The isomers are separated by steam distillation: o -nitrophenol is steam volatile because of intramolecular hydrogen bonding, while p -nitrophenol is less volatile because intermolecular hydrogen bonding causes association. With concentrated nitric acid phenol gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid), though in poor yield; today picric acid is made by first converting phenol to phenol-2,4-disulphonic acid with concentrated sulphuric acid and then treating it with concentrated nitric acid. 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol is a strong acid because the three electron-withdrawing —NO 2 groups facilitate release of the hydrogen ion. (ii) Halogenation. On treating phenol with bromine, different products form under different conditions: In solvents of low polarity such as CHCl 3 or CS 2 at low temperature, monobromophenols are formed. With bromine water , 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed as a white precipitate. The usual halogenation of benzene needs a Lewis acid such as FeBr 3 to polarise the haloge

blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/Formula"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/ConceptCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/EquationLadder"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/chemistry/MoleculeStructure"; import from "./structures.generated"; export default function AldehydesKetonesCarboxylicAcidsChapter() { return ( <> In the previous Unit you studied organic compounds with a carbon–oxygen single bond. This Unit is about compounds containing the carbon–oxygen double bond (>C=O) — the carbonyl group , one of the most important functional groups in organic chemistry. Carbonyl compounds are constituents of fabrics, flavourings, plastics and drugs. Aldehyde — the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a carbon and a hydrogen. Ketone — the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms. Carboxylic acid — the carbonyl carbon is bonded to carbon or hydrogen and to the oxygen of a hydroxyl moiety (–OH). Amide — the carbonyl carbon is bonded to the nitrogen of an –NH 2 moiety. Acyl halide — the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a halogen. Esters and anhydrides are derivatives of carboxylic acids. Aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids are widespread in the plant and animal kingdoms and play an important role in biochemical processes of life. They also add fragrance and flavour to nature — vanillin (from vanilla beans), salicylaldehyde (from meadow sweet) and cinnamaldehyde (from cinnamon) all have very pleasant fragrances. Many of these families are manufactured for use as solvents (acetone) and for preparing adhesives, paints, resins, perfumes, plastics and fabrics. 8.1 Nomenclature and Structure of the Carbonyl Group 8.1.1 Nomenclature Aldehydes and ketones are the simplest and most important carbonyl compounds. There are two systems of naming them. (a) Common names The common names of most aldehydes are derived from the common names of the corresponding carboxylic acids by replacing the ending –ic of the acid with aldehyde . These names also reflect the Latin or Greek term for the original source of the acid or aldehyde. The position of a substituent in the chain is shown by Greek letters α, β, γ, δ, … — the α-carbon is the one directly linked to the aldehyde group, β the next, and so on. The common names of ketones are derived by naming the two alkyl or aryl groups bonded to the carbonyl group. For ketones the positions are marked αα′, ββ′, … starting from the carbon atoms next to the carbonyl group. Some ketones have historical common names — the simplest dimethyl ketone is called acetone . Alkyl phenyl ketones are named by adding the name of the acyl group as a prefix to the word phenone (acetophenone, propiophenone, butyrophenone). (b) IUPAC names The IUPAC names of open-chain aliphatic aldehydes and ketones are derived from the corresponding alkanes by replacing the ending –e with –al and –one respectively. For aldehydes the longest chain is numbered starting from the carbon of the aldehyde group. For ketones the numbering begins from the end nearer to the carbonyl group. Substituents are prefixed in alphabetical order with numerals showing their positions. In cyclic ketones the carbonyl carbon is numbered one. When the aldehyde group is attached to a ring, the suffix carbaldehyde is added after the full name of the cycloalkane; ring numbering starts from the carbon carrying the –CHO group. The simplest aromatic aldehyde is benzenecarbaldehyde ; the common name benzaldehyde is also accepted by IUPAC, and other aromatic aldehydes are named as substituted benzaldehydes. 8.1.2 Structure of the Carbonyl Group The carbonyl carbon is sp 2 -hybridised and forms three sigma (σ) bonds. The fourth valence electron of carbon remains in its p-orbital and forms a π-bond with oxygen by overlap with a p-orbital of oxygen. Oxygen also has two non-bonding electron pairs. The carbonyl carbon and the three atoms attached to it lie in the same plane, with the π-electron cloud above and below it. Bond angles are approximately 120° — a trigonal coplanar structure. The carbon–oxygen double bond is polarised because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon. Hence the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic (a Lewis acid) and the carbonyl oxygen is nucleophilic (a Lewis base) . Carbonyl compounds have substantial dipole moments and are more polar than ethers. The high polarity is explained by resonance between a neutral structure and a dipolar structure: C=O} \ \longleftrightarrow \ \text ^ -\text ^ `} label="Neutral form ↔ dipolar form" /> 8.2 Preparation of Aldehydes and Ketones 8.2.1 Preparation of Aldehydes The general routes, then the specific named methods: By oxidation of alcohols — primary alcohols give aldehydes (Unit 7). By dehydrogenation of alcohols — alcohol vapours are passed over heavy metal catalysts (Ag or Cu); suitable for volatile alcohols and used industrially. Primary alcohols → aldehydes, secondary alcohols → ketones. By ozonolysis of alkenes — ozonolysis followed by reaction with zinc dust and water gives aldehydes, ketones or a mixture, depending on the substitution pattern of the alkene (Unit 9). By hydration of alkynes — addition of water to ethyne in the presence of H 2 SO 4 and HgSO 4 gives acetaldehyde; all other alkynes give ketones. Aromatic aldehydes from aromatic hydrocarbons Strong oxidising agents oxidise toluene and its derivatives all the way to benzoic acids. The oxidation can be stopped at the aldehyde stage with reagents that convert the methyl group into an intermediate difficult to oxidise further. 8.2.2 Preparation of Ketones Problem: Give the names of the reagents to bring about the following transformations: (i) Hexan-1-ol to hexanal (ii) Cyclohexanol to cyclohexanone (iii) p-Fluorotoluene to p-fluorobenzaldehyde (iv) Ethanenitrile to ethanal (v) Allyl alcohol to propenal (vi) But-2-ene to ethanal Solution: (i) Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) — it oxidises a primary alcohol only up to the aldehyde. (ii) Anhydrous CrO 3 (a secondary alcohol gives a ketone). (iii) CrO 3 in the presence of acetic anhydride, followed by hydrolysis. (iv) Diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL-H), followed by hydrolysis. (v) PCC. (vi) O 3 /H 2 O–Zn dust (ozonolysis). Question: Write the structures of the products of the given reactions. How to read them: each of these is a “stop at the carbonyl” reaction, so the product keeps the carbonyl group intact — an acid chloride with H 2 /Pd–BaSO 4 gives the aldehyde with the same number of carbons; a nitrile with SnCl 2 /HCl followed by hydrolysis gives the aldehyde ; a methylbenzene with CrO 2 Cl 2 then H 3 O + gives the benzaldehyde ; an alkyne with Hg 2+ /H 2 SO 4 gives the ketone (except ethyne, which gives ethanal). 8.3 Physical Properties Methanal is a gas at room temperature and ethanal a volatile liquid; other aldehydes and ketones are liquids or solids. Boiling points are higher than those of hydrocarbons and ethers of comparable molecular mass, because of weak molecular association through dipole–dipole interactions. They are lower than those of alcohols of similar molecular mass, because there is no intermolecular hydrogen bonding. The lower members (methanal, ethanal, propanone) are miscible with water in all proportions — they form hydrogen bonds with water. Solubility falls rapidly as the alkyl chain lengthens; all aldehydes and ketones are fairly soluble in benzene, ether, methanol, chloroform, etc. The lower aldehydes have sharp pungent odours; as the molecule grows the odour becomes less pungent and more fragrant — many occur in perfumes and flavouring agents. Problem: Arrange the following in increasing order of boiling point: CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 CHO, CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 CH 2 OH, H 5 C 2 –O–C 2 H 5 , CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 CH 3 . Solution: the molecular masses of these compounds are in the range 72–74. Only butan-1-ol molecules are associated through extensive intermolecular hydrogen bonding, so butan-1-ol has the highest boiling point. Butanal is more polar than ethoxyethane, so the intermolecular dipole–dipole attraction is stronger in the aldehyde. The alkane molecules have only weak van der Waals forces. Increasing order: Question: Arrange CH 3 CHO, CH 3 CH 2 OH, CH 3 OCH 3 and CH 3 CH 2 CH 3 in increasing order of boiling points. Answer: Propane has only van der Waals forces; ethoxyethane is weakly polar; ethanal is more polar (dipole–dipole); ethanol alone has intermolecular hydrogen bonding. 8.4 Chemical Reactions Because both aldehydes and ketones carry the carbonyl group, they undergo similar chemical reactions. 1. Nucleophilic addition reactions Contrary to the electrophilic additions of alkenes, aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition . C=O} + \text ^ \longrightarrow \text \xrightarrow ^ } \text `} label="Nucleophilic addition" /> Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition, for two reasons: Steric — two relatively large substituents in a ketone hinder the approach of the nucleophile; an aldehyde has only one such substituent. Electronic — two alkyl groups reduce the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon more effectively than one does. Problem: Would you expect benzaldehyde to be more or less reactive than propanal in nucleophilic addition reactions? Explain. Solution: Less reactive. The carbonyl carbon of benzaldehyde is less electrophilic than that of propanal, because the polarity of the carbonyl group is reduced by resonance with the ring: The ring donates electron density into the carbonyl group, so the partial positive charge on carbon is smaller and the nucleophile attacks more slowly. 2. Important addition reactions Addition of ammonia and its derivatives Nucleophiles of the type H 2 N–Z add to the carbonyl group. The reaction is reversible and acid-catalysed; the equilibrium favours the product because the intermediate dehydrates rapidly to >C=N–Z. Oxidation This is where aldehydes and ketones part ways. The reaction occurs in an alkaline medium. ), }, { title: "Fehling's test", children: ( Solution A is aqueous copper sulphate; solution B is alkaline sodium potassium tartarate (Rochelle salt). Mix equal amounts before the test. On heating an aldehyde, a reddish-brown precipitate of Cu 2 O forms. The aldehyde is oxidised to the carboxylate anion. Aromatic aldehydes do not respond to this test. ), }, ]} /> Haloform reaction of methyl ketones Aldehydes and ketones having at least one methyl group attached to the carbonyl carbon are oxidised by sodium hypohalite to the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid with one carbon less than the carbonyl compound. The methyl group becomes haloform. A C=C bond elsewhere in the molecule is not affected. The iodoform reaction with sodium hypoiodite also detects a –CH 3 CO group, or a –CH 3 CH(OH)– group which produces –CH 3 CO on oxidation. Problem: An organic compound (A), C 8 H 8 O, forms an orange-red precipitate with 2,4-DNP reagent and gives a yellow precipitate on heating with iodine in the presence of sodium hydroxide. It neither reduces Tollens’ or Fehling’s reagent, nor decolourises bromine water or Baeyer’s reagent. On drastic oxidation with chromic acid it gives a carboxylic acid (B), C 7 H 6 O 2 . Identify (A) and (B) and explain the reactions. Solution: (A) forms a 2,4-DNP derivative — so it is an aldehyde or a ketone. (A) does not reduce Tollens’ or Fehling’s reagent — so it must be a ketone . (A) responds to the iodoform test — so it is a methyl ketone . The high degree of unsaturation (C 8 H 8 O) yet no reaction with bromine water or Baeyer’s reagent means the unsaturation is due to an aromatic ring . (B), the oxidation product of a ketone, is a carboxylic acid of formula C 7 H 6 O 2 — that is benzoic acid . So (A) is a monosubstituted aromatic methyl ketone: acetophenone (phenyl methyl ketone). 5. Reactions due to α-hydrogens The α-hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic . The acidity comes from the strong electron-withdrawing effect of the carbonyl group and from resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base. When aldol condensation is carried out between two different aldehydes and/or ketones it is called cross aldol condensation. If both carry α-hydrogens the result is a mixture of four products — for example, the reaction of a mixture of ethanal and propanal. Ketones can also be used as one component. 6. Other reactions Aldehydes which have no α-hydrogen undergo self oxidation and reduction (disproportionation) on heating with concentrated alkali. One molecule of the aldehyde is reduced to the alcohol while another is oxidised to the carboxylic acid salt. Electrophilic substitution: aromatic aldehydes and ketones undergo electrophilic substitution on the ring, where the carbonyl group acts as a deactivating and meta-directing group. Question: Arrange in increasing order of reactivity in nucleophilic addition: (i) ethanal, propanal, propanone, butanone; (ii) benzaldehyde, p-tolualdehyde, p-nitrobenzaldehyde, acetophenone. Answer: (i) Butanone < propanone < propanal < ethanal — the more and the larger the alkyl groups, the slower the addition. In nature they occur among proteins, vitamins, alkaloids and hormones . Synthetic examples include polymers, dye stuffs and drugs . Adrenaline and ephedrine , both containing a secondary amino group, are used to increase blood pressure. Novocain , a synthetic amino compound, is used as an anaesthetic in dentistry. Benadryl , a well known antihistaminic drug, contains a tertiary amino group. Quaternary ammonium salts are used as surfactants. Diazonium salts are intermediates in the preparation of a variety of aromatic compounds including dyes. “The chief commercial use of amines is as intermediates in the synthesis of medicines and fibres .” 9.1 Structure of Amines Amines can be considered as derivatives of ammonia , obtained by replacement of one, two or all the three hydrogen atoms by alkyl and/or aryl groups. Like ammonia, the nitrogen atom of amines is trivalent and carries an unshared pair of electrons . Nitrogen orbitals in amines are therefore sp 3 hybridised and the geometry of amines is pyramidal . Each of the three sp 3 hybridised orbitals of nitrogen overlaps with orbitals of hydrogen or carbon, depending upon the composition of the amine. The fourth orbital of nitrogen in all amines holds an unshared pair of electrons. Because of that lone pair, the angle C–N–E (E = C or H) is less than 109.5° ; in trimethylamine it is 108° . In trimethylamine the three methyl groups sit at the corners of a pyramid with nitrogen at the apex — the same shape as ammonia. Nitrogen keeps its lone pair in an sp 3 orbital, so every amine is pyramidal, not planar — and that lone pair is what makes amines basic and nucleophilic. 9.2 Classification of Amines Amines are classified as primary (1°) , secondary (2°) and tertiary (3°) depending upon the number of hydrogen atoms replaced by alkyl or aryl groups in the ammonia molecule. Replacement of one hydrogen atom of ammonia by R or Ar gives RNH 2 or ArNH 2 — a primary amine. Replacement of a second hydrogen atom (of ammonia, or of R–NH 2 ) by another alkyl/aryl group R′ gives R–NHR′ — a secondary amine. The second alkyl/aryl group may be the same as the first, or different. Replacement of a third hydrogen atom by an alkyl/aryl group gives a tertiary amine, R 3 N. Amines are said to be simple when all the alkyl or aryl groups are the same, and mixed when they are different. Count the hydrogens of NH 3 that have been replaced: one replaced → 1°, two → 2°, three → 3°. Every class still keeps one unshared pair on nitrogen, so all three behave as Lewis bases . 9.3 Nomenclature In the IUPAC system, primary amines are named as alkanamines . The name is derived by replacement of ‘e’ of alkane by the word amine — CH 3 NH 2 is methanamine. Common names An aliphatic amine is named by prefixing the alkyl group to amine, i.e. alkylamine as one word (methylamine). In secondary and tertiary amines with identical groups, the prefix di or tri is appended before the name of the alkyl group (dimethylamine, trimethylamine). IUPAC names More than one –NH 2 group: positions are specified by numbering the carbon atoms bearing –NH 2 , with a prefix di, tri, etc. The letter ‘e’ of the suffix of the hydrocarbon part is retained — H 2 N–CH 2 –CH 2 –NH 2 is ethane-1,2-diamine. For secondary and tertiary amines the locant N designates a substituent attached to the nitrogen atom. CH 3 NHCH 2 CH 3 is N-methylethanamine; (CH 3 CH 2 ) 3 N is N,N-diethylethanamine. Arylamines In arylamines the –NH 2 group is attached directly to the benzene ring; C 6 H 5 NH 2 is the simplest example. Its common name aniline is also an accepted IUPAC name; by the systematic rule (suffix ‘e’ of arene replaced by ‘amine’) it is benzenamine . 9.4 Preparation of Amines Amines are prepared by the following methods. 1. Reduction of nitro compounds Nitro compounds are reduced to amines by passing hydrogen gas in the presence of finely divided nickel, palladium or platinum . They are also reduced by metals in acidic medium. Nitroalkanes can be similarly reduced to the corresponding alkanamines. Reduction with iron scrap and hydrochloric acid is preferred because the FeCl 2 formed gets hydrolysed to release hydrochloric acid during the reaction — so only a small amount of acid is needed to start it. 2. Ammonolysis of alkyl halides The C–X bond of an alkyl or benzyl halide is cleaved by a nucleophile; with an ethanolic solution of ammonia the halogen is replaced by –NH 2 . This cleavage of the C–X bond by ammonia is called ammonolysis ; it is carried out in a sealed tube at 373 K . The primary amine formed is itself a nucleophile, so it reacts with more alkyl halide to give secondary and tertiary amines and finally a quaternary ammonium salt. A large excess of ammonia makes the primary amine the major product. Order of reactivity of halides with amines: RI > RBr > RCl . The free amine is obtained from the ammonium salt by treatment with a strong base: Disadvantage of ammonolysis: it gives a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines together with a quaternary ammonium salt, so the product must be separated. 3. Reduction of nitriles Nitriles on reduction with LiAlH 4 or by catalytic hydrogenation give primary amines. The reaction is used for the ascent of the amine series — it makes an amine with one carbon atom more than the starting amine. 4. Reduction of amides Amides on reduction with LiAlH 4 yield amines. 5. Gabriel phthalimide synthesis Gabriel synthesis is used for the preparation of primary amines . Phthalimide is treated with ethanolic potassium hydroxide to form the potassium salt of phthalimide. Heating that salt with an alkyl halide, followed by alkaline hydrolysis, gives the corresponding primary amine. Aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared this way because aryl halides do not undergo nucleophilic substitution with the anion formed by phthalimide. 6. Hoffmann bromamide degradation reaction Hoffmann developed a method for the preparation of primary amines by treating an amide with bromine in an aqueous or ethanolic solution of sodium hydroxide . In this degradation, an alkyl or aryl group migrates from the carbonyl carbon of the amide to the nitrogen atom . The amine so formed contains one carbon less than that present in the amide — a descent of the series. Every method above gives a mixture except two: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis and Hoffmann bromamide degradation both give pure primary amines . Gabriel works only for alkyl halides; Hoffmann works for both alkyl and aryl amides. Problem: Write chemical equations for the following reactions: (i) Reaction of ethanolic NH 3 with C 2 H 5 Cl. (ii) Ammonolysis of benzyl chloride and reaction of the amine so formed with two moles of CH 3 Cl. Solution: (i) Ammonolysis of ethyl chloride: (ii) Benzyl chloride first gives benzylamine, which is then alkylated twice: The final product is N,N-dimethylbenzylamine (N,N-dimethyl-1-phenylmethanamine). Convert the halide to the nitrile with KCN, then reduce the nitrile with LiAlH 4 . Solution: (i) Propanamine contains three carbons, so the amide molecule must contain four carbons: CH 3 –CH 2 –CH 2 –CONH 2 — butanamide (ii) Benzamide is an aromatic amide with seven carbons, so the amine formed is an aromatic primary amine with six carbons: C 6 H 5 –NH 2 — aniline (benzenamine) Question: (i) Write structures of different isomeric amines corresponding to the molecular formula C 4 H 11 N. (ii) Write IUPAC names of all the isomers. (iii) What type of isomerism is exhibited by different pairs of amines? Answer: (i) and (ii) — four primary, three secondary and one tertiary amine: CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 CH 2 NH 2 — butan-1-amine CH 3 CH 2 CH(NH 2 )CH 3 — butan-2-amine (CH 3 ) 2 CHCH 2 NH 2 — 2-methylpropan-1-amine (CH 3 ) 3 CNH 2 — 2-methylpropan-2-amine CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 NHCH 3 — N-methylpropan-1-amine (CH 3 ) 2 CHNHCH 3 — N-methylpropan-2-amine CH 3 CH 2 NHCH 2 CH 3 — N-ethylethanamine (CH 3 ) 2 NCH 2 CH 3 — N,N-dimethylethanamine (iii) Chain isomerism (straight vs branched skeleton), position isomerism (the –NH 2 group at different carbons) and metamerism (different alkyl groups distributed around the nitrogen atom, e.g. N-ethylethanamine versus N,N-dimethylethanamine). Answer: (i) Nitration, then reduction of the nitro group: C 6 H 6 → (conc. HNO 3 / conc. H 2 SO 4 ) C 6 H 5 NO 2 → (Fe / HCl) C 6 H 5 NH 2 (ii) Aniline is then exhaustively alkylated: C 6 H 5 NH 2 → (excess CH 3 I, Na 2 CO 3 ) C 6 H 5 N(CH 3 ) 2 (iii) Two successive one-carbon ascents on a dihalide give the C 6 diamine: 9.5 Physical Properties The lower aliphatic amines are gases with a fishy odour . Primary amines with three or more carbon atoms are liquids ; still higher ones are solids . Aniline and other arylamines are usually colourless but get coloured on storage due to atmospheric oxidation . Solubility Lower aliphatic amines are soluble in water because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules . Solubility decreases with increase in molar mass because the hydrophobic alkyl part grows. Higher amines are essentially insoluble in water. Amines are soluble in organic solvents like alcohol, ether and benzene. Boiling points Primary and secondary amines are associated through intermolecular hydrogen bonding between the nitrogen of one molecule and the hydrogen of another. This association is greater in primary amines than in secondary amines, because a primary amine has two hydrogens available for hydrogen bonding and a secondary amine only one. Tertiary amines have no hydrogen on nitrogen , so no intermolecular association — hence the lowest boiling points. \text > \text `} important label="Order of boiling points" /> Nitrogen electronegativity 3.0 — N–H is only weakly polar. The number of hydrogen atoms attached to nitrogen also decides the course of the reaction — that is why primary (–NH 2 ), secondary (>N–H) and tertiary (>N–) amines differ in many reactions. Amines behave as nucleophiles because of the unshared pair. 1. Basic character of amines Amines, being basic in nature, react with acids to form salts . Amine salts on treatment with a base like NaOH regenerate the parent amine . Amine salts are soluble in water but insoluble in organic solvents like ether. This is the basis for separating amines from non-basic organic compounds that are insoluble in water. Reaction with mineral acids to form ammonium salts shows amines are basic; the unshared pair on nitrogen makes them Lewis bases . Basic character is better understood through K b and pK b values: Larger the value of K b , or smaller the value of pK b , stronger is the base. pK b of ammonia is 4.75 . Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia because of the +I effect of alkyl groups, which raises electron density on nitrogen; their pK b values lie between 3 and 4.22 . Aromatic amines are weaker bases than ammonia because of the electron withdrawing nature of the aryl group (pK b of aniline 9.38). Structure–basicity relationship Basicity depends upon the ease of formation of the cation by accepting a proton from the acid. The more stable the cation is relative to the amine, the more basic the amine. (a) Alkanamines versus ammonia The electron releasing alkyl group pushes electrons towards nitrogen, making the unshared pair more available for sharing with the proton. The substituted ammonium ion is stabilised by dispersal of the positive charge through the +I effect of the alkyl group. So in the gaseous phase basicity rises with the number of alkyl groups. In the aqueous phase the trend is not regular: the ammonium cations are also stabilised by solvation with water. The greater the size of the ion, the lesser the solvation and the less stabilised the ion. When the alkyl group is bigger than –CH 3 there is steric hindrance to hydrogen bonding , which again changes the order. (b) Arylamines versus ammonia In aniline the –NH 2 group is attached directly to the benzene ring, so the unshared pair on nitrogen is in conjugation with the ring . That makes the lone pair less available for protonation, so pK b is high. Aniline is a resonance hybrid of five structures . The anilinium ion formed by accepting a proton has only two resonating (Kekulé) structures. Greater number of resonating structures means greater stability — aniline is more stable than the anilinium ion, so its proton acceptability is lower. In substituted anilines, electron releasing groups (–OCH 3 , –CH 3 ) increase basic strength. Electron withdrawing groups (–NO 2 , –SO 3 H, –COOH, –X) decrease it. Aniline: 5 resonance structures → ring-delocalised lone pair → low proton affinity. Anilinium ion: only 2 Kekulé structures → less stabilised than aniline. Consequence: aniline (pK b 9.38) is about five orders of magnitude weaker as a base than ammonia (pK b 4.75). Benzylamine (pK b 4.70) keeps the –NH₂ on a CH₂, so the lone pair stays free — it is as basic as an aliphatic amine. blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/Formula"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/ConceptCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/TreeDiagram"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/EquationLadder"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/chemistry/MoleculeStructure"; import from "./structures.generated"; export default function BiomoleculesChapter() { return ( <> A living system grows, sustains and reproduces itself. The most amazing thing about a living system is that it is composed of non-living atoms and molecules. The pursuit of knowledge of what goes on chemically within a living system falls in the domain of biochemistry . Living systems are made up of various complex biomolecules like carbohydrates , proteins , nucleic acids , lipids , etc. Proteins and carbohydrates are essential constituents of our food. These biomolecules interact with each other and constitute the molecular logic of life processes. In addition, some simple molecules like vitamins and mineral salts also play an important role in the functions of organisms. 10.1 Carbohydrates Carbohydrates are primarily produced by plants and form a very large group of naturally occurring organic compounds. Some common examples are cane sugar, glucose, starch, etc. Most of them have a general formula, C x (H 2 O) y , and were considered as hydrates of carbon from where the name carbohydrate was derived. For example, the molecular formula of glucose (C 6 H 12 O 6 ) fits into this general formula, C 6 (H 2 O) 6 . But all the compounds which fit into this formula may not be classified as carbohydrates. For example acetic acid (CH 3 COOH) fits into this general formula, C 2 (H 2 O) 2 but is not a carbohydrate. Similarly, rhamnose, C 6 H 12 O 5 is a carbohydrate but does not fit in this definition. Chemically, the carbohydrates may be defined as optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or the compounds which produce such units on hydrolysis. Some of the carbohydrates, which are sweet in taste, are also called sugars . Carbohydrates are also called saccharides (Greek: sakcharon means sugar). 10.1.1 Classification of Carbohydrates Carbohydrates are classified on the basis of their behaviour on hydrolysis. They have been broadly divided into following three groups. The carbohydrates may also be classified as either reducing or non-reducing sugars . All those carbohydrates which reduce Fehling’s solution and Tollens’ reagent are referred to as reducing sugars . All monosaccharides whether aldose or ketose are reducing sugars. 10.1.2 Monosaccharides Monosaccharides are further classified on the basis of number of carbon atoms and the functional group present in them. If a monosaccharide contains an aldehyde group , it is known as an aldose and if it contains a keto group , it is known as a ketose . The number of carbon atoms is also introduced in the name as shown in Table 10.1 . 10.1.2.1 Glucose Glucose occurs freely in nature as well as in the combined form. It is present in sweet fruits and honey. Ripe grapes also contain glucose in large amounts. It is prepared as follows: Sucrose is boiled with dilute HCl or H 2 SO 4 in alcoholic solution; glucose and fructose are obtained in equal amounts. ), }, { label: "From starch", description: ( <> Commercially glucose is obtained by hydrolysis of starch by boiling it with dilute H 2 SO 4 at 393 K under pressure. ), }, ]} /> Glucose is an aldohexose and is also known as dextrose . It is the monomer of many larger carbohydrates, namely starch, cellulose. It is probably the most abundant organic compound on earth. It was assigned the structure given below on the basis of the following evidences: 1. Its molecular formula was found to be C 6 H 12 O 6 . 2. On prolonged heating with HI, it forms n-hexane , suggesting that all the six carbon atoms are linked in a straight chain. 3. Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine to form an oxime and adds a molecule of hydrogen cyanide to give cyanohydrin . These reactions confirm the presence of a carbonyl group (>C = O) in glucose. 4. Glucose gets oxidised to six carbon carboxylic acid ( gluconic acid ) on reaction with a mild oxidising agent like bromine water. This indicates that the carbonyl group is present as an aldehydic group . 5. Acetylation of glucose with acetic anhydride gives glucose pentaacetate which confirms the presence of five –OH groups . Since it exists as a stable compound, five –OH groups should be attached to different carbon atoms. 6. On oxidation with nitric acid, glucose as well as gluconic acid both yield a dicarboxylic acid, saccharic acid . This indicates the presence of a primary alcoholic (–OH) group in glucose. The exact spatial arrangement of different –OH groups was given by Fischer. Glucose is correctly named as D(+)-glucose . ‘D’ before the name represents the configuration whereas ‘(+)’ represents dextrorotatory nature of the molecule. ‘D’ and ‘L’ have no relation with the optical activity of the compound. For assigning configuration of monosaccharides, it is the lowest asymmetric carbon atom which is compared to D-(+)- glyceraldehyde. (+) Isomer of glyceraldehyde has ‘D’ configuration (–OH on right hand side in Fischer projection). All compounds correlated to D-(+) glyceraldehyde are said to have D-configuration , those correlated to L-(–) glyceraldehyde have L-configuration (–OH on left). In (+) glucose, —OH on the lowest asymmetric carbon is on the right side (comparable to (+) glyceraldehyde), so (+) glucose is assigned D-configuration. Cyclic Structure of Glucose (Anomers) The open chain structure (I) of glucose explained most of its properties but the following could not be explained: 1. Despite having the aldehyde group, glucose does not give Schiff’s test and it does not form the hydrogensulphite addition product with NaHSO 3 . 2. The pentaacetate of glucose does not react with hydroxylamine indicating the absence of free —CHO group . 3. Glucose is found to exist in two different crystalline forms named α and β . The α-form (m.p. 419 K) is obtained by crystallisation from concentrated solution of glucose at 303 K while the β-form (m.p. 423 K) is obtained by crystallisation from hot and saturated aqueous solution at 371 K. It was proposed that one of the —OH groups may add to the —CHO group and form a cyclic hemiacetal structure. Glucose forms a six-membered ring in which —OH at C-5 is involved in ring formation. This explains the absence of —CHO group and the existence of glucose in two forms. The two cyclic hemiacetal forms of glucose differ only in the configuration of the hydroxyl group at C1 , called the anomeric carbon . Such isomers (α-form and β-form) are called anomers . The six-membered cyclic structure of glucose is called pyranose structure (α– or β–), in analogy with pyran . The cyclic structure is more correctly represented by Haworth structures. 10.1.2.2 Fructose Fructose is an important ketohexose . It is obtained along with glucose by the hydrolysis of disaccharide, sucrose. It is a natural monosaccharide found in fruits, honey and vegetables. In its pure form it is used as a sweetner. It has the molecular formula C 6 H 12 O 6 and contains a ketonic functional group at carbon number 2 and six carbons in straight chain as in the case of glucose. It belongs to D-series and is a laevorotatory compound. It is appropriately written as D-(–)-fructose . Fructose also exists in two cyclic forms which are obtained by the addition of —OH at C5 to the (>C=O) group. The ring, thus formed is a five membered ring and is named as furanose with analogy to the compound furan (a five membered cyclic compound with one oxygen and four carbon atoms). The cyclic structures of the two anomers of fructose are represented by Haworth structures. 10.1.3 Disaccharides Disaccharides on hydrolysis with dilute acids or enzymes yield two molecules of either the same or different monosaccharides. The two monosaccharides are joined together by an oxide linkage formed by the loss of a water molecule. Such a linkage between two monosaccharide units through oxygen atom is called a glycosidic linkage . In disaccharides, if the reducing groups of monosaccharides i.e., aldehydic or ketonic groups are bonded , these are non-reducing sugars , e.g., sucrose . On the other hand, sugars in which these functional groups are free , are called reducing sugars , for example, maltose and lactose . Sucrose is dextrorotatory but after hydrolysis gives dextrorotatory glucose and laevorotatory fructose. Since the laevorotation of fructose (–92.4°) is more than dextrorotation of glucose (+52.5°), the mixture is laevorotatory . Thus, hydrolysis of sucrose brings about a change in the sign of rotation, from dextro (+) to laevo (–) and the product is named as invert sugar . 10.1.4 Polysaccharides Polysaccharides contain a large number of monosaccharide units joined together by glycosidic linkages. These are the most commonly encountered carbohydrates in nature. They mainly act as the food storage or structural materials . 10.1.5 Importance of Carbohydrates Carbohydrates are essential for life in both plants and animals. They form a major portion of our food. Honey has been used for a long time as an instant source of energy by ‘Vaids’ in ayurvedic system of medicine. Used as storage molecules as starch in plants and glycogen in animals. Cell wall of bacteria and plants is made up of cellulose . We build furniture, etc. from cellulose in the form of wood and clothe ourselves with cellulose in the form of cotton fibre. Provide raw materials for many important industries like textiles, paper, lacquers and breweries. Two aldopentoses viz. D-ribose and 2-deoxy-D-ribose are present in nucleic acids. Carbohydrates are found in biosystem in combination with many proteins and lipids. 10.1 Glucose or sucrose are soluble in water but cyclohexane or benzene (simple six membered ring compounds) are insoluble in water. Explain. 10.2 What are the expected products of hydrolysis of lactose? 10.3 How do you explain the absence of aldehyde group in the pentaacetate of D-glucose? 10.2 Proteins Proteins are the most abundant biomolecules of the living system. Chief sources of proteins are milk, cheese, pulses, peanuts, fish, meat, etc. They occur in every part of the body and form the fundamental basis of structure and functions of life. They are also required for growth and maintenance of body. The word protein is derived from Greek word, “proteios” which means primary or of prime importance . All proteins are polymers of α-amino acids . 10.2.1 Amino Acids Amino acids contain amino (–NH 2 ) and carboxyl (–COOH) functional groups. Depending upon the relative position of amino group with respect to carboxyl group, the amino acids can be classified as α, β, γ, δ and so on. Only α-amino acids are obtained on hydrolysis of proteins . They may contain other functional groups also. All α-amino acids have trivial names, which usually reflect the property of that compound or its source (glycine — sweet, glykos ; tyrosine — first obtained from cheese, tyros ). Amino acids are generally represented by a three letter symbol, sometimes one letter symbol is also used. Structures of some commonly occurring amino acids along with their 3-letter and 1-letter symbols are given in Table 10.2 . 10.2.2 Classification of Amino Acids Amino acids are classified as acidic, basic or neutral depending upon the relative number of amino and carboxyl groups in their molecule. Neutral Basic Acidic ), }, { title: "Condition", children: ( Equal number of –NH 2 and –COOH groups More number of –NH 2 than –COOH groups More number of –COOH groups than –NH 2 groups ), }, ]} /> The amino acids, which can be synthesised in the body, are known as non-essential amino acids . On the other hand, those which cannot be synthesised in the body and must be obtained through diet, are known as essential amino acids (marked with asterisk in Table 10.2). Amino acids are usually colourless, crystalline solids. They are water-soluble, high melting solids and behave like salts rather than simple amines or carboxylic acids. In aqueous solution, the carboxyl group can lose a proton and amino group can accept a proton, giving rise to a dipolar ion known as zwitter ion . This is neutral but contains both positive and negative charges. In zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour as they react both with acids and bases. Except glycine, all other naturally occurring α-amino acids are optically active , since the α-carbon atom is asymmetric. These exist both in ‘D’ and ‘L’ forms. Most naturally occurring amino acids have L-configuration . L-Amino acids are represented by writing the –NH 2 group on left hand side. 10.2.3 Structure of Proteins Proteins are the polymers of α-amino acids and they are connected to each other by peptide bond or peptide linkage . Chemically, peptide linkage is an amide formed between –COOH group and –NH 2 group with elimination of a water molecule (–CO–NH–). Two amino acids → dipeptide (e.g. glycylalanine from glycine + alanine) Three amino acids → tripeptide (two peptide linkages) Four, five or six amino acids → tetrapeptide, pentapeptide or hexapeptide More than ten amino acids → polypeptides . A polypeptide with more than hundred amino acid residues, having molecular mass higher than 10,000 u is called a protein . However, the distinction between a polypeptide and a protein is not very sharp (e.g. insulin contains 51 amino acids). Polypeptide chains run parallel and are held together by hydrogen and disulphide bonds. Fibre–like structure. Generally insoluble in water. Examples: keratin (hair, wool, silk), myosin (muscles). ), }, { title: "Globular proteins", children: ( Chains of polypeptides coil around to give a spherical shape. Usually soluble in water. Examples: insulin and albumins . ), }, ]} /> Structure and shape of proteins can be studied at four different levels — primary , secondary , tertiary and quaternary , each more complex than the previous one. α-Helix: Polypeptide chain forms all possible hydrogen bonds by twisting into a right handed screw (helix) with the –NH group of each amino acid residue hydrogen bonded to the –C(=O) of an adjacent turn of the helix. β-Pleated sheet: All peptide chains are stretched out to nearly maximum extension and then laid side by side which are held together by intermolecular hydrogen bonds . The structure resembles the pleated folds of drapery. 10.2.4 Denaturation of Proteins Protein found in a biological system with a unique three-dimensional structure and biological activity is called a native protein . blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/Formula"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/ConceptCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/chemistry/MoleculeStructure"; import from "./structures.generated"; export default function CoordinationCompoundsChapter() { return ( <> Introduction: Coordination Compounds 5.1 Werner's Theory of Coordination Compounds Alfred Werner (1866–1919) was the first to formulate ideas about the structures of coordination compounds. He proposed the concept of a primary valence and a secondary valence for a metal ion. Binary compounds such as CrCl 3 , CoCl 2 , PdCl 2 have primary valences of 3, 2 and 2 respectively. In cobalt(III) chloride–ammonia complexes, some chloride ions precipitate as AgCl on adding excess AgNO 3 in cold, and some do not. The last two compounds have the same empirical formula CoCl 3 ·4NH 3 but different properties — they are isomers . The atoms inside the square brackets form a single entity that does not dissociate under the reaction conditions. Metals in coordination compounds show two types of linkages — primary and secondary. Primary valences are normally ionisable and are satisfied by negative ions. Secondary valences are non-ionisable ; they are satisfied by neutral molecules or negative ions. The secondary valence equals the coordination number and is fixed for a metal. Ions/groups bound by secondary linkages to the metal have characteristic spatial arrangements corresponding to different coordination numbers (coordination polyhedra). Species inside the bracket are coordination entities (complexes); ions outside the bracket are counter ions . Octahedral, tetrahedral and square planar geometries are most common: [Co(NH 3 ) 6 ] 3+ , [CoCl(NH 3 ) 5 ] 2+ and [CoCl 2 (NH 3 ) 4 ] + are octahedral, while [Ni(CO) 4 ] is tetrahedral and [PtCl 4 ] 2− is square planar. Formed from two or more stable compounds in stoichiometric ratio. Dissociates completely into simple ions in water. Examples: carnallite KCl·MgCl₂·6H₂O, Mohr's salt FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O, potash alum KAl(SO₄)₂·12H₂O. ), }, { title: "Complex", children: ( Also formed in stoichiometric ratio. The complex ion does not dissociate into its constituent ions — [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ in K₄[Fe(CN)₆] does not give Fe²⁺ and CN⁻. Example: K₄[Fe(CN)₆]. ), }, ]} /> Question: On the basis of the observations made with aqueous solutions, assign secondary valences to metals in: (i) PdCl 2 ·4NH 3 — 2 mol AgCl (ii) NiCl 2 ·6H 2 O — 2 mol AgCl (iii) PtCl 4 ·2HCl — 0 mol AgCl (iv) CoCl 3 ·4NH 3 — 1 mol AgCl (v) PtCl 2 ·2NH 3 — 0 mol AgCl. Solution: The number of chloride ions precipitated gives the number of ionisable chlorides; the rest stay bound to the metal. (i) Secondary 4 — [Pd(NH 3 ) 4 ]Cl 2 (ii) Secondary 6 — [Ni(H 2 O) 6 ]Cl 2 (iii) Secondary 6 — H 2 [PtCl 6 ] (iv) Secondary 6 — [CoCl 2 (NH 3 ) 4 ]Cl (v) Secondary 4 — [PtCl 2 (NH 3 ) 2 ] 5.2 Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds A central metal atom or ion bonded to a fixed number of ions or molecules — e.g. [CoCl 3 (NH 3 ) 3 ], [Ni(CO) 4 ], [Fe(CN) 6 ] 4− , [Co(NH 3 ) 6 ] 3+ . The atom/ion to which a fixed number of ions/groups are bound in a definite geometrical arrangement. In [NiCl 2 (H 2 O) 4 ], [CoCl(NH 3 ) 5 ] 2+ and [Fe(CN) 6 ] 3− the central ions are Ni 2+ , Co 3+ and Fe 3+ . They act as Lewis acids . Unidentate — binds through a single donor atom (Cl − , H 2 O, NH 3 ). Didentate — binds through two donor atoms (ethane-1,2-diamine en, oxalate C 2 O 4 2− ). Polydentate — several donor atoms in one ligand (N(CH 2 CH 2 NH 2 ) 3 ). Hexadentate — EDTA 4− binds through two N and four O atoms. Chelate — a di- or polydentate ligand using two or more donor atoms simultaneously for one metal ion; the number of ligating groups is the denticity . Chelate complexes are more stable than similar unidentate complexes. Ambidentate — two different donor atoms, either of which can bind: NO 2 − (through N or O) and SCN − (through S or N). The number of ligand donor atoms to which the metal is directly bonded. In [PtCl 6 ] 2− CN = 6; in [Ni(NH 3 ) 4 ] 2+ CN = 4. Both [Fe(C 2 O 4 ) 3 ] 3− and [Co(en) 3 ] 3+ have CN = 6 because the ligands are didentate. Coordination sphere — the central atom/ion plus attached ligands, enclosed in square brackets. Ionisable groups outside are the counter ions: in K 4 [Fe(CN) 6 ] the sphere is [Fe(CN) 6 ] 4− and the counter ion is K + . Coordination polyhedron — the spatial arrangement of ligand atoms directly attached to the central atom. Common ones: octahedral, square planar, tetrahedral. Oxidation number — the charge the central atom would carry if all ligands were removed along with the shared electron pairs. Written as a Roman numeral in parentheses: copper in [Cu(CN) 4 ] 3− is Cu(I). Homoleptic — one kind of donor group, e.g. [Co(NH 3 ) 6 ] 3+ . Heteroleptic — more than one kind, e.g. [Co(NH 3 ) 4 Cl 2 ] + . 5.3 Nomenclature of Coordination Compounds 5.3.1 Formulas of Mononuclear Coordination Entities The central atom is listed first. Ligands are then listed in alphabetical order ; the placement does not depend on charge. Polydentate ligands are also listed alphabetically; for abbreviated ligands the first letter of the abbreviation decides the position. The entire entity is enclosed in square brackets; polyatomic ligands and abbreviations go in parentheses. No space between ligands and metal inside the sphere. Charge is shown outside the brackets as a right superscript, number before sign: [Co(CN) 6 ] 3− , [Cr(H 2 O) 6 ] 3+ . The charge of the cation(s) balances the charge of the anion(s). 5.3.2 Naming of Mononuclear Coordination Compounds The cation is named first. Ligands are named alphabetically before the central atom — the reverse of formula order. Anionic ligand names end in -o ; neutral and cationic ligands keep their names, except aqua (H 2 O), ammine (NH 3 ), carbonyl (CO) and nitrosyl (NO). Prefixes mono, di, tri indicate the number of each ligand. If the ligand name itself has a numerical prefix, use bis, tris, tetrakis with the ligand in parentheses — e.g. [NiCl 2 (PPh 3 ) 2 ] is dichloridobis(triphenylphosphine)nickel(II). The oxidation state of the metal is a Roman numeral in parentheses. In a complex cation the metal keeps its element name; in a complex anion the name ends in -ate (cobaltate), with Latin names for some metals (ferrate for Fe). A neutral complex molecule is named like a complex cation. The 2004 IUPAC draft recommends sorting ligands alphabetically irrespective of charge, and ending anionic ligand names in -ido (chloro → chlorido). Current NCERT usage follows the -o form. Question: Write formulas for (a) tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride (b) potassium tetrahydroxidozincate(II) (c) potassium trioxalatoaluminate(III) (d) dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) (e) tetracarbonylnickel(0). Solution: (a) [Co(NH 3 ) 4 (H 2 O)Cl]Cl 2 (b) K 2 [Zn(OH) 4 ] (c) K 3 [Al(C 2 O 4 ) 3 ] (d) [CoCl 2 (en) 2 ] + (e) [Ni(CO) 4 ] Question: Name (a) [Pt(NH 3 ) 2 Cl(NO 2 )] (b) K 3 [Cr(C 2 O 4 ) 3 ] (c) [CoCl 2 (en) 2 ]Cl (d) [Co(NH 3 ) 5 (CO 3 )]Cl (e) Hg[Co(SCN) 4 ]. Solution: (a) diamminechloridonitrito-N-platinum(II) (b) potassium trioxalatochromate(III) (c) dichloridobis(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) chloride (d) pentaamminecarbonatocobalt(III) chloride (e) mercury(I) tetrathiocyanato-S-cobaltate(III) 5.4 Isomerism in Coordination Compounds Isomers have the same chemical formula but a different arrangement of atoms, and hence differ in one or more physical or chemical properties. 5.4.1 Geometric Isomerism Arises in heteroleptic complexes from different possible geometric arrangements of ligands; important for coordination numbers 4 and 6. Square planar [MX 2 L 2 ]: the two X ligands may be adjacent ( cis ) or opposite ( trans ). Square planar MABXL gives three isomers — two cis and one trans. Not possible for tetrahedral geometry. Octahedral [MX 2 L 4 ]: the two X ligands may be cis or trans. Also arises with didentate ligands in [MX 2 (L–L) 2 ]. Octahedral [Ma 3 b 3 ]: facial (fac) when the three donor atoms of the same ligand occupy adjacent corners of an octahedral face; meridional (mer) when they lie around the meridian. Solution: Tetrahedral complexes do not show geometrical isomerism because the relative positions of the unidentate ligands attached to the central metal atom are the same with respect to each other. 5.4.2 Optical Isomerism Optical isomers are mirror images that cannot be superimposed on one another — enantiomers . The molecules or ions that cannot be superimposed are chiral . The two forms are called dextro (d) and laevo (l) according to the direction in which they rotate the plane of polarised light ( d rotates to the right, l to the left). Optical isomerism is common in octahedral complexes involving didentate ligands, e.g. [Co(en) 3 ] 3+ . In [PtCl 2 (en) 2 ] 2+ , only the cis isomer shows optical activity. Solution: Of the two, cis-[CrCl 2 (ox) 2 ] 3− is chiral (optically active). The trans isomer has a plane of symmetry. 5.4.3 Linkage Isomerism Arises in a compound containing an ambidentate ligand . The thiocyanate ligand NCS − may bind through nitrogen (M–NCS) or through sulphur (M–SCN). Jørgensen discovered this in [Co(NH 3 ) 5 (NO 2 )]Cl 2 : the red form has nitrite bound through oxygen (–ONO), the yellow form through nitrogen (–NO 2 ). 5.4.4 Coordination Isomerism Arises from interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions. Example: [Co(NH 3 ) 6 ][Cr(CN) 6 ] and its coordination isomer [Cr(NH 3 ) 6 ][Co(CN) 6 ]. 5.4.5 Ionisation Isomerism Arises when the counter ion is itself a potential ligand and can displace a ligand that then becomes the counter ion: [Co(NH 3 ) 5 (SO 4 )]Br and [Co(NH 3 ) 5 Br]SO 4 . 5.4.6 Solvate Isomerism Also called hydrate isomerism when water is the solvent. Solvate isomers differ in whether a solvent molecule is directly bonded to the metal or merely present as free solvent in the crystal lattice: [Cr(H 2 O) 6 ]Cl 3 (violet) and [Cr(H 2 O) 5 Cl]Cl 2 ·H 2 O (grey-green). 5.5 Bonding in Coordination Compounds Werner's theory could not answer why only certain elements form complexes, why the bonds are directional, or why the compounds have characteristic magnetic and optical properties. The main approaches are Valence Bond Theory (VBT), Crystal Field Theory (CFT), Ligand Field Theory (LFT) and Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT). 5.5.1 Valence Bond Theory The metal atom or ion uses its (n−1)d, ns, np — or ns, np, nd — orbitals for hybridisation, giving equivalent orbitals of definite geometry. These hybridised orbitals overlap with ligand orbitals that donate electron pairs. Co is +3 with 3d⁶. The 3d electrons pair up, leaving two 3d orbitals free. Hybridisation is d²sp³ — inner d orbital used. Six electron pairs from six NH₃ molecules occupy the hybrid orbitals. Octahedral; no unpaired electron → low spin / spin paired . ), }, { title: "[CoF₆]³⁻ — outer orbital, paramagnetic", children: ( Co is +3 with 3d⁶; F⁻ is a weak ligand and does not pair the electrons. Hybridisation is sp³d² — outer 4d orbital used. Octahedral; unpaired electrons remain → high spin / spin free . ), }, ]} /> [NiCl 4 ] 2− : Ni is +2, 3d 8 ; one s and three p orbitals hybridise (sp 3 ) → tetrahedral, paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons. [Ni(CO) 4 ]: nickel is in zero oxidation state, tetrahedral, diamagnetic — no unpaired electrons. [Ni(CN) 4 ] 2− : Ni is +2, 3d 8 ; hybridisation is dsp² → square planar; each hybrid orbital receives a pair from a cyanide ion, so it is diamagnetic. Hybrid orbitals do not actually exist. Hybridisation is a mathematical manipulation of the wave equation for the atomic orbitals involved. 5.5.2 Magnetic Properties of Coordination Compounds Magnetic susceptibility measurements give the number of unpaired electrons and hence the structure. The magnetic moment follows the spin-only formula. For ions with up to three d electrons — Ti 3+ (d 1 ), V 3+ (d 2 ), Cr 3+ (d 3 ) — two vacant d orbitals are available for octahedral hybridisation, so the magnetic behaviour matches the free ion. With more than three 3d electrons the required pair of 3d orbitals is not directly available (Hund's rule). For d 4 (Cr 2+ , Mn 3+ ), d 5 (Mn 2+ , Fe 3+ ) and d 6 (Fe 2+ , Co 3+ ), a vacant pair of d orbitals results only by pairing, leaving two, one and zero unpaired electrons respectively. Question: The spin-only magnetic moment of [MnBr 4 ] 2− is 5.9 BM. Predict the geometry of the complex ion. Solution: The coordination number of Mn 2+ is 4, so the ion is either tetrahedral (sp 3 ) or square planar (dsp 2 ). A moment of 5.9 BM corresponds to five unpaired electrons, which is possible only in the tetrahedral case — dsp 2 would force pairing and leave fewer unpaired electrons. 5.5.3 Limitations of Valence Bond Theory It involves a number of assumptions. It does not give a quantitative interpretation of magnetic data. It does not explain the colour of coordination compounds. It does not quantitatively interpret thermodynamic or kinetic stabilities. It does not make exact predictions regarding tetrahedral and square planar structures of 4-coordinate complexes. It does not distinguish between weak and strong ligands. 5.5.4 Crystal Field Theory CFT is an electrostatic model : the metal–ligand bond is ionic, arising from electrostatic interaction between the metal ion and the ligand. Ligands are point charges (anions) or point dipoles (neutral molecules). The five d orbitals of an isolated gaseous metal ion are degenerate. A spherically symmetrical field keeps them degenerate, but a ligand field is asymmetrical — the degeneracy is lifted and the d orbitals split. The pattern depends on the geometry. The d x²−y² and d z² orbitals point towards the ligands, so they experience more repulsion and are raised in energy — the e g set. The d xy , d yz and d xz orbitals point between the axes and are lowered — the t 2g set. The separation is ; the e g orbitals rise by (3/5)Δ o and the t 2g fall by (2/5)Δ o . This is an experimentally determined series based on the absorption of light by complexes with different ligands. Larger splitting is produced by strong-field ligands. P", "t₂g⁴ e_g⁰", "strong field", "low spin"] }, ]} /> Calculations show that d 4 to d 7 coordination entities are more stable for strong fields than for weak fields. In tetrahedral entities the splitting is inverted and smaller: \Delta_o`} . The splitting is not large enough to force pairing, so low-spin tetrahedral configurations are rarely observed. The subscript g is used only for octahedral and square planar complexes, which have a centre of symmetry. 5.5.5 Colour in Coordination Compounds The colour of a complex is complementary to the light absorbed: if green light is absorbed, the complex looks red. CFT attributes the colour to d–d transitions . Ti 3+ is a 3d 1 system. The single electron sits in the t 2g level. Absorption of blue-green light excites it to the empty e g level (t 2g 1 e g 0 → t 2g 0 e g 1 ), so the complex appears violet. Without a ligand there is no crystal field splitting and no colour — removing water from [Ti(H 2 O) 6 ]Cl 3 on heating renders it colourless. Anhydrous CuSO 4 is white; CuSO 4 ·5H 2 O is blue.
