blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/Formula"; import from "@/components/content/Stepper"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/EquationLadder"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; export default function DAndFBlockElementsChapter() { return ( <> 4.1 Position in the Periodic Table The d-block of the periodic table contains the elements of the groups 3–12 in which the d orbitals are progressively filled in each of the four long periods. The f-block consists of elements in which 4f and 5f orbitals are progressively filled. The f-block elements are placed in a separate panel at the bottom of the periodic table. The names transition metals and inner transition metals are used for the d- and f-block elements respectively. The name transition was originally derived from the fact that their chemical properties were transitional between those of s- and p-block elements. Transition metals are metals which have incomplete d subshell either in the neutral atom or in their ions . Zinc, cadmium and mercury of group 12 have full d 10 configuration in their ground state as well as in their common oxidation states, and hence are not regarded as transition metals . However, being the end members of the 3d, 4d and 5d series, their chemistry is studied along with that of the transition metals. The presence of partly filled d or f orbitals in their atoms makes transition elements different from non-transition elements. Ions of a given d n configuration (n = 1–9) have similar magnetic and electronic properties, and partly filled d orbitals give a variety of oxidation states, coloured ions, complex formation, catalytic property and paramagnetic behaviour. 4.2 Electronic Configurations of the d-Block Elements The d-orbitals of the penultimate energy level receive electrons, giving the four rows of transition metals — 3d, 4d, 5d and 6d. Exception: Pd has the configuration 5s^ `} . The generalisation also breaks for Cr and Cu because the energy gap between (n−1)d and ns orbitals is very small and half-filled and completely filled sets of orbitals are relatively more stable . Cr: 4s^ `} instead of 4s^ `} . Cu: 4s^ `} instead of 4s^ `} . Zn, Cd, Hg, Cn: general formula ns^ `} — completely filled d orbitals, so not transition elements. Question: On what ground can you say that scandium (Z = 21) is a transition element but zinc (Z = 30) is not? Solution: Scandium has incompletely filled 3d orbitals in its ground state (3d 1 ), so it is a transition element. Zinc has completely filled d orbitals (3d 10 ) in its ground state as well as in its oxidised state, so it is not a transition element. Silver (Z = 47) can exhibit the +2 oxidation state, in which it has incompletely filled 4d orbitals. Hence it behaves as a transition element. 4.3 General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block) The properties of the first transition series (3d) are discussed here; the heavier series follow the same pattern. 4.3.1 Physical Properties Nearly all transition elements show typical metallic properties — high tensile strength, ductility, malleability, high thermal and electrical conductivity, metallic lustre. With the exceptions of Zn, Cd, Hg and Mn, they have one or more typical metallic structures at normal temperatures (bcc, hcp, ccp). The metals (except Zn, Cd and Hg) are very hard and have low volatility ; melting and boiling points are high. Greater number of electrons from (n−1)d, in addition to the ns electrons, take part in interatomic metallic bonding. In any row the melting points rise to a maximum at d 5 (except the anomalous Mn and Tc) and then fall regularly. The maxima near the middle of each series indicate that one unpaired electron per d orbital is particularly favourable for strong interatomic interaction. Higher enthalpy of atomisation makes a metal noble in its reactions. Metals of the second and third series have greater enthalpies of atomisation than the corresponding first-series metals — this accounts for the much more frequent metal–metal bonding in compounds of the heavy transition metals. Solution: Because of a large number of unpaired electrons in their atoms, they have stronger interatomic interaction and hence stronger bonding between atoms, resulting in higher enthalpies of atomisation. In the formation of metallic bonds no electrons from 3d orbitals are involved in zinc (3d 10 ), while in all other metals of the 3d series d electrons do take part in metallic bonding. 4.3.2 Variation in Atomic and Ionic Sizes Ions of the same charge in a given series show a progressive decrease in radius with increasing atomic number. Reason: each new electron enters a d orbital while nuclear charge rises by unity, and the shielding effect of a d electron is not effective. The variation within a series is quite small. Radii increase from the 3d to the 4d series, but the 5d radii are virtually the same as those of the corresponding 4d elements. The filling of 4f orbitals before the 5d orbitals results in a regular decrease in atomic radii called lanthanoid contraction . It compensates for the expected increase in atomic size with increasing atomic number, because the shielding of one 4f electron by another is less than that of one d electron by another. Net result: the second and third d series have similar radii — e.g. Zr = 160 pm, Hf = 159 pm — and therefore very similar physical and chemical properties. Decreasing metallic radius coupled with increasing atomic mass gives a general increase in density : from titanium (3.43 g cm −3 ) to copper (8.9 g cm −3 ). 4.3.3 Ionisation Enthalpies Ionisation enthalpy increases along each series from left to right, due to increasing nuclear charge while inner d orbitals are filled. Successive enthalpies do not rise as steeply as in non-transition elements; variation along the series is much smaller. The first ionisation enthalpy increases in general, but the second and third rise much more steeply. The irregular trend in the first ionisation enthalpy of the 3d metals is of little chemical significance; it arises because removing one electron alters the relative energies of 4s and 3d orbitals. Attraction of each electron towards the nucleus. Repulsion between the electrons. Exchange energy — approximately proportional to the total number of possible pairs of parallel spins in degenerate orbitals; the lowest energy state has maximum single occupation with parallel spins (Hund's rule). Loss of exchange energy increases stability, so ionisation becomes more difficult. Breaks occur at Mn 2+ (3d 5 ) and Fe 3+ (3d 5 ) because of the extra stability of the half-filled d 5 configuration. The lowest common oxidation state is +2. Forming M 2+ (g) needs the enthalpy of atomisation plus the first and second ionisation enthalpies; the second ionisation enthalpy dominates, giving unusually high values for Cr and Cu (M + has d 5 and d 10 ) and a low value for Zn. Third ionisation enthalpies are quite high and show the difficulty of removing an electron from d 5 (Mn 2+ ) and d 10 (Zn 2+ ). The high values for Cu, Ni and Zn explain why an oxidation state greater than +2 is difficult for them. 4.3.4 Oxidation States The elements with the greatest number of oxidation states occur in or near the middle of the series; manganese shows all states from +2 to +7. Fewer states at the ends: either too few electrons to lose or share (Sc, Ti) or too many d electrons leaving fewer orbitals for higher valence (Cu, Zn). Maximum oxidation state of reasonable stability corresponds to the sum of s and d electrons up to manganese: TiO 2 , VO 2 + , CrO 4 2− , MnO 4 − . Beyond Mn there is an abrupt decrease in the stability of higher states, so the typical species are Fe II,III , Co II,III , Ni II , Cu I,II , Zn II . Transition-metal oxidation states differ from each other by unity (V II , V III , V IV , V V ), whereas non-transition element states normally differ by two. In groups 4–10 the heavier members favour higher oxidation states — the opposite of the inert pair effect in the p-block. In group 6, Mo(VI) and W(VI) are more stable than Cr(VI): dichromate in acid is a strong oxidising agent, whereas MoO 3 and WO 3 are not. Low oxidation states occur when ligands have π-acceptor character: nickel and iron are zero in Ni(CO) 4 and Fe(CO) 5 . Question: Name a transition element which does not exhibit variable oxidation states. Solution: Scandium (Z = 21) does not exhibit variable oxidation states. Manganese (Z = 25), because its atom has the maximum number of unpaired electrons (3d 5 4s 2 ). 4.3.5 Trends in the M²⁺/M Standard Electrode Potentials The general trend is towards less negative E° values across the series, related to the increase in the sum of the first and second ionisation enthalpies. E° for Mn, Ni and Zn is more negative than the trend predicts: Mn 2+ (d 5 ) and Zn 2+ (d 10 ) have extra stability, while Ni 2+ has the most negative enthalpy of hydration. Copper has a positive E° and so cannot liberate H 2 from acids. Only oxidising acids (nitric acid, hot concentrated sulphuric acid) react with it, and they are reduced. Solution: Cr 2+ is reducing because its configuration changes from d 4 to d 3 , the latter having a half-filled t 2g level. The change from Mn 3+ to Mn 2+ gives the half-filled d 5 configuration, which has extra stability — so Mn 3+ readily accepts an electron. 4.3.6 Trends in the M³⁺/M²⁺ Standard Electrode Potentials The low value for Sc reflects the stability of Sc 3+ , which has a noble gas configuration. The highest value for Zn is due to removal of an electron from the stable d 10 configuration of Zn 2+ . The high value for Mn shows that Mn 2+ (d 5 ) is particularly stable; the low value for Fe shows the extra stability of Fe 3+ (d 5 ). The low value for V is related to the stability of V 2+ (half-filled t 2g level). Mn 3+ and Co 3+ are the strongest oxidising agents in aqueous solution; Ti 2+ , V 2+ and Cr 2+ are strong reducing agents. The high energy needed to transform Cu(s) to Cu 2+ (aq) (high Δ a H°, and high Δ i H₁° + Δ i H₂°) is not balanced by its hydration enthalpy. 4.3.7 Trends in Stability of Higher Oxidation States The highest oxidation numbers are achieved in TiX 4 , VF 5 and CrF 6 . The +7 state of Mn is not represented in simple halides, but MnO 3 F is known; beyond Mn no metal gives a trihalide except FeX 3 and CoF 3 . Fluorine stabilises the highest state through higher lattice energy (CoF 3 ) or higher bond enthalpy terms (VF 5 , CrF 6 ). Oxidation number Halides of the 3d metals +6 CrF₆ +5 VF₅, CrF₅ +4 TiX₄, VX₄, CrX₄, MnF₄ +3 TiX₃, VX₃, CrX₃, MnF₃, FeX₃, CoF₃ +2 TiX₂, VX₂, CrX₂, MnX₂, FeX₂, CoX₂, NiX₂, CuX₂, ZnX₂ +1 CuX Table 4.5: Formulas of halides of 3d metals. X = F→I; X′ = F→Br; X″ = F, Cl; X‴ = Cl→I. All Cu II halides are known except the iodide, because Cu 2+ oxidises I − to I 2 . Many copper(I) compounds are unstable in aqueous solution and disproportionate. Cu 2+ (aq) is more stable than Cu + (aq) because the much more negative Δ hyd H° of Cu 2+ more than compensates for the second ionisation enthalpy. The highest oxidation number in oxides coincides with the group number and is attained from Sc 2 O 3 to Mn 2 O 7 . Thus the highest Mn fluoride is MnF 4 while the highest oxide is Mn 2 O 7 . Oxygen wins because it forms multiple bonds to metals. Oxocations also stabilise high states: VO 2 + (V V ), VO 2+ (V IV ), TiO 2+ (Ti IV ). Solution: This is due to the increasing stability of the lower species to which they are reduced. Because of the small size and high electronegativity of oxygen and fluorine, they can oxidise the metal to its highest oxidation state. 4.3.8 Chemical Reactivity and E° Values Transition metals vary widely in reactivity. Many dissolve in mineral acids, but a few are ‘noble’ and unaffected by single acids. In the first series, all metals except copper are relatively reactive and are oxidised by 1 M H + , though the rate may be slow. Titanium and vanadium are passive to dilute non-oxidising acids at room temperature. E° values for M 2+ /M show a decreasing tendency to form divalent cations across the series. Question: The values are V −1.18, Cr −0.91, Mn −1.18, Fe −0.44, Co −0.28, Ni −0.25, Cu +0.34 V. Explain the irregularity. Solution: The E°(M 2+ /M) values are not regular because of the irregular variation of ionisation enthalpies (Δ i H₁ + Δ i H₂) and also the sublimation enthalpies, which are relatively much less for manganese and vanadium. Solution: The much larger third ionisation enthalpy of Mn (the change is d 5 → d 4 ) is mainly responsible. This also explains why the +3 state of Mn is of little importance. Cr 2+ is the stronger reducing agent: it changes from d 4 to d 3 , whereas Fe 2+ changes from d 6 to d 5 . In aqueous medium d 3 is more stable than d 5 when crystal field stabilisation is considered. 4.3.9 Magnetic Properties Diamagnetic substances are repelled by an applied field; paramagnetic substances are attracted. Substances attracted very strongly are ferromagnetic — an extreme form of paramagnetism. Paramagnetism arises from unpaired electrons, each with spin and orbital angular momentum. For first-series compounds the orbital contribution is effectively quenched, so the spin-only formula is used. Here n is the number of unpaired electrons and μ is in Bohr magnetons (BM). A single unpaired electron gives 1.73 BM. Solution: Z = 25 is manganese; the divalent ion is Mn 2+ with 3d 5 , i.e. five unpaired electrons. Z = 27 is cobalt; Co 2+ is 3d 7 with three unpaired electrons, so = 3.87\ \text `} . 4.3.10 Formation of Coloured Ions When an electron from a lower energy d orbital is excited to a higher energy d orbital, the energy of excitation corresponds to the frequency of light absorbed. This frequency generally lies in the visible region, and the colour observed is the complementary colour of the light absorbed. 4.3.11 Formation of Complex Compounds Complex compounds are those in which metal ions bind a number of anions or neutral molecules, giving species with characteristic properties — e.g. [Fe(CN) 6 ] 3− , [Fe(CN) 6 ] 4− , [Cu(NH 3 ) 4 ] 2+ , [PtCl 4 ] 2− . Comparatively small size of the metal ions. High ionic charges . Availability of d orbitals for bond formation. 4.3.12 Catalytic Properties Catalytic activity is ascribed to the ability to adopt multiple oxidation states and to form complexes. Examples: V 2 O 5 in the Contact process, finely divided iron in the Haber process, nickel in catalytic hydrogenation. At a solid surface, bonds form between reactant molecules and atoms of the catalyst surface, increasing reactant concentration and weakening bonds in the reacting molecules (lowering activation energy). 4.3.13 Formation of Interstitial Compounds Interstitial compounds are formed when small atoms like H, C or N are trapped inside the crystal lattices of metals. They are usually non-stoichiometric and are neither typically ionic nor covalent — e.g. TiC, Mn 4 N, Fe 3 H, VH 0.56 , TiH 1.7 . They have high melting points, higher than those of the pure metals. They are very hard — some borides approach diamond in hardness. They retain metallic conductivity. They are chemically inert. 4.3.14 Alloy Formation An alloy is a blend of metals prepared by mixing the components. Alloys may be homogeneous solid solutions in which atoms of one metal are distributed randomly among atoms of the other; such alloys form when metallic radii are within about 15 percent of each other. Ferrous alloys: chromium, vanadium, tungsten, molybdenum and manganese are used to make steels and stainless steel. Alloys w

title: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
headings: 6.1.1 On the Basis of Number of Halogen Atoms
6.1.2 Compounds Containing sp³ C—X Bond (X = F, Cl, Br, I)
blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/Formula"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/Stepper"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/ConceptCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/chemistry/MoleculeStructure"; import from "./structures.generated"; export default function HaloalkanesAndHaloarenesChapter() { return ( <> Introduction: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes Definition Haloalkanes (Alkyl Halides): Aliphatic hydrocarbon + Halogen atom. Haloarenes (Aryl Halides): Aromatic hydrocarbon + Halogen atom. The Core Difference Haloalkanes: Halogen is attached to an sp³-hybridized carbon (alkyl group). Haloarenes: Halogen is attached to an sp²-hybridized carbon (aromatic/aryl group). Significance: This hybridization difference (sp³ vs. sp²) governs their distinct chemistry. Quick Examples Haloalkane: Chloroethane (CH₃—CH₂—Cl) Haloarene: Chlorobenzene (C₆H₅—Cl) 6.1 Classification 6.1.1 On the Basis of Number of Halogen Atoms 6.1.2 Compounds Containing sp³ C—X Bond (X = F, Cl, Br, I) (a) Alkyl halides or haloalkanes (R—X). The halogen is bonded to an alkyl group (R). They form a homologous series _n\text _ \text `} and are classed as primary, secondary or tertiary by the carbon bearing the halogen. 6.1.3 Compounds Containing sp² C—X Bond The hybridisation of the carbon holding the halogen decides how easily the C—X bond breaks. An sp 3 carbon gives up its halogen readily (nucleophilic substitution); an sp 2 carbon holds it tightly, so haloarenes and vinylic halides are far less reactive. 6.2 Nomenclature 1. Alkyl Halides Common System: Named as [alkyl group] + [halide name] . IUPAC System: Named as halosubstituted hydrocarbons . 2. Benzene Derivatives (Haloarenes) Monohalogen Derivatives: Common and IUPAC names are identical . Dihalogen Derivatives: Common System: uses the prefixes o- (ortho), m- (meta) and p- (para). IUPAC System: uses locant numbers ( 1,2 ; 1,3 ; 1,4 ). 3. Dihaloalkanes (Same Halogen Type) Geminal (gem-) Dihalides: both halogen atoms on the same carbon (also called alkylidene dihalides). Vicinal (vic-) Dihalides: halogen atoms on adjacent carbons (also called alkylene dihalides). IUPAC System: both are simply named as dihaloalkanes using locant numbers. Draw the structures of all the eight structural isomers that have the molecular formula C 5 H 11 Br. Name each isomer according to the IUPAC system and classify them as primary, secondary or tertiary bromide. Solution Write the structures of the following compounds: (i) 4-bromopent-2-ene (ii) 3-bromo-2-methylbut-1-ene (iii) 4-bromo-3-methylpent-2-ene (iv) 1-bromo-2-methylbut-2-ene (v) 1-bromobut-2-ene (vi) 3-bromo-2-methylpropene. Solution Number the chain from the end that gives the double bond the lower locant, then the halogen the lower locant consistent with that choice. (i) 2-Chloro-3-methylpentane (ii) 1-Chloro-4-ethylcyclohexane (iii) 4- tert -butyl-3-iodoheptane (iv) 1,4-Dibromobut-2-ene (v) 1-Bromo-4- sec -butyl-2-methylbenzene. 6.3 Nature of C—X Bond Halogen atoms are more electronegative than carbon, so the carbon–halogen bond of an alkyl halide is polarised : the carbon bears a partial positive charge (δ+) and the halogen a partial negative charge (δ−). This is why the carbon is attacked by nucleophiles and the halogen leaves as a halide ion. Going down the group the halogen atom gets larger — fluorine is the smallest, iodine the largest — so the C—X bond length increases from C—F to C—I. Bond enthalpy falls steeply from C—F to C—I while the bond gets longer, so the order of ease of breaking the bond — and hence of reactivity in substitution — is: \text > \text > \text `} important /> 6.4 Methods of Preparation of Haloalkanes 6.4.1 From Alcohols Alkyl halides are best prepared from alcohols, which are easily accessible. The hydroxyl group of an alcohol is replaced by halogen on reaction with concentrated halogen acids, phosphorus halides or thionyl chloride. The preparation of an alkyl chloride is carried out either by passing dry hydrogen chloride gas through a solution of the alcohol, or by heating a mixture of the alcohol and concentrated aqueous halogen acid. Reactions of primary and secondary alcohols with HCl need a catalyst, ZnCl 2 ; tertiary alcohols react simply on shaking with concentrated HCl at room temperature. Constant boiling HBr (48%) is used for alkyl bromides, and good yields of R—I are obtained by heating the alcohol with sodium or potassium iodide in 95% ortho phosphoric acid. The order of reactivity of alcohols with a given haloacid is 3° > 2° > 1° . Phosphorus tribromide and triiodide are usually generated in situ by the reaction of red phosphorus with bromine and iodine respectively. Thionyl chloride is the reagent of choice because the alkyl halide is formed along with gases SO 2 and HCl. Both gaseous products escape, so the reaction gives pure alkyl halides . These methods are not applicable to aryl halides: the carbon–oxygen bond in phenols has partial double bond character and is stronger than a single bond, so it is difficult to break. 6.4.2 From Hydrocarbons (I) From alkanes by free radical halogenation. Free radical chlorination or bromination of alkanes gives a complex mixture of isomeric mono- and polyhaloalkanes which is difficult to separate as pure compounds. Consequently the yield of any single compound is low. Identify all the possible monochloro structural isomers expected to be formed on free radical monochlorination of (CH 3 ) 2 CHCH 2 CH 3 . Solution The molecule has four different types of hydrogen atoms. Replacing each type gives one product, so four isomeric monochloro compounds are formed: (II) From alkenes. An alkene is converted to the corresponding alkyl halide by reaction with HCl, HBr or HI. Propene yields two products, but only one predominates according to Markovnikov's rule — the halogen goes to the carbon carrying fewer hydrogens. Addition of halogens gives vic-dibromides . Adding bromine in CCl 4 to an alkene discharges the reddish brown colour of bromine — an important test for a double bond. 6.4.3 Halogen Exchange Alkyl iodides are often prepared by the reaction of alkyl chlorides/bromides with NaI in dry acetone — the Finkelstein reaction . NaCl or NaBr formed is precipitated in dry acetone, which drives the forward reaction according to Le Chatelier's principle. Alkyl fluorides are best made by heating an alkyl chloride/bromide with a metallic fluoride such as AgF, Hg 2 F 2 , CoF 2 or SbF 3 — the Swarts reaction . Why is sulphuric acid not used during the reaction of alcohols with KI? Answer H 2 SO 4 cannot be used along with KI in the conversion of an alcohol to an alkyl iodide, because it converts KI into the corresponding acid HI, which is then oxidised by it to I 2 . 6.5 Preparation of Haloarenes (i) From hydrocarbons by electrophilic substitution Aryl chlorides and bromides are easily prepared by electrophilic substitution of arenes with chlorine and bromine in the presence of Lewis acid catalysts such as iron or iron(III) chloride. The ortho and para isomers are easily separated because of the large difference in their melting points. Reactions with iodine are reversible and need an oxidising agent (HNO 3 , HIO 4 ) to oxidise the HI formed. Fluoro compounds are not prepared this way because of the high reactivity of fluorine. (ii) From amines by Sandmeyer's reaction When a primary aromatic amine, dissolved or suspended in cold aqueous mineral acid, is treated with sodium nitrite, a diazonium salt is formed. Mixing a freshly prepared solution of the diazonium salt with cuprous chloride or cuprous bromide replaces the diazonium group by —Cl or —Br. ), }, { label: "Sandmeyer substitution with CuCl / CuBr", description: ( ), }, { label: "For the iodide, no cuprous halide is needed", description: ( ), }, ]} /> Replacement of the diazonium group by iodine is done simply by shaking the diazonium salt with potassium iodide. 6.6 Physical Properties Alkyl halides are colourless when pure, but bromides and iodides develop colour on exposure to light. Many volatile halogen compounds have a sweet smell. Melting and boiling points Methyl chloride, methyl bromide, ethyl chloride and some chlorofluoromethanes are gases at room temperature; higher members are liquids or solids. Organic halogen compounds are generally polar, and their molecular masses are higher than those of the parent hydrocarbons, so dipole–dipole and van der Waals forces are stronger. That is why the boiling points of chlorides, bromides and iodides are considerably higher than those of hydrocarbons of comparable molecular mass. For the same alkyl group, boiling points decrease in the order RI > RBr > RCl > RF , because van der Waals forces increase with the size and mass of the halogen. Boiling points of isomeric haloalkanes decrease with increasing branching — 2-bromo-2-methylpropane has the lowest boiling point of its three isomers. Boiling points of isomeric dihalobenzenes are very nearly the same, but para-isomers have much higher melting points — their symmetry lets them fit into the crystal lattice better than the ortho and meta forms. Solubility Haloalkanes are very slightly soluble in water. Energy is needed to overcome the attractions between haloalkane molecules and to break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules, while less energy is released when new haloalkane–water attractions form (they are weaker than the original hydrogen bonds). By contrast, haloalkanes dissolve readily in organic solvents, because the new intermolecular attractions are of much the same strength as those being broken. Density Bromo, iodo and polychloro derivatives of hydrocarbons are heavier than water, and density increases with the number of carbon atoms, the number of halogen atoms and the atomic mass of the halogen. (i) Bromomethane, bromoform, chloromethane, dibromomethane. (ii) 1-Chloropropane, isopropyl chloride, 1-chlorobutane. Answer (i) Chloromethane < bromomethane < dibromomethane < bromoform — boiling point increases with molecular mass. (ii) Isopropyl chloride < 1-chloropropane < 1-chlorobutane — the branched isomer has a lower boiling point than the straight chain, and the C 4 compound boils higher than the C 3 compounds. 6.7 Chemical Reactions The reactions of haloalkanes fall into three categories: Nucleophilic substitution Elimination reactions Reaction with metals 6.7.1 Reactions of Haloalkanes (1) Nucleophilic substitution reactions Nucleophiles are electron-rich species, so they attack the electron-deficient carbon of the substrate. In a nucleophilic substitution reaction a nucleophile replaces an already existing nucleophile (the leaving group , which departs as a halide ion) in the molecule. Haloalkanes are the substrate; the reaction is initiated by the nucleophile, and the halogen-bonded carbon carries a partial positive charge. Groups such as cyanide and nitrite possess two nucleophilic centres and are called ambident nucleophiles . The cyanide group is a hybrid of two contributing structures, so it can link through carbon (giving alkyl cyanides) or through nitrogen (giving isocyanides). Similarly the nitrite ion links through oxygen to give alkyl nitrites and through nitrogen to give nitroalkanes. Haloalkanes react with KCN to form alkyl cyanides as the main product, while AgCN forms isocyanides as the chief product. Explain. Solution KCN is predominantly ionic and provides cyanide ions in solution. Although both carbon and nitrogen can donate electron pairs, attack takes place mainly through carbon, because the C—C bond is more stable than the C—N bond. AgCN, however, is mainly covalent, so nitrogen is free to donate its electron pair and isocyanide becomes the main product. (a) Substitution nucleophilic bimolecular (S N 2) The reaction between CH 3 Cl and hydroxide ion to give methanol and chloride ion follows second order kinetics — the rate depends on the concentration of both reactants. Because the nucleophile must approach the carbon bearing the leaving group, bulky substituents on or near that carbon have a dramatic inhibiting effect. Of the simple alkyl halides, methyl halides react most rapidly in S N 2 reactions (only three small hydrogens), while tertiary halides are least reactive because bulky groups hinder the approaching nucleophile. 1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ`} important /> (b) Substitution nucleophilic unimolecular (S N 1) S N 1 reactions are generally carried out in polar protic solvents (water, alcohol, acetic acid). The reaction between tert -butyl bromide and hydroxide ion follows first order kinetics — the rate depends only on the concentration of the alkyl halide. The more stable the carbocation, the easier it forms and the faster the reaction. For alkyl halides, 3° halides undergo S N 1 very fast because of the high stability of 3° carbocations. Allylic and benzylic halides are also highly reactive towards S N 1, because their carbocations are stabilised by resonance. 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \text _3\text `} important /> One step, bimolecular, second order. Rate = k[RX][Nu⁻]. No carbocation; a five-coordinate transition state. Product has inverted configuration. Reactivity: CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°. ), }, { title: "S_N1", children: ( <> Two steps, unimolecular, first order. Rate = k[RX]. Planar carbocation intermediate; polar protic solvent helps. Product is racemised. Reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X. ), }, ]} /> In the following pairs of halogen compounds, which would undergo S N 2 reaction faster? Solution (i) The primary halide reacts faster, because a primary carbon offers little steric hindrance to the approaching nucleophile. blob: "use client"; import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/Formula"; import from "@/components/content/FormulaCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/SpeedTricks"; export default function LinearProgrammingChapter() { return ( <> 12.1 Introduction Linear programming (LP) is the method of optimising a linear objective subject to linear constraints. A typical problem asks: how to use limited resources (labour, money, material) so as to maximise profit or minimise cost. 12.2 Linear Programming Problem and its Mathematical Formulation Every LP problem contains: Decision variables — the quantities to be determined. Objective function to be maximised or minimised. Constraints x_1+\cdots+a_ x_n\le (\text \ge,=)\,b_i`} , typically representing limits on resources (with ). Non-negativity — quantities cannot be negative. A solution satisfying all constraints is a feasible solution ; a feasible solution optimising is an optimal solution . The set of all feasible solutions is the feasible region — a closed, bounded, convex polygon (in 2-D) or polyhedron (in 3-D). 12.3 Graphical Method for Solving LP Problems in Two Variables When there are only two decision variables, the feasible region is drawn in the plane: plot each inequality as a half-plane, the intersection is the feasible region. The objective is maximised (or minimised) at a corner point (vertex) of the feasible region (corner point theorem), provided the region is bounded. 12.4 Vertex / Corner-Point Method — Algorithm Step 1. Write the constraints including non-negativity. Step 2. Draw each line and shade the half-plane satisfying the inequality (test origin). Step 3. Identify the feasible polygon and list its vertices (intersections of boundary lines). Step 4. Evaluate at every vertex. Step 5. The largest (or smallest) value is the answer; note the multiple optima if two adjacent vertices give the same value. title: Biodiversity and Conservation
headings: 13.1.1 How Many Species Are There on Earth and How Many in India?
13.1.3 The Importance of Species Diversity to the Ecosystem
The four major causes — the "Evil Quartet"
blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/Formula"; import from "@/components/content/Stepper"; import from "@/components/content/study/MetricCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/ConceptCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/TreeDiagram"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; export default function BiodiversityAndConservationChapter() { return ( <> 13.1 Biodiversity In our biosphere immense diversity (or heterogeneity) exists not only at the species level but at all levels of biological organisation ranging from macromolecules within cells to biomes. Biodiversity is the term popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson to describe the combined diversity at all the levels of biological organisation. The three most important levels of biodiversity are genetic, species and ecological diversity: It has taken millions of years of evolution to accumulate this rich diversity in nature, but we could lose all that wealth in less than two centuries if the present rates of species losses continue. Biodiversity and its conservation are now vital environmental issues of international concern. 13.1.1 How Many Species Are There on Earth and How Many in India? Published records tell us how many species have been discovered and named, but it is not easy to answer how many species there are on earth. According to the IUCN (2004), the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than 1.5 million. Estimates of the total range widely, from 20 to 50 million at the extreme, with a more conservative and scientifically sound estimate by Robert May placing global species diversity at about 7 million. Species inventories are more complete in temperate than in tropical countries, and the overwhelming majority of species still waiting to be discovered live in the tropics. So biologists extrapolate from the temperate-tropical richness ratio of an exhaustively studied group (insects) to the whole living world. div]:my-0"> More than 70 per cent of all species recorded are animals, while plants (algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) comprise no more than 22 per cent of the total. Among animals, insects are the most species-rich taxonomic group — more than 70 per cent of the total. The fungi alone have more species than all the fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals combined. Prokaryotes are not counted in any of these figures; their diversity, by molecular criteria, might run into millions, and many are not culturable under laboratory conditions. India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, but holds 8.1 per cent of global species diversity. Nearly 45,000 plant species and twice as many animal species have been recorded from India. If only 22 per cent of species have been recorded so far, then more than 1,00,000 plant and 3,00,000 animal species may still be waiting to be discovered in India. 13.1.2 Patterns of Biodiversity Latitudinal gradients Species diversity is uneven across the globe: in general it decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles. Tropics (23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas. Colombia near the equator has nearly 1,400 bird species; New York at 41° N has 105; Greenland at 71° N only 56. India, with much of its land in the tropical latitudes, hosts more than 1,200 bird species. A tropical forest such as in Ecuador can have up to 10 times as many vascular-plant species as a temperate forest of equal area, and the Amazonian rain forest — the most biodiverse place on earth — holds over 40,000 plant species, 3,000 fishes, 1,300 birds, 427 mammals, 427 amphibians, 378 reptiles and 1,25,000+ invertebrates. More evolutionary time: unlike temperate regions that suffered frequent past glaciations, the tropics have stayed relatively undisturbed for millions of years, allowing species to diversify. Less seasonal environments: constant, predictable conditions promote niche specialisation. More solar energy: higher productivity in the tropics indirectly supports greater diversity. Species-area relationships Alexander von Humboldt observed that species richness increases with explored area, but only up to a limit; for a wide variety of taxa the relationship is a rectangular hyperbola. On a logarithmic scale this becomes a straight line: where S is species richness, A is area, Z is the slope of the regression line and C is the Y-intercept. 13.1.3 The Importance of Species Diversity to the Ecosystem Does the number of species in a community really matter to how the ecosystem functions? Ecologists have suspected for decades that communities richer in species tend to be more stable. A stable community shows little year-to-year variation in productivity, resists or recovers from disturbances, and resists invasion by alien species. David Tilman's long-term outdoor-plot experiments suggest that plots with more species show less year-to-year variation in total biomass and are more productive. An ecosystem is an aeroplane and each species is a rivet. Popping out a few rivets at first may not affect the flight, but as more are removed the plane weakens dangerously; rivets on the wings (key species that drive major ecosystem functions) are far more critical than rivets on the seats or windows. 13.1.4 Loss of Biodiversity New species are probably not being added as fast as old ones are being lost. The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species in the last 500 years. Examples of recent extinctions include the dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's Sea Cow (Russia) and three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan, Caspian). The last twenty years alone saw 27 species disappear. Loss is not random across taxa — amphibians appear especially vulnerable. More than 15,500 species world-wide, including over 650 from India, face the threat of extinction. At present 12 per cent of all bird species, 23 per cent of all mammal species, 32 per cent of all amphibian species and 31 per cent of all gymnosperm species are threatened. Five mass-extinction episodes occurred during the more than 3 billion years of life on earth. The current sixth episode differs only in rate: present extinction rates are 100 to 1,000 times faster than pre-human times. If current trends continue, nearly half of all species may be wiped out within 100 years. It generally leads to (a) decline in plant production, (b) lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought and (c) increased variability in ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use and pest and disease cycles. The four major causes — the "Evil Quartet" 13.2 Biodiversity Conservation 13.2.1 Why Should We Conserve Biodiversity? Conservation arguments fall into three categories: Countless direct economic benefits from nature — food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material. Industrial products — tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes. More than 25 per cent of drugs sold world-wide are derived from plants; 25,000 plant species serve traditional medicine. Bioprospecting promises nations with rich biodiversity enormous benefits. ), }, { title: "Broadly utilitarian", children: ( Ecosystem services — the Amazon forest alone produces an estimated 20 per cent of atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis. Pollination by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats sustains our fruits and seeds. Intangible benefits — aesthetics, recreation, cultural and spiritual value. Climate moderation, pest control and flood control. ), }, ]} /> Every species has an intrinsic value, even if it has no economic value to us. We share this planet with millions of plant, animal and microbe species, and owe it to future generations to pass on our biological legacy in good order. 13.2.2 How Do We Conserve Biodiversity? Conserve the whole ecosystem to protect its biodiversity at all levels — save the entire forest to save the tiger. Preferred whenever the species still lives in its natural habitat. ), }, { title: "Ex situ (off site) conservation", children: ( Remove threatened animals and plants from their natural habitat into settings where they can be protected and given special care — zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks, cryopreservation of gametes, in-vitro fertilisation, tissue culture, seed banks. ), }, ]} /> In situ conservation in practice Nations cannot conserve everything, so conservationists identified "biodiversity hotspots" — regions with very high species richness and high endemism (species confined to that region and found nowhere else). Initially 25 hotspots were identified; 9 more were added, bringing the total to 34. Although hotspots cover less than 2 per cent of the earth's land area, they harbour an enormous share of species, and strict protection could cut ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent. Three of these hotspots (Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya) cover India's exceptionally rich biodiversity regions. div]:my-0"> In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as biosphere reserves, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries — 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks and 448 wildlife sanctuaries. Indian cultural and religious traditions also protected nature through sacred groves: tracts of forest set aside and given total protection, found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills (Meghalaya), Aravalli Hills (Rajasthan), the Western Ghats of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh. In Meghalaya these sacred groves are the last refuges for many rare and threatened plants. div]:my-0"> Ex situ conservation in practice Threatened species are removed from their natural habitat and protected with special care. Many animals survive only in captivity today. Modern ex situ methods go well beyond enclosures: gametes preserved by cryopreservation, eggs fertilised in vitro, plants propagated by tissue culture, and genetic strains of commercially important plants maintained in seed banks. Biodiversity does not respect political boundaries, so conservation is a collective responsibility of all nations. The Convention on Biological Diversity (the Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro, 1992) called on all nations to conserve biodiversity and use it sustainably; the World Summit on Sustainable Development (Johannesburg, 2002) pledged a significant reduction in the rate of biodiversity loss by 2010. title: Biotechnology and its Applications
headings: Recovery of healthy plants from diseased plants
Bt cotton — how the toxin works
blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/Stepper"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/RevealAnswer"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/ConceptCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MetricCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; export default function BiotechnologyAndItsApplicationsChapter() { return ( <> Biotechnology, as you would have learnt from the previous chapter, essentially deals with industrial scale production of biopharmaceuticals and biologicals using genetically modified microbes, fungi, plants and animals. Therapeutics Diagnostics Genetically modified crops for agriculture Processed food Bioremediation Waste treatment Energy production Human beings have used biotechnology to improve the quality of human life, especially in the field of food production and health — and those two arenas are exactly the two halves of this chapter. 10.1 Biotechnological Applications in Agriculture Let us take a look at the three options that can be thought for increasing food production. Agro-chemical based agriculture. Organic agriculture. Genetically engineered crop-based agriculture. Why was a third option even needed? The Green Revolution succeeded in tripling the food supply, but yet it was not enough to feed the growing human population. Increased yields have partly been due to the use of improved crop varieties. But they were mainly due to better management practices and the use of agrochemicals — fertilisers and pesticides. For farmers in the developing world, agrochemicals are often too expensive . Further increases in yield with existing varieties are not possible using conventional breeding . Traditional breeding techniques failed to keep pace with demand and to provide sufficiently fast and efficient systems for crop improvement. Two technologies were developed to fill that gap — tissue culture and, later, genetically modified crops . Tissue culture and micro-propagation It was learnt by scientists, during the 1950s, that whole plants could be regenerated from explants — any part of a plant taken out and grown in a test tube, under sterile conditions in special nutrient media. This capacity to generate a whole plant from any cell/explant is called totipotency . The nutrient medium must provide a carbon source such as sucrose, and also inorganic salts , vitamins , amino acids and growth regulators like auxins and cytokinins. By application of these methods it is possible to achieve propagation of a large number of plants in very short durations . Many important food plants — tomato , banana , apple — have been produced on commercial scale using this method. Recovery of healthy plants from diseased plants Even if the plant is infected with a virus, the meristem (apical and axillary) is free of virus. Hence, one can remove the meristem and grow it in vitro to obtain virus-free plants. Scientists have succeeded in culturing meristems of banana , sugarcane , potato , etc. Somatic hybrids Scientists have even isolated single cells from plants and, after digesting their cell walls, have been able to isolate naked protoplasts (surrounded by plasma membranes). A protoplast of tomato was fused with that of potato and grown — forming new hybrid plants combining tomato and potato characteristics. This was achieved, giving pomato . Unfortunately, the plant did not have all the desired combination of characteristics for its commercial utilisation. Genetically modified crops Is there an alternative path that our understanding of genetics can show, so that farmers may obtain maximum yield from their fields, and the use of fertilisers and chemicals can be minimised? Use of genetically modified crops is a possible solution. Plants, bacteria, fungi and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation are called Genetically Modified Organisms (GMO) . In addition to these uses, GM has been used to create tailor-made plants to supply alternative resources to industries, in the form of starches , fuels and pharmaceuticals . The application studied in detail here is the production of pest resistant plants , which could decrease the amount of pesticide used. Bt toxin is produced by a bacterium called Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt for short). The Bt toxin gene has been cloned from the bacteria and expressed in plants to provide resistance to insects without the need for insecticides — in effect creating a bio-pesticide . Examples are Bt cotton , Bt corn , rice , tomato , potato and soyabean . Bt cotton — how the toxin works Some strains of Bacillus thuringiensis produce proteins that kill certain insects. B. thuringiensis forms protein crystals during a particular phase of its growth. These crystals contain a toxic insecticidal protein. The Bt toxin protein exists as an inactive protoxin . It becomes active only after an insect ingests it — so the bacterium that stores the crystal is never harmed by its own product. Specific Bt toxin genes were isolated from Bacillus thuringiensis and incorporated into several crop plants such as cotton. The choice of genes depends upon the crop and the targeted pest, as most Bt toxins are insect-group specific . Pest resistant plants — RNA interference Several nematodes parasitise a wide variety of plants and animals, including human beings. A nematode, Meloidegyne incognitia , infects the roots of tobacco plants and causes a great reduction in yield. A novel strategy was adopted to prevent this infestation, based on the process of RNA interference (RNAi) . RNAi takes place in all eukaryotic organisms as a method of cellular defense. This method involves silencing of a specific mRNA due to a complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation of the mRNA (silencing). The source of this complementary RNA could be an infection by viruses having RNA genomes . It could also come from mobile genetic elements (transposons) that replicate via an RNA intermediate. In the Bt strategy the plant makes a toxic protein . In the RNAi strategy the plant makes an RNA that silences the nematode's own mRNA . Both protect the plant, but only the first is a toxin. 10.2 Biotechnological Applications in Medicine The recombinant DNA technological processes have made immense impact in the area of healthcare by enabling mass production of safe and more effective therapeutic drugs. Recombinant therapeutics do not induce unwanted immunological responses as is common in case of similar products isolated from non-human sources. div]:my-0"> 10.2.1 Genetically Engineered Insulin Management of adult-onset diabetes is possible by taking insulin at regular time intervals. What would a diabetic patient do if enough human insulin was not available? One would have to isolate and use insulin from other animals. Insulin used for diabetes was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs . Insulin from an animal source, though, caused some patients to develop allergy or other types of reactions to the foreign protein . Imagine if a bacterium were available that could make human insulin — you could grow a large quantity of the bacteria and make as much insulin as you need. Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains — chain A and chain B — that are linked together by disulphide bridges . In mammals, including humans, insulin is synthesised as a pro-hormone (like a pro-enzyme, the pro-hormone also needs to be processed before it becomes a fully mature and functional hormone) which contains an extra stretch called the C peptide . The main challenge for production of insulin using rDNA techniques was getting insulin assembled into a mature form — not making the chains, but joining them correctly. 10.2.2 Gene Therapy If a person is born with a hereditary disease, can a corrective therapy be taken for such a disease? Gene therapy is an attempt to do this. Gene therapy is a collection of methods that allows correction of a gene defect that has been diagnosed in a child/embryo. Here genes are inserted into a person's cells and tissues to treat a disease. Correction of a genetic defect involves delivery of a normal gene into the individual or embryo to take over the function of, and compensate for, the non-functional gene. The first clinical gene therapy was given in 1990 to a 4-year old girl with adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency . ADA is an enzyme crucial for the immune system to function. The disorder is caused due to the deletion of the gene for adenosine deaminase . Can cure ADA deficiency in some children. The patient receives bone marrow from a donor. Not completely curative. ), }, { title: "Enzyme replacement therapy", children: ( Used for other children with the same disorder. Functional ADA is given to the patient by injection. Not completely curative. ), }, ]} /> Both approaches work, but neither is a complete cure — which is what pushed the search towards gene therapy. 10.2.3 Molecular Diagnosis For effective treatment of a disease, early diagnosis and understanding its pathophysiology is very important. Using conventional methods of diagnosis — serum and urine analysis, etc. — early detection is not possible. Presence of a pathogen (bacteria, viruses, etc.) is normally suspected only when it has produced a disease symptom . By this time the concentration of the pathogen is already very high in the body. Very low concentration of a bacteria or virus — at a time when the symptoms of the disease are not yet visible — can be detected by amplification of their nucleic acid by PCR. The clone having the mutated gene will not appear on the photographic film, because the probe will not have complementarity with the mutated gene. 10.3 Transgenic Animals Animals that have had their DNA manipulated to possess and express an extra (foreign) gene are known as transgenic animals . div]:my-0"> Medicines required to treat certain human diseases can contain biological products, but such products are often expensive to make . Similar attempts to the α-1-antitrypsin work are being made for treatment of phenylketonuria (PKU) and cystic fibrosis . Transgenic mice are being used to test the safety of the polio vaccine; if successful and found to be reliable, they could replace the use of monkeys to test the safety of batches of the vaccine. Understand (physiology, disease) and manufacture or test (biological products, vaccine safety, chemical safety). Every reason in the table falls under one of those two. 10.4 Ethical Issues The manipulation of living organisms by the human race cannot go on any further, without regulation. Some ethical standards are required to evaluate the morality of all human activities that might help or harm living organisms. Genetic modification of organisms can have unpredictable results when such organisms are introduced into the ecosystem. The modification/usage of living organisms for public services — as food and medicine sources, for example — has also created problems with patents granted for the same. Certain companies are being granted patents for products and technologies that make use of the genetic materials, plants and other biological resources that have long been identified, developed and used by farmers and indigenous people of a specific region or country. The Basmati rice patent Rice is an important food grain, the presence of which goes back thousands of years in Asia's agricultural history. The diversity of rice in India is one of the richest in the world. Basmati rice is distinct for its unique aroma and flavour, and there is reference to Basmati in ancient texts, folklore and poetry, as it has been grown for centuries. Several attempts have also been made to patent uses, products and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines — e.g., turmeric , neem . If we are not vigilant and do not immediately counter these patent applications, other countries/individuals may encash on our rich legacy, and we may not be able to do anything about it. Biopiracy Biopiracy is the term used to refer to the use of bio-resources by multinational companies and other organisations without proper authorisation from the countries and people concerned without compensatory payment . Rich financially. Poor in biodiversity. Poor in traditional knowledge related to bio-resources. ), }, { title: "Developing and underdeveloped world", children: ( Rich in biodiversity. Rich in traditional knowledge related to bio-resources. Traditional knowledge can be exploited to develop modern applications, and can save time, effort and expenditure during commercialisation. ), }, ]} /> There has been growing realisation of the injustice, inadequate compensation, and benefit sharing between developed and developing countries. Therefore, some nations are developing laws to prevent such unauthorised exploitation of their bio-resources and traditional knowledge. The Indian Parliament has recently cleared the second amendment of the Indian Patents Bill . The amendment takes such issues into consideration, including patent terms, emergency provisions, research, and development initiatives. blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/Stepper"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/CycleDiagram"; import from "@/components/content/study/MetricCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; export default function BiotechnologyPrinciplesAndProcessesChapter() { return ( <> Making curd, bread or wine — all microbe-mediated processes — could also be thought of as a form of biotechnology. In the restricted sense used today, it refers to those processes which use genetically modified organisms to achieve the same on a larger scale. Many other techniques are included too — in vitro fertilisation leading to a ‘test-tube’ baby, synthesising a gene and using it, developing a DNA vaccine, or correcting a defective gene. The European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB) has given a definition of biotechnology that encompasses both the traditional view and modern molecular biotechnology: ‘ The integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services ’. Herbert Boyer was born in 1936 and brought up in a corner of western Pennsylvania where railroads and mines were the destiny of most young men. He completed graduate work at the University of Pittsburgh in 1963, followed by three years of post-graduate studies at Yale. In 1966, Boyer took over assistant professorship at the University of California at San Francisco. By 1969, he performed studies on a couple of restriction enzymes of the E. coli bacterium with especially useful properties. Boyer observed that these enzymes have the capability of cutting DNA strands in a particular fashion, which left what has become known as ‘sticky ends’ on the strands. These clipped ends made pasting together pieces of DNA a precise exercise. This discovery, in turn, led to a rich and rewarding conversation in Hawaii with a Stanford scientist named Stanley Cohen. Cohen had been studying small ringlets of DNA called plasmids, which float about freely in the cytoplasm of certain bacterial cells and replicate independently from the coding strand of DNA. Cohen had developed a method of removing these plasmids from the cell and then reinserting them in other cells. Combining this process with that of DNA splicing enabled Boyer and Cohen to recombine segments of DNA in desired configurations and insert the DNA in bacterial cells, which could then act as manufacturing plants for specific proteins. This breakthrough was the basis upon which the discipline of biotechnology was founded. 9.1 Principles of Biotechnology Among many, the two core techniques that enabled birth of modern biotechnology are: Techniques to alter the chemistry of genetic material — DNA and RNA. Introduce these into host organisms . Thus change the phenotype of the host organism. ), }, { title: "Bioprocess engineering", children: ( Maintenance of a sterile (microbial contamination-free) ambience in chemical engineering processes. Enables growth of only the desired microbe/eukaryotic cell in large quantities. For manufacture of biotechnological products like antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes , etc. ), }, ]} /> The conceptual development of genetic engineering Sexual reproduction provides opportunities for variations and formulation of unique combinations of genetic setup, some of which may be beneficial to the organism as well as the population. Asexual reproduction preserves the genetic information, while sexual reproduction permits variation. Traditional hybridisation procedures used in plant and animal breeding very often lead to inclusion and multiplication of undesirable genes along with the desired genes. The techniques of genetic engineering — creation of recombinant DNA, use of gene cloning and gene transfer — overcome this limitation. They allow us to isolate and introduce only one or a set of desirable genes without introducing undesirable genes into the target organism. Why an alien piece of DNA needs an origin of replication Most likely, a piece of DNA transferred into an alien organism would not be able to multiply itself in the progeny cells of the organism. But when it gets integrated into the genome of the recipient, it may multiply and be inherited along with the host DNA — because the alien piece has become part of a chromosome , which has the ability to replicate. In a chromosome there is a specific DNA sequence called the origin of replication , which is responsible for initiating replication. An alien DNA is linked with the origin of replication, so that this alien piece of DNA can replicate and multiply itself in the host organism. A mosquito acts as an insect vector to transfer the malarial parasite into the human body. In the same way, a plasmid can be used as a vector to deliver an alien piece of DNA into the host organism. The first artificial recombinant DNA molecule The construction of the first recombinant DNA emerged from the possibility of linking a gene encoding antibiotic resistance with a native plasmid — autonomously replicating circular extra-chromosomal DNA — of Salmonella typhimurium . Stanley Cohen and Herbert Boyer accomplished this in 1972 . Three basic steps in genetically modifying an organism 9.2 Tools of Recombinant DNA Technology Genetic engineering or recombinant DNA technology can be accomplished only if we have the key tools. Five of them are named in the chapter: 9.2.1 Restriction Enzymes In the year 1963 , the two enzymes responsible for restricting the growth of bacteriophage in Escherichia coli were isolated. One of these added methyl groups to DNA, while the other cut DNA. The latter was called restriction endonuclease . The first restriction endonuclease — Hind II — whose functioning depended on a specific DNA nucleotide sequence, was isolated and characterised five years later. Hind II always cut DNA molecules at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of six base pairs . This specific base sequence is known as the recognition sequence for Hind II. Today we know more than 900 restriction enzymes , isolated from over 230 strains of bacteria , each of which recognises different recognition sequences. div]:my-0"> How these enzymes are named The convention is that the first letter of the name comes from the genus and the second two letters come from the species of the prokaryotic cell from which they were isolated. Roman numbers following the names indicate the order in which the enzymes were isolated from that strain of bacteria. Nucleases: exo and endo Restriction enzymes belong to a larger class of enzymes called nucleases . Remove nucleotides from the ends of the DNA. They nibble inwards from a terminus. ), }, { title: "Endonucleases", children: ( Make cuts at specific positions within the DNA. Restriction endonucleases belong to this group. ), }, ]} /> How a restriction endonuclease works Each restriction endonuclease functions by ‘ inspecting ’ the length of a DNA sequence. Once it finds its specific recognition sequence, it binds to the DNA. It then cuts each of the two strands of the double helix at specific points in their sugar-phosphate backbones. Each restriction endonuclease recognises a specific palindromic nucleotide sequence in the DNA. Palindromes are groups of letters that form the same words when read both forward and backward, e.g. “MALAYALAM”. As against a word-palindrome, where the same word is read in both directions, the palindrome in DNA is a sequence of base pairs that reads the same on the two strands when the orientation of reading is kept the same. These sequences read the same on the two strands in the 5′ → 3′ direction — and this is also true if read in the 3′ → 5′ direction. Sticky ends Restriction enzymes cut the strand of DNA a little away from the centre of the palindrome sites, but between the same two bases on the opposite strands. This leaves single stranded portions at the ends. These overhanging stretches are called sticky ends , on each strand. They are named so because they form hydrogen bonds with their complementary cut counterparts. This stickiness of the ends facilitates the action of the enzyme DNA ligase . Restriction endonucleases are used in genetic engineering to form ‘recombinant’ molecules of DNA, which are composed of DNA from different sources/genomes. When cut by the same restriction enzyme, the resultant DNA fragments have the same kind of sticky ends, and these can be joined together (end-to-end) using DNA ligases. Unless one cuts the vector and the source DNA with the same restriction enzyme, the recombinant vector molecule cannot be created. Separation and isolation of DNA fragments The cutting of DNA by restriction endonucleases results in fragments of DNA. These fragments can be separated by a technique known as gel electrophoresis . The DNA fragments purified in this way are used in constructing recombinant DNA by joining them with cloning vectors. 9.2.2 Cloning Vectors Plasmids and bacteriophages have the ability to replicate within bacterial cells independent of the control of chromosomal DNA . Bacteriophages, because of their high number per cell, have very high copy numbers of their genome within the bacterial cells. Some plasmids may have only one or two copies per cell. Others may have 15–100 copies per cell, and their numbers can go even higher. Link an alien piece of DNA with bacteriophage or plasmid DNA, and its numbers can be multiplied equal to the copy number of the plasmid or bacteriophage. Vectors used at present are engineered in such a way that they help easy linking of foreign DNA and selection of recombinants from non-recombinants. Origin of replication (ori) This is a sequence from where replication starts . Any piece of DNA, when linked to this sequence, can be made to replicate within the host cells. This sequence is also responsible for controlling the copy number of the linked DNA. So, if one wants to recover many copies of the target DNA, it should be cloned in a vector whose origin supports a high copy number . Selectable marker In addition to ‘ori’, the vector requires a selectable marker , which helps in identifying and eliminating non-transformants and selectively permitting the growth of the transformants. Normally, the genes encoding resistance to antibiotics such as ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin , etc., are considered useful selectable markers for E. coli . The normal E. coli cells do not carry resistance against any of these antibiotics. Cloning sites In order to link the alien DNA, the vector needs to have very few, preferably single , recognition sites for the commonly used restriction enzymes. Presence of more than one recognition site within the vector will generate several fragments, which will complicate the gene cloning. The ligation of alien DNA is carried out at a restriction site present in one of the two antibiotic resistance genes. For example, you can ligate a foreign DNA at the BamH I site of the tetracycline resistance gene in the vector pBR322 . The E. coli cloning vector pBR322 shows restriction sites (Hind III, EcoR I, BamH I, Sal I, Pvu II, Pst I, Cla I), an ori and the antibiotic resistance genes (amp R and tet R ). rop codes for the proteins involved in the replication of the plasmid. The recombinant plasmids will lose tetracycline resistance due to insertion of foreign DNA, but can still be selected out from non-recombinant ones by plating the transformants on an ampicillin containing medium. The transformants growing on ampicillin containing medium are then transferred on a medium containing tetracycline. Selection of recombinants due to inactivation of antibiotics is a cumbersome procedure, because it requires simultaneous plating on two plates having different antibiotics. Alternative selectable markers therefore differentiate recombinants from non-recombinants on the basis of their ability to produce colour in the presence of a chromogenic substrate . In this, a recombinant DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of an enzyme, β-galactosidase . This results into inactivation of the gene for synthesis of this enzyme — referred to as insertional inactivation . The presence of a chromogenic substrate gives blue coloured colonies if the plasmid in the bacteria does not have an insert. Presence of an insert results in insertional inactivation of the β-galactosidase gene, so the colonies do not produce any colour — these are identified as recombinant colonies. Identifies and eliminates non-transformants ; permits growth of the transformants only. Usually a gene for resistance to an antibiotic the normal host cell is not resistant to. Tells you that DNA got into the cell — nothing about whether that DNA is recombinant. ), }, { title: "Insertional inactivation", children: ( Separates recombinants from non-recombinants, both of which are already transformants. Works because the insert disrupts a second gene — an antibiotic resistance gene, or the gene for β-galactosidase. The antibiotic version needs two plates; the chromogenic version reads the colour of the colonies on one plate. ), }, ]} /> Vectors for cloning genes in plants and animals We have learnt the lesson of transferring genes into plants and animals from bacteria and viruses, which have known this for ages — how to deliver genes to transform eukaryotic cells and force them to do what the bacteria or viruses want. Once a gene or a DNA fragment has been ligated into a suitable vector, it is transferred into a bacterial, plant or animal host — where it multiplies. 9.2.3 Competent Host (For Transformation with Recombinant DNA) DNA is a hydrophilic molecule, so it cannot pass through cell membranes. In order to force bacteria to take up the plasmid, the bacterial cells must first be made ‘ competent ’ to take up DNA. This is not the only way to introduce alien DNA into host cells. 9.3 Processes of Recombinant DNA Technology Recombinant DNA technology involves several steps in a specific sequence: 9.3.1 Isolation of the Genetic Material (DNA) Nucleic acid is the genetic material of all organisms without exception; in the majority of organisms this is deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA . In order to cut the DNA with restriction enzymes, it needs to be in pure form , free from other macro-molecules. DNA is enclosed within membranes, so the cell has to be broken open. That releases DNA along with other macromolecules — RNA, proteins, polysaccharides and also lipids . Genes are located on long molecules of DNA intertwined with proteins such as histones . 9.3.2 Cutting of DNA at Specific Locations Restriction enzyme digestions are performed by incubating purified DNA molecules with the restriction enzyme, at the optimal conditions for that specific enzyme. Agarose gel electrophoresis is employed to check the progression of a restriction enzyme digestion. DNA is a negatively charged molecule, hence it moves towards the positive electrode (anode). The process is repeated with the vector DNA also. After having cut the source DNA as well as the vector DNA with a specific restriction enzyme, the cut out ‘gene of interest’ from the source DNA and the cut vector with space are mixed and ligase is added. This results in the preparation of recombinant DNA. 9.3.3 Amplification of Gene of Interest using PCR PCR stands for Polymerase Chain Reaction . In this reaction, multiple copies of the gene (or DNA) of interest is synthesised in vitro usin

blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/CycleDiagram"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/ConceptCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MetricCard"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; export default function EcosystemChapter() { return ( <> An ecosystem varies greatly in size, from a small pond to a large forest or a sea. Many ecologists regard the entire biosphere as a global ecosystem — a composite of all the local ecosystems on Earth. Because that system is too large and complex to study at once, it is convenient to divide it into two basic categories: terrestrial and aquatic . Forest, grassland and desert are terrestrial; pond, lake, wetland, river and estuary are aquatic. Crop fields and an aquarium are man-made ecosystems. To understand how an ecosystem works we look at its structure first, then at the input (productivity) , the transfer of energy (food chain / food web, nutrient cycling) and the output (degradation and energy loss) . Along the way we meet the cycles, chains and webs created by these energy flows. 12.1 Ecosystem – Structure and Function In earlier classes you looked at the abiotic and biotic components of the environment. Here we take a more integrated view and follow how energy moves through those components. Interaction of biotic and abiotic components produces a physical structure characteristic of each ecosystem. Identification and enumeration of the plant and animal species present gives the species composition . The vertical distribution of different species at different levels is called stratification — trees in the top layer of a forest, shrubs below them, herbs and grasses at the bottom. Productivity — capture and storage of energy / biomass. Decomposition — breakdown of dead organic matter into inorganic nutrients. Energy flow — movement of energy from producers up the trophic levels. Nutrient cycling — repeated reuse of nutrient elements within the system. 12.2 Productivity A constant input of solar energy is the basic requirement for any ecosystem to function and sustain. Primary production is the amount of biomass or organic matter produced per unit area over a time period by plants during photosynthesis, expressed as weight (g m⁻²) or energy (kcal m⁻²). The rate of biomass production is called productivity , expressed in g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹ so that different ecosystems can be compared. NPP is the biomass actually available for consumption by heterotrophs — herbivores and decomposers. Primary productivity varies with plant species, environmental factors, nutrient availability and the photosynthetic capacity of plants. 12.3 Decomposition Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide, water and nutrients. The process is called decomposition . The raw material is detritus — dead plant remains (leaves, bark, flowers) and dead remains of animals, including faecal matter. 12.4 Energy Flow Except for the deep-sea hydrothermal ecosystems, the sun is the only source of energy for all ecosystems on Earth. Less than 50% of the incident solar radiation is photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) , and plants capture only 2–10% of the PAR — yet this small amount sustains the entire living world. Energy flow is unidirectional — sun → producers → consumers — consistent with the first law. Energy is lost as heat at every transfer (second law), so ecosystems need a constant energy supply to maintain order. The green plants are the producers . Consumers are heterotrophs that depend on plants directly or indirectly. If they feed on producers they are primary consumers (herbivores); if they eat other animals that eat plants they are secondary consumers ; tertiary consumers exist too. An animal that eats herbivores is a carnivore, or more precisely a primary carnivore (still a secondary consumer). A simple grazing food chain (GFC): Grass (Producer) → Goat (Primary Consumer) → Man (Secondary Consumer) The detritus food chain (DFC) begins with dead organic matter and is driven by decomposers (fungi and bacteria, i.e., saprotrophs). GFC dominates energy flow in aquatic ecosystems; in terrestrial ecosystems a much larger fraction flows through the DFC. The two chains interconnect (omnivores, predators of detritivores) to form a food web . Each level has a standing crop — the biomass (fresh or, more accurately, dry weight) or number of organisms present in a unit area at a given time. Successive trophic levels are limited by the 10 per cent law : only about 10% of the energy of a level is transferred to the next; the rest is lost, mostly as heat. 12.5 Ecological Pyramids An ecological pyramid expresses the food / energy relationship between organisms at different trophic levels in terms of number, biomass or energy . The base is always the producers (first trophic level); the apex is the top carnivore. Three types are studied: Producers far exceed consumers in number and biomass. Energy at a lower trophic level is always greater than at the next. Most terrestrial ecosystems show this. ), }, { title: "Inverted pyramid", children: ( Biomass of consumers exceeds that of producers. Typical of the sea, where a small standing crop of fast-reproducing phytoplankton supports a large biomass of zooplankton / fish. Pyramid of energy can never be inverted. ), }, ]} /> They ignore the same species occupying two or more trophic levels (e.g., a sparrow as both primary and secondary consumer). They assume a simple food chain, not a food web. Saprotrophs are not shown even though they play a vital role. Nutrient cycling — a brief note Nutrient cycling is the storage and movement of nutrient elements through the components of an ecosystem, with nutrients being used repeatedly. It is of two types: gaseous (atmosphere or hydrosphere as reservoir — carbon) and sedimentary (Earth's crust as reservoir — phosphorus). Products of ecosystem processes are called ecosystem services, e.g., purification of air and water by forests. Exercises ); }
