blob: import Image from "next/image"; import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Stepper"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/Formula"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/Timeline"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/biology/BrainSizeBars"; import from "@/components/content/biology/FinchBeaksDiagram"; import from "@/components/content/biology/MillerApparatusDiagram"; import from "@/components/content/PocketGrid"; export default function EvolutionChapter() { return ( <> 6.1 Origin of Life The origin of life is considered a unique event in the history of the universe. The universe is vast, and relatively speaking the earth itself is almost only a speck. From the Big Bang to the first oceans The Big Bang theory explains the origin of the universe as a singular, huge explosion. What followed can be read as four steps. Where did the first life come from? Special creation Life was created by a supernatural power — God (mythological; associated with Father Suarez). Three connotations: all present creatures were created as such; diversity never changes; earth about 4,000 years old. Abiogenesis (spontaneous generation) Life arose from decaying matter — straw, mud, etc. (living from non-living). Rejected by Louis Pasteur via the swan-neck flask experiment (sterile broth, no growth; growth appeared only when the neck was removed). Biogenesis Core maxim: "Omnis vivum ex ovo or vivo" — new life can originate only from pre-existing life. The experiment here set out to disprove abiogenesis (spontaneous generation from mud, straw, etc.). Swan-neck flask experiment: Louis Pasteur boiled nutrient broth in swan-neck flasks to kill existing microbes; the curved neck allowed air in but trapped airborne dust and spores. Results: broth in the curved flask stayed sterile (free of life); once the neck was removed or opened, microbial growth appeared. Conclusion and limitation: it permanently rejected spontaneous generation without explaining how the very first life itself emerged on earth. Panspermia (cosmic theory) Early Greek astronomers suggested units of life called spores were transferred from outer space to earth and other planets. Chemical evolution (modern theory) Proposed by Oparin (Russia) and Haldane (England); principle: "abiogenesis first, but biogenesis ever since" . Evolutionary sequence: inorganic constituents (NH₃, CH₄, etc.) → organic molecules (RNA, proteins) → life. Conditions: high temperature, volcanic storms, reducing atmosphere of methane and ammonia. Key note: first life originated in water ; water is therefore essential for the origin of life. Chemical evolution and the Urey-Miller experiment To prove the theory of chemical evolution — that the organic molecules of life could form from inorganic gases on the early earth. Oparin (Russia) and Haldane (England) had proposed that the first form of life came from pre-existing non-living organic molecules, and that life was preceded by chemical evolution . The Urey-Miller experiment put that idea to the test. Amino acids. Sugars, nitrogenous bases, pigments and fats. It showed that organic molecules can be built from inorganic gases under the conditions of the early earth — that is, it supported chemical evolution. It said nothing about how those molecules came together into a self-replicating, metabolising capsule of life. 6.2 Evolution of Life Forms – A Theory The theory of special creation held that every species was created as it is today, that diversity never changes, and that the earth is only about 4,000 years old. Charles Darwin challenged it after sailing round the world on H.M.S. Beagle and concluding the following. Existing living forms share similarities to varying degrees — not only among themselves but also with life forms that existed millions of years ago. Many such life forms do not exist any more. Extinctions of different life forms happened in the years gone by, just as new forms of life arose at different periods of the history of earth. There has been gradual evolution of life forms. Alfred Wallace, a naturalist who worked in the Malay Archipelago, had also come to similar conclusions around the same time. In due course of time, new types of organisms become recognisable. All living forms share similarities and common ancestors — but those ancestors lived at different periods of earth's history (epochs, periods and eras). The geological history of the earth closely matches the biological history of life — a common permissible conclusion is that the earth is billions of years old, not thousands . 6.3 What are the Evidences for Evolution? Palaeontology is the study of fossils. Fossils are hard remains of life-forms preserved in rocks. Rocks are formed by sedimentation . A cross-section of the earth's crust therefore shows sediments arranged one over the other across the long history of the earth, and different-aged sediments contain the fossils of life-forms that died while that sediment was forming. A fossil that bridges two groups by carrying features of both. Archaeopteryx shows reptilian as well as avian characters, so it is a connecting link between reptiles and birds. ), }, { id: "h-6-3-homology", icon: "🫀", label: "2. Morphological and anatomical", note: "Homology and analogy.", content: ( <> Organs with a similar internal structure but different functions , suited to different environmental conditions. Homology is the result of divergent evolution and indicates common ancestry . Forelimbs of mammals — the human hand, whale's flippers, bat's wings and cheetah's foot — are all built from the same bones: humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals and phalanges . Homology is also seen in internal organs such as the heart and brain . In plants, the thorns of Bougainvillea and the tendrils of Cucurbita . The same bones in seven forelimbs. Image: "Various vertebrate limbs" by Ruth Lawson (Otago Polytechnic), CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Organs with different internal structures but the same function , suited to similar environmental conditions. Analogy is the result of convergent evolution . Wings of insects (a thin flap of chitin) and wings of birds (modified forelimbs). Eyes of the octopus (retina formed from skin) and eyes of mammals (retina from the embryonic brain). Flippers of penguins and dolphins. Sweet potato (a modified root) and potato (a modified stem), both for food storage. Structure — similar. Function — different. Cause — divergent evolution. Shows — common ancestry. ), }, { title: "Analogous organs", children: ( Structure — different. Function — same. Cause — convergent evolution. Shows — similar habitat, not ancestry. ), }, ]} /> ), }, { id: "h-6-3-biochemistry", icon: "🧬", label: "3. Biochemical", note: "Proteins, genes and the central dogma.", content: ( <> Organisms show striking similarities in proteins, genes, other biomolecules and metabolic pathways. Such biochemical uniformity is strong evidence of common ancestry for diverse life forms. DNA → mRNA → Protein — the same flow of information in all of them. ), }, { id: "h-6-3-biogeography", icon: "🗺️", label: "4. Biogeographical and adaptive radiation", note: "Distribution, finches and marsupials.", content: ( <> The distribution of organisms over geographical areas is itself evidence of evolution: an ancestral stock that reaches an isolated area diversifies into many forms. Evolution of different species in a given geographical area starting from one point and radiating into other habitats is called adaptive radiation . On the Galapagos Islands , Darwin found small black birds — Darwin's finches . Many varieties — several kinds of finch lived on the same island. One origin — he conjectured that all of them evolved on the island itself. Beaks changed with diet — from the original seed-eating form arose insectivorous and vegetarian finches. When more than one adaptive radiation occurs in the same isolated area, the resemblance between the independently evolved forms is called convergent evolution . ), }, { id: "h-6-3-embryology", icon: "🥚", label: "5. Embryological", note: "Features shared by embryos.", content: ( <> Embryological support for evolution was proposed by Ernst Heckel , based upon the observation of certain features during the embryonic stage that are common to all vertebrates but absent in the adult. For example, the embryos of all vertebrates including human develop a row of vestigial gill slit just behind the head. But it is a functional organ only in fish , and is not found in any other adult vertebrates. On careful study performed by Karl Ernst von Baer , the proposal was disapproved. He noted that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals . ), }, { id: "h-6-3-moth", icon: "🦋", label: "6. Natural selection", note: "Industrial melanism and resistance.", content: ( <> A famous test case comes from England — the peppered moth, sampled before and after industrialisation. Trees — covered in white lichen. Moths — white-winged common; dark-winged rare. Why — dark moths stood out against pale bark and were picked off. ), }, { title: "After 1920", children: ( Trees — darkened by soot; lichens died. Moths — dark-winged common; white-winged declined. Why — now the pale moths were the conspicuous ones. ), }, ]} /> Lichens do not grow in polluted air. Their disappearance left the trunks bare and dark. That changed which moth was conspicuous. In a mixed population, the better-adapted form survives and increases — but no variant is completely wiped out . The whole case is called industrial melanism . Evolution by anthropogenic action Excess use of herbicides, pesticides, etc. has only resulted in selection of resistant varieties in a much lesser time scale. This is also true for microbes against which we employ antibiotics, or drugs against eukaryotic organisms/cells. Hence resistant organisms/cells are appearing in a time scale of months or years and not centuries. Evolution is not a directed process in the sense of determinism . It is a stochastic process based on chance events in nature and chance mutation in the organisms. ), }, ]} /> 6.4 Biological Evolution Evolution by natural selection, in a true sense, would have started when cellular forms of life with differences in metabolic capability originated on earth. The essence of Darwinian theory about evolution is natural selection . The rate of appearance of new forms is linked to the life cycle or the life span. Here we say that the fitness of B is better than that of A under the new conditions. Nature selects for fitness. Microbes that divide fast multiply into millions within hours — which is why their evolution is visible on a human timescale. The so-called fitness is based on characteristics which are inherited . Hence there must be a genetic basis for getting selected and to evolve. Adaptive ability is inherited; it has a genetic basis. Fitness is the end result of the ability to adapt and get selected by nature. Branching descent and natural selection are the two key concepts of the Darwinian theory of evolution. Lamarck — use and disuse of organs Even before Darwin, the French naturalist Lamarck argued that evolution is driven by use and disuse of organs . The claim — an organ used more develops; one used less withers. The giraffe — stretching for tall leaves elongated the neck, and the elongated neck was passed on to the offspring. The verdict — acquired characters are not inherited; nobody believes this conjecture any more. The world we see, inanimate and animate, is only the success stories of evolution. When we describe the story of this world we describe evolution as a process ; when we describe the story of life on earth we treat evolution as a consequence of a process called natural selection. We are still not very clear whether to regard evolution and natural selection as processes or as the end result of unknown processes. Malthus and the logic of natural selection It is possible that the work of Thomas Malthus on populations influenced Darwin. Natural selection is based on certain observations which are factual. Natural resources are limited. Populations are stable in size except for seasonal fluctuation. Members of a population vary in characteristics — in fact no two individuals are alike — even though they look superficially similar. Most of the variations are inherited. Left unchecked, a population would grow exponentially — as a growing bacterial culture shows. Real populations stay limited, which means there has been competition for resources : only some survived and grew at the cost of others. Variations which are heritable, and which make resource utilisation better for a few (adapted to the habitat better), will enable only those to reproduce and leave more progeny. Over many generations, survivors leave more progeny, there is a change in population characteristic, and hence new forms appear to arise. 6.5 Mechanism of Evolution What is the origin of variation, and how does speciation occur? Darwin either ignored Mendel's inheritable 'factors' or stayed silent about them. In the first decade of the twentieth century, Hugo deVries — working on evening primrose — proposed mutations: large differences arising suddenly in a population . 6.6 Hardy-Weinberg Principle In a population, the frequency of alleles of a gene or locus tends to remain fixed through the generations. The Hardy-Weinberg principle states this in algebraic form. Allele frequencies in a population are stable and are constant from generation to generation. The gene pool (total genes and their alleles in a population) remains a constant. This is called genetic equilibrium . The sum of all allelic frequencies is 1. In a diploid, p and q are the frequencies of allele A and allele a . When the frequency measured differs from expected values, the difference (direction) indicates the extent of evolutionary change. Disturbance in genetic equilibrium — a change of frequency of alleles in a population — would then be interpreted as resulting in evolution. Since p + q = 1, q = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4 . Frequency of AA = p ² = (0.6)² = 0.36 . Frequency of Aa = 2 pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48 . Frequency of aa = q ² = (0.4)² = 0.16 . Check: 0.36 + 0.48 + 0.16 = 1 , as the equation demands. Five factors that disturb the equilibrium A critical analysis makes us believe that variation due to mutation, variation due to recombination during gametogenesis, or variation due to gene flow or genetic drift results in a changed frequency of genes and alleles in the future generation. Coupled to enhanced reproductive success, natural selection makes the population look like a different population altogether. What natural selection does to a trait 6.7 A Brief Account of Evolution About 2000 mya the first cellular life appeared. Some cells could release O₂ — much as the light reaction of photosynthesis splits water — and single cells slowly became multicellular. How non-cellular aggregates of giant molecules became cells with a membranous envelope is still unknown. Plants first — the first organisms to invade land were plants; they were widespread before animals followed. Coal from ferns — giant ferns (pteridophytes) fell and slowly formed coal deposits. From fish to mammals In 1938 a fish caught in South Africa turned out to be a Coelacanth , thought extinct. These lobefins evolved into the first amphibians ; no transitional specimens survive, only their descendants — frogs

How HIV disables the immune system
Other drugs, and what drug abuse means
blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/Stepper"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MetricCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/ConceptCard"; export default function HumanHealthAndDiseasesChapter() { return ( <> Health was once explained as a balance of certain ‘humors’ — the view of early Greeks like Hippocrates and of the Indian Ayurveda system of medicine. Persons with ‘blackbile’ were thought to have a hot personality and to get fevers. That idea came from pure reflective thought, not experiment. It was overturned by experiment: William Harvey discovered blood circulation, and a thermometer showed that persons with blackbile had normal body temperature. Later biology showed that the mind influences the immune system through the neural system and the endocrine system , and the immune system maintains our health. Healthy people are more efficient at work — this increases productivity and brings economic prosperity. Health increases longevity of people and reduces infant and maternal mortality. Balanced diet, personal hygiene and regular exercise are very important to maintain good health. Yoga has been practised since time immemorial to achieve physical and mental health. Awareness about diseases, vaccination (immunisation) against infectious diseases, proper disposal of wastes, control of vectors and hygiene in food and water resources are necessary for good health. When the functioning of one or more organs or systems of the body is adversely affected, characterised by appearance of various signs and symptoms, we say that we are not healthy, i.e., we have a disease . Easily transmitted from one person to another. Very common — everyone suffers from them at sometime or other. Some, like AIDS, are fatal. ), }, { title: "Non-infectious diseases", children: ( Not transmitted from person to person. Cancer is the major cause of death among them. Drug and alcohol abuse also affect our health adversely. ), }, ]} /> 7.1 Common Diseases in Humans A wide range of organisms belonging to bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, helminths, etc., could cause diseases in man. Such disease-causing organisms are called pathogens . Most parasites are therefore pathogens — they cause harm to the host by living in (or on) them. Pathogens enter the body by various means, multiply, and interfere with normal vital activities — resulting in morphological and functional damage . A pathogen must adapt to life inside the host. Pathogens that enter the gut must survive the low pH of the stomach and resist the various digestive enzymes. Typhoid Salmonella typhi is a pathogenic bacterium which causes typhoid fever in human beings. The pathogens generally enter the small intestine through food and water contaminated with them, and migrate to other organs through blood . In severe cases, intestinal perforation and death may occur. Typhoid fever could be confirmed by the Widal test . Mary Mallon, nicknamed Typhoid Mary , was a cook by profession and was a typhoid carrier who continued to spread typhoid for several years through the food she prepared. Pneumonia Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae cause pneumonia in humans, infecting the alveoli (air filled sacs) of the lungs. As a result of the infection, the alveoli get filled with fluid, leading to severe problems in respiration. A healthy person acquires the infection by inhaling the droplets/aerosols released by an infected person, or even by sharing glasses and utensils with an infected person. Dysentery, plague, diphtheria, etc., are some of the other bacterial diseases in man. Common cold Rhino viruses cause one of the most infectious human ailments — the common cold. They infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs . Symptoms usually last for 3–7 days . Droplets from cough or sneezes of an infected person are either inhaled directly or transmitted through contaminated objects — pens, books, cups, doorknobs, computer keyboard or mouse, etc. Malaria Plasmodium , a tiny protozoan, is responsible for malaria. Different species cause different types of malaria; malignant malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum is the most serious one and can even be fatal. The malarial parasite requires two hosts — human and mosquitoes — to complete its life cycle, and the female Anopheles mosquito is the vector (transmitting agent) too. Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery) Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite in the large intestine of human which causes amoebiasis. Houseflies act as mechanical carriers — they transmit the parasite from the faeces of an infected person to food and food products, thereby contaminating them. Drinking water and food contaminated by faecal matter are the main source of infection. Ascariasis Ascaris , the common round worm, is an intestinal parasite that causes ascariasis. The eggs of the parasite are excreted along with the faeces of infected persons, which contaminate soil, water, plants, etc. A healthy person acquires this infection through contaminated water, vegetables, fruits, etc. Filariasis (elephantiasis) Wuchereria ( W. bancrofti and W. malayi ), the filarial worms, live for many years in the organ they infect, causing a slowly developing chronic inflammation . The disease is called elephantiasis or filariasis. The pathogens are transmitted to a healthy person through the bite of female mosquito vectors. Ringworms Ringworms are one of the most common infectious diseases in man. Heat and moisture help these fungi to grow , which makes them thrive in skin folds such as those in the groin or between the toes. Ringworms are generally acquired from soil or by using towels, clothes or even the comb of infected individuals. Prevention and control of infectious diseases Maintenance of personal and public hygiene is very important for prevention and control of many infectious diseases. Recent widespread incidences of vector-borne ( Aedes mosquitoes) diseases like dengue and chikungunya in many parts of India have made these precautions more important. Vaccines, immunisation and antibiotics The use of vaccines and immunisation programmes has enabled us to completely eradicate a deadly disease like smallpox . Polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus have been controlled to a large extent by the use of vaccines. Biotechnology is at the verge of making available newer and safer vaccines. Discovery of antibiotics and various other drugs has enabled us to effectively treat infectious diseases. 7.2 Immunity Everyday we are exposed to a large number of infectious agents, yet only a few of these exposures result in disease. The body is able to defend itself from most of these foreign agents. This overall ability of the host to fight the disease-causing organisms, conferred by the immune system is called immunity . Immunity is of two types: Innate immunity Acquired immunity 7.2.1 Innate Immunity Innate immunity is non-specific type of defence, that is present at the time of birth . This is accomplished by providing different types of barriers to the entry of the foreign agents into our body. Innate immunity consist of four types of barriers. 7.2.2 Acquired Immunity Acquired immunity, on the other hand, is pathogen specific . It is characterised by memory . Produced on the first encounter with a pathogen. Of low intensity. ), }, { title: "Secondary (anamnestic) response", children: ( Produced on a subsequent encounter with the same pathogen. Highly intensified — the body appears to have memory of the first encounter. ), }, ]} /> Both responses are carried out with the help of two special types of lymphocytes present in our blood — B-lymphocytes and T-lymphocytes . B-lymphocytes produce an army of proteins in response to pathogens into our blood to fight with them. These proteins are called antibodies . T-cells themselves do not secrete antibodies but help B cells to produce them. Each antibody molecule has four peptide chains — two small called light chains and two longer called heavy chains . Hence, an antibody is represented as H₂L₂ . Different types of antibodies are produced in our body. IgA, IgM, IgE and IgG are some of them. Also called antibody mediated response. Carried out by antibodies produced by B-lymphocytes. Antibodies circulate in the blood. ), }, { title: "Cell-mediated immune response (CMI)", children: ( Mediated by T-lymphocytes. Responsible for graft rejection. Lets the body differentiate ‘self’ and ‘nonself’. ), }, ]} /> Why transplanted organs are rejected When organs like heart, eye, liver or kidney fail, transplantation is the only remedy. Grafts from just any source — an animal, another primate, or any human being — cannot be made, since the grafts would be rejected sooner or later. Tissue matching and blood group matching are essential before any graft/transplant. Even after this, the patient has to take immuno-suppressants all his/her life. 7.2.3 Active and Passive Immunity The host is exposed to antigens — living or dead microbes, or other proteins — and antibodies are produced in the host body. Slow, and takes time to give its full effective response. Induced by injecting microbes during immunisation, or by infectious organisms gaining access during natural infection. ), }, { title: "Passive immunity", children: ( Ready-made antibodies are directly given to protect the body against foreign agents. Example: the foetus receives some antibodies from the mother through the placenta during pregnancy. Ready-made preparations — antitoxin, antivenom — are covered under passive immunisation. ), }, ]} /> The yellowish fluid colostrum , secreted by the mother during the initial days of lactation, has abundant antibodies (IgA) to protect the infant. The infant has not made them itself — this borrowed protection is passive immunity. 7.2.4 Vaccination and Immunisation The principle of immunisation or vaccination is based on the property of ‘memory’ of the immune system. For deadly microbes needing a quick immune response — as in tetanus — preformed antibodies, or antitoxin (a preparation containing antibodies to the toxin), are injected directly. In cases of snakebites , the injection given to the patient contains preformed antibodies against the snake venom. This type of immunisation is called passive immunisation. Recombinant DNA technology has allowed the production of antigenic polypeptides of pathogen in bacteria or yeast. Vaccines produced this way allow large scale production and hence greater availability for immunisation. Example: the hepatitis B vaccine produced from yeast . 7.2.5 Allergies The exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens present in the environment is called allergy . The substances to which such an immune response is produced are called allergens . The antibodies produced to these are of IgE type. Common allergens: mites in dust, pollens, animal dander, etc. Symptoms: sneezing, watery eyes, running nose and difficulty in breathing. Allergy is due to the release of chemicals like histamine and serotonin from the mast cells. For determining the cause, the patient is exposed to or injected with very small doses of possible allergens, and the reactions are studied. Drugs like anti-histamine, adrenalin and steroids quickly reduce the symptoms of allergy. Modern-day life style has resulted in lowering of immunity and more sensitivity to allergens — more and more children in metro cities of India suffer from allergies and asthma. This could be because of the protected environment provided early in life. 7.2.6 Auto Immunity Memory-based acquired immunity evolved in higher vertebrates based on the ability to differentiate foreign organisms (e.g., pathogens) from self-cells. Two corollaries follow: Higher vertebrates can distinguish foreign molecules as well as foreign organisms — most experimental immunology deals with this aspect. Sometimes, due to genetic and other unknown reasons, the body attacks self-cells. This results in damage to the body and is called auto-immune disease . 7.2.7 Immune System in the Body The human immune system consists of lymphoid organs, tissues, cells and soluble molecules like antibodies . It recognises foreign antigens, responds to these and remembers them. It also plays an important role in allergic reactions, auto-immune diseases and organ transplantation. These are the organs where origin and/or maturation and proliferation of lymphocytes occur. 7.3 AIDS The word AIDS stands for Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome . This means deficiency of immune system, acquired during the lifetime of an individual, indicating that it is not a congenital disease. ‘Syndrome’ means a group of symptoms. div]:my-0"> AIDS is caused by the Human Immuno deficiency Virus (HIV) , a member of a group of viruses called retrovirus , which have an envelope enclosing the RNA genome. People at high risk of getting this infection include: Individuals who have multiple sexual partners. Drug addicts who take drugs intravenously. Individuals who require repeated blood transfusions. Children born to an HIV infected mother. HIV/AIDS is not spread by mere touch or physical contact ; it spreads only through body fluids . It is, hence, imperative, for the physical and psychological well-being of the infected, that HIV/AIDS infected persons are not isolated from family and society. The chapter asks you to find out and make a list. Conditions in which repeated transfusion is needed include: Thalassaemia and other inherited haemoglobin disorders. Haemophilia and other severe bleeding disorders. Severe anaemia, including that caused by chronic kidney disease. Major surgery, trauma and severe blood loss. Cancer chemotherapy and bone-marrow disorders, where blood cells are not produced adequately. How HIV disables the immune system Simultaneously, HIV enters helper T-lymphocytes (T H ), replicates and produces progeny viruses. ), }, { label: "Progressive loss of helper T-cells", description: "Progeny viruses released in the blood attack other helper T-lymphocytes. This is repeated, leading to a progressive decrease in the number of helper T-lymphocytes.", }, { label: "Opportunistic infections take over", description: "The person suffers from bouts of fever, diarrhoea and weight loss, then from infections that could otherwise be overcome — bacteria especially Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and even parasites like Toxoplasma.", }, ]} /> A widely used diagnostic test for AIDS is enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay (ELISA) . Treatment with anti-retroviral drugs is only partially effective. These drugs can only prolong the life of the patient but cannot prevent death, which is inevitable. Prevention of AIDS As AIDS has no cure, prevention is the best option . HIV infection, more often, spreads due to conscious behaviour patterns and is not something that happens inadvertently, like pneumonia or typhoid. Making blood (from blood banks) safe from HIV. Ensuring the use of only disposable needles and syringes in public and private hospitals and clinics. Free distribution of condoms. Controlling drug abuse. Advocating safe sex. Promoting regular check-ups for HIV in susceptible populations. In our country the National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) and other non-governmental organisations (NGOs) are doing a lot to educate people about AIDS. WHO has started a number of programmes to prevent the spreading of HIV infection. “Don’t die of ignorance.” Infection with HIV or having AIDS is something that should not be hidden

title: Human Reproduction
headings: Sex of the baby is decided at fertilisation
blob: import from "@/components/content/Callout"; import from "@/components/content/KeyPoint"; import from "@/components/content/Comparison"; import from "@/components/content/Expandable"; import from "@/components/content/ExerciseQa"; import from "@/components/content/Highlight"; import from "@/components/content/Stepper"; import from "@/components/content/process/ProcessCard"; import from "@/components/content/process/CycleDiagram"; import from "@/components/content/process/Timeline"; import from "@/components/content/study/MetricCard"; import from "@/components/content/study/MistakeCard"; import from "@/components/content/data/TableCard"; import from "@/components/content/data/Checklist"; import from "@/components/content/concept/FactCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/ConceptCard"; import from "@/components/content/concept/TreeDiagram"; export default function HumanReproductionChapter() { return ( <> Sperm formation continues even in old men . Formation of ovum ceases in women around the age of fifty years . 2.1 The Male Reproductive System The male reproductive system is located in the pelvis region . It includes a pair of testes alongwith accessory ducts, glands and the external genitalia. The testes and the scrotum The testes are situated outside the abdominal cavity , within a pouch called the scrotum . Each testis is oval in shape. Length is about 4 to 5 cm ; width is about 2 to 3 cm . The testis is covered by a dense covering . Each testis has about 250 compartments called testicular lobules . Each lobule contains one to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules , in which sperms are produced. The scrotum helps in maintaining the low temperature of the testes — about 2–2.5 °C lower than the normal internal body temperature — which is necessary for spermatogenesis . A temperature this close to core temperature is what the process cannot tolerate. div]:my-0"> Inside a seminiferous tubule Each seminiferous tubule is lined on its inside by two types of cells — male germ cells (spermatogonia) and Sertoli cells . Lie on the inside wall of the tubule. Undergo meiotic divisions . Finally lead to sperm formation . ), }, { title: "Sertoli cells", children: ( Also line the inside of the tubule. Provide nutrition to the germ cells. Later nurse the developing sperms — sperm heads become embedded in them. ), }, ]} /> The regions outside the seminiferous tubules are called interstitial spaces . They contain: Small blood vessels. Interstitial cells, or Leydig cells . Other immunologically competent cells. Leydig cells synthesise and secrete testicular hormones called androgens . They sit in the interstitial spaces, not inside the seminiferous tubule. The male sex accessory ducts The ducts store and transport the sperms from the testis to the outside through the urethra. The penis The penis is the male external genitalia . It is made of special tissue that helps in erection of the penis, which facilitates insemination. The enlarged end is called the glans penis . The glans penis is covered by a loose fold of skin called the foreskin . The male accessory glands Paired seminal vesicles . A prostate . Paired bulbourethral glands . The seminal plasma supplies fructose — the sugar the sperms use — along with calcium and certain enzymes . The secretions of the bulbourethral glands also help in the lubrication of the penis . Testis makes the sperms and the androgens; the ducts carry them; the glands make the seminal plasma that keeps them alive and motile. 2.2 The Female Reproductive System The female reproductive system consists of a pair of ovaries alongwith a pair of oviducts , uterus , cervix , vagina and the external genitalia , all located in the pelvic region. These parts, alongwith the pair of mammary glands, are integrated structurally and functionally to support ovulation, fertilisation, pregnancy, birth and child care . The ovaries Ovaries are the primary female sex organs . They produce the female gamete ( ovum ) and several steroid hormones ( ovarian hormones ). The ovaries are located one on each side of the lower abdomen . Each ovary is about 2 to 4 cm in length. Each ovary is connected to the pelvic wall and the uterus by ligaments . Each ovary is covered by a thin epithelium which encloses the ovarian stroma . The stroma is divided into two zones — a peripheral cortex and an inner medulla . The oviducts The oviducts (fallopian tubes), uterus and vagina constitute the female accessory ducts . Each fallopian tube is about 10–12 cm long and extends from the periphery of each ovary to the uterus. The ampullary region of the fallopian tube is where the ovum and the sperms meet — and therefore where fertilisation takes place. Section 2.5 returns here. The uterus The uterus is single and is also called the womb . Its shape is like an inverted pear . It is supported by ligaments attached to the pelvic wall. The uterus opens into the vagina through a narrow cervix . The cavity of the cervix is called the cervical canal ; alongwith the vagina it forms the birth canal . The endometrium is rebuilt and shed every cycle; the myometrium is the muscle that pushes the baby out at birth. Do not swap them. The female external genitalia The hymen is often torn during the first coitus (intercourse). However, it can also be broken by a sudden fall or jolt, insertion of a vaginal tampon, or active participation in some sports like horseback riding, cycling, etc. In some women the hymen persists even after coitus. In fact, the presence or absence of hymen is not a reliable indicator of virginity or sexual experience . The mammary glands A functional mammary gland is characteristic of all female mammals . The mammary glands are paired structures (breasts) that contain glandular tissue and a variable amount of fat . The glandular tissue of each breast is divided into 15–20 mammary lobes . Each lobe contains clusters of cells called alveoli . The cells of the alveoli secrete milk , which is stored in the cavities (lumens) of the alveoli. 2.3 Gametogenesis The primary sex organs — the testis in the males and the ovaries in the females — produce gametes, i.e., sperms and ovum, respectively, by the process called gametogenesis . Occurs in the testis . Immature male germ cells (spermatogonia) produce sperms. Begins at puberty . ), }, { title: "Oogenesis", children: ( Occurs in the ovary . Produces the mature female gamete (ovum). Initiated during embryonic development . ), }, ]} /> Spermatogenesis In the testis, the immature male germ cells ( spermatogonia ) produce sperms by spermatogenesis, which begins at puberty. The spermatogonia (sing. spermatogonium) present on the inside wall of the seminiferous tubules multiply by mitotic division and increase in numbers. Each spermatogonium is diploid and contains 46 chromosomes . Some of the spermatogonia, called primary spermatocytes , periodically undergo meiosis. A spermatogonium is diploid with 46 chromosomes . Meiosis I halves the number and meiosis II keeps it unchanged, so every spermatid carries 23 chromosomes . There are four spermatids from one primary spermatocyte, and each of them is haploid. Mitosis multiplies the stock of spermatogonia; meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles the chromosomes; spermiogenesis merely remodels a round cell into a swimming one. Hormonal control of spermatogenesis Spermatogenesis starts at the age of puberty due to a significant increase in the secretion of gonadotropin releasing hormone (GnRH) — a hypothalamic hormone. Structure of a sperm A sperm is a microscopic structure composed of a head , neck , a middle piece and a tail . A plasma membrane envelops the whole body of the sperm. div]:my-0"> Sperms released from the seminiferous tubules are transported by the accessory ducts. Secretions of the epididymis , vas deferens , seminal vesicle and prostate are essential for maturation and motility of sperms. The seminal plasma along with the sperms constitute the semen . The functions of the male sex accessory ducts and glands are maintained by the testicular hormones ( androgens ). Oogenesis The process of formation of a mature female gamete is called oogenesis , which is markedly different from spermatogenesis. Oogenesis is initiated during the embryonic development stage . A couple of million gamete mother cells ( oogonia ) are formed within each fetal ovary . No more oogonia are formed and added after birth. These cells start division and enter prophase-I of the meiotic division. They get temporarily arrested at that stage and are then called primary oocytes . A large number of these follicles degenerate between birth and puberty. Therefore, at puberty only 60,000–80,000 primary follicles are left in each ovary. The secondary oocyte retains bulk of the nutrient-rich cytoplasm of the primary oocyte. That store is the only provision the early embryo has before implantation, so the cell that is going to be fertilised keeps almost all of it; the first polar body gets very little. The first polar body is born out of the first meiotic division, which is unequal — it receives barely any cytoplasm. NCERT states plainly: at present we are not very certain about this. It may divide further or it may degenerate. What is certain is that it does not become a gamete. Spermatogenesis vs oogenesis Site: seminiferous tubules of the testis. Starts at puberty and continues through life. Both meiotic divisions are equal . One primary spermatocyte gives four sperms . No reserve is built before birth; new cells are made all the time. Millions of gametes are released in one ejaculation. ), }, { title: "Oogenesis", children: ( Site: ovary. Initiated in the fetal ovary; no new oogonia after birth. Both meiotic divisions are unequal — polar bodies are set aside. One primary oocyte gives one ovum (plus polar bodies). Meiosis II is completed only after the sperm enters. One ovum is released per menstrual cycle. ), }, ]} /> 2.4 Menstrual Cycle The reproductive cycle in the female primates (e.g. monkeys, apes and human beings) is called the menstrual cycle . The first menstruation begins at puberty and is called menarche . In human females, menstruation is repeated at an average interval of about 28/29 days , and the cycle of events starting from one menstruation till the next one is called the menstrual cycle. div]:my-0"> The cycle starts with the menstrual phase , when menstrual flow occurs. The menstrual flow results due to breakdown of the endometrial lining of the uterus and its blood vessels, which forms a liquid that comes out through the vagina. Menstruation only occurs if the released ovum is not fertilised. Lack of menstruation may be indicative of pregnancy. During pregnancy all events of the menstrual cycle stop and there is no menstruation. However, it may also be caused due to some other underlying causes like stress , poor health , etc. Hormonal control of the cycle LH surge — the rapid mid-cycle rise of luteinising hormone — ruptures the Graafian follicle. If a question asks which hormone induces ovulation, the answer is LH. Cyclic menstruation is an indicator of a normal reproductive phase, and it extends between menarche and menopause . In human beings, menstrual cycles cease around 50 years of age; that is termed menopause . Menstrual hygiene Maintenance of hygiene and sanitation during menstruation is very important. 2.5 Fertilisation and Implantation During copulation (coitus) semen is released by the penis into the vagina ( insemination ). The motile sperms swim rapidly, pass through the cervix, enter into the uterus and finally reach the ampullary region of the fallopian tube. The ovum released by the ovary is also transported to the ampullary region, where fertilisation takes place. Fertilisation can only occur if the ovum and sperms are transported simultaneously to the ampullary region. This is the reason why not all copulations lead to fertilisation and pregnancy. The process of fusion of a sperm with an ovum is called fertilisation . Each gamete is haploid with 23 chromosomes . Fusion restores the diploid number, so the zygote has 46 chromosomes — 23 from the sperm and 23 from the ovum. Sex of the baby is decided at fertilisation The chromosome pattern in the human female is XX and that in the male is XY . All the haploid gametes (ova) produced by the female have the sex chromosome X . In the male gametes (sperms) the sex chromosome could be either X or Y . Hence 50 per cent of sperms carry the X chromosome while the other 50 per cent carry the Y . After fusion, the zygote would carry either XX or XY , depending on whether the sperm carrying X or Y fertilised the ovum. The zygote carrying XX would develop into a female baby and XY would form a male . Scientifically it is correct to say that the sex of the baby is determined by the father and not by the mother. Cleavage, morula, blastocyst and implantation Trophoblast — the outer layer; it attaches to the endometrium and later forms the chorionic villi. Inner cell mass — the group of cells attached to the trophoblast; it differentiates as the embryo. 2.6 Pregnancy and Embryonic Development After implantation, finger-like projections appear on the trophoblast called chorionic villi , which are surrounded by the uterine tissue and maternal blood. The chorionic villi and uterine tissue become interdigitated with each other and jointly form a structural and functional unit between the developing embryo (foetus) and the maternal body, called the placenta . Facilitates the supply of oxygen and nutrients to the embryo. Also the removal of carbon dioxide and excretory/waste materials produced by the embryo. Is connected to the embryo through an umbilical cord , which helps in the transport of substances to and from the embryo. Acts as an endocrine tissue and produces several hormones. Increased production of these hormones is essential for supporting fetal growth , metabolic changes in the mother and maintenance of pregnancy . The three germ layers Immediately after implantation, the inner cell mass (embryo) differentiates: An outer layer called ectoderm . An inner layer called endoderm . A mesoderm soon appears between the ectoderm and the endoderm. These three layers give rise to all tissues (organs) in adults . The inner cell mass also contains certain cells called stem cells , which have the potency to give rise to all the tissues and organs. Month by month The human pregnancy lasts 9 months. Here is what is visible at each stage. 2.7 Parturition and Lactation The average duration of human pregnancy is about 9 months , which is called the gestation period . Vigorous contraction of the uterus at the end of pregnancy causes expulsion/delivery of the foetus. This process of delivery of the foetus (childbirth) is called parturition . Parturition is induced by a complex neuroendocrine mechanism. The stimulatory reflex between the uterine contraction and oxytocin secretion continues, resulting in stronger and stronger contractions. This leads to expulsion of the baby out of the uterus through the birth canal — parturition. Soon after the infant is delivered, the placenta is also expelled out of the uterus. Oxytocin. Since oxytocin is the hormone that drives the contraction–secretion feedback loop, an injection of oxytocin starts the same loop and brings on labour. Lactation The mammary glands of the female undergo differentiation during pregnancy . They start producing milk towards the end of pregnancy by the process called lactation . This helps the mother in feeding the new-born. Breast-feeding during the initial period of infant growth is recommended by doctors for bringing up a healthy baby. Everywhere — in water, air, soil, and inside the bodies of animals and plants. Even where nothing else survives — the extreme addresses below. Deep inside the geysers (thermal vents), at temperatures up to 100 °C . Deep in the soil. Under layers of snow several metres thick. In highly acidic environments. How diverse are they? Bacteria Fungi Protozoa Viruses — microscopic, of animals and of plants Viroids Prions — proteinaceous infectious agents Bacteria and many fungi grow on nutritive media as colonies visible to the naked eye — which is what makes them studyable in the lab. 8.1 Microbes in Household Products We use microbes, or products derived from them, every day. The most familiar example is the production of curd from milk. Curd from milk Micro-organisms such as Lactobacillus and others commonly called lactic acid bacteria (LAB) grow in milk and convert it to curd. During growth, the LAB produce acids that coagulate and partially digest the milk proteins. Curd is not just soured milk — it is a better food than the milk it came from. More vitamin B₁₂ — the nutritional quality of the milk improves. Fewer pathogens — in our stomach the same LAB check disease-causing microbes. Other fermented foods Several everyday foods are made by letting microbes ferment the raw material. Saccharomyces cerevisiae , "Baker’s yeast ferments the dough; CO₂ raises it.", ], }, { cells: [ "Toddy", "Microbes in the palm sap", "Sap from palms ferments into a traditional drink.", ], }, { cells: ["Fish, soyabean, bamboo-shoots", "Microbes", "Fermented to make foods."], }, ]} caption="Idli and bread rise by the same gas — CO₂ from fermentation." /> The bacteria break down the sugars of the dough anaerobically — fermentation. The sugar is not fully oxidised, so CO₂ escapes as a gas. The same breakdown raises bread and produces ethanol in fermented drinks. They are not added as a pure laboratory culture. The bacteria are already present in the ingredients and in the surroundings, and the dough is simply left at a suitable temperature so that these naturally occurring microbes multiply and ferment it. Cheese Cheese is one of the oldest food items in which microbes were used. Its variety is decided by the microbe. Propionibacterium sharmanii , "Produces a large amount of CO₂ — that is what makes the large holes.", ], }, { cells: [ "Roquefort cheese", "A specific fungus grown on the cheese", "Ripens the cheese and gives it a particular flavour.", ], }, ]} caption="Different varieties are known by their texture, flavour and taste — and that specificity comes from the microbe used." /> 8.2 Microbes in Industrial Products Even in industry, microbes are used to synthesise a number of products valuable to human beings. Beverages and antibiotics are some examples. 8.2.1 Fermented Beverages Microbes, especially yeasts, have been used from time immemorial for the production of beverages like wine, beer, whisky, brandy or rum. The same yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae used for bread-making — commonly called brewer’s yeast — is used for fermenting malted cereals and fruit juices. The product of that fermentation is ethanol . Depending on the raw material used for fermentation and the type of processing, different types of alcoholic drinks are obtained. Yeast ferments the sugars of the malted cereal or the fruit juice anaerobically . A sugar such as glucose becomes ethanol and carbon dioxide . That is the same reaction that raises bread dough — only what is fermented and what is collected differ. Wine Beer The fermented broth itself is the drink. ), }, { title: "Produced by distillation", children: ( Whisky Brandy Rum These are produced by distillation of the fermented broth. ), }, ]} /> 8.2.2 Antibiotics Antibiotics produced by microbes are regarded as one of the most significant discoveries of the twentieth century, and have greatly contributed towards the welfare of human society. Antibiotics are chemical substances, which are produced by some microbes and can kill or retard the growth of other (disease-causing) microbes . Anti is a Greek word that means “against”, and bio means “life”; together they mean “against life” — in the context of disease-causing organisms. With reference to human beings they are “pro life” and not against . Penicillin is the antibiotic everyone knows. It was the first antibiotic to be discovered , and it was a chance discovery . After penicillin, other antibiotics were also purified from other microbes. Penicillin was only the first. Streptomycin — from Streptomyces griseus . Erythromycin — from Streptomyces erythraeus . Tetracyclines — from other Streptomyces species. NCERT asks you to find these out for yourself — keep adding to the list from your library. Antibiotics have greatly improved our capacity to treat deadly diseases such as: Plague. Whooping cough ( kali khansi ). Diphtheria ( gal ghotu ). Leprosy ( kusht rog ). These diseases used to kill millions all over the globe. Today, we cannot imagine a world without antibiotics. 8.2.3 Chemicals, Enzymes and other Bioactive Molecules Microbes are also used for commercial and industrial production of certain chemicals like organic acids, alcohols and enzymes. Aspergillus niger , "A fungus", ], }, { cells: [ "Acetic acid", Acetobacter aceti , "A bacterium", ], }, { cells: [ "Butyric acid", Clostridium butylicum , "A bacterium", ], }, { cells: [ "Lactic acid", Lactobacillus , "A bacterium", ], }, ]} /> Yeast ( Saccharomyces cerevisiae ) is used for commercial production of ethanol . Microbes are also used for production of enzymes . Streptococcus (modified by genetic engineering) , "Used as a “clot buster” for removing clots from the blood vessels of patients who have undergone myocardial infarction leading to heart attack.", ], }, { cells: [ "Cyclosporin A", Trichoderma polysporum (a fungus) , "An immunosuppressive agent used in organ-transplant patients.", ], }, { cells: [ "Statins", Monascus purpureus (a yeast) , "Commercialised as blood-cholesterol lowering agents; acts by competitively inhibiting the enzyme responsible for synthesis of cholesterol.", ], }, ]} /> Organic acids, ethanol, enzymes, a clot buster, an immunosuppressant and a cholesterol-lowering drug — all six come out of microbial cultures, and all six are industrial products. 8.3 Microbes in Sewage Treatment Large quantities of waste water are generated every day in cities and towns. A major component of this waste water is human excreta. This huge quantity of sewage cannot be discharged into natural water bodies like rivers and streams directly. Before disposal, therefore, sewage is treated in sewage treatment plants (STPs) to make it less polluting. Treatment of waste water is done by the heterotrophic microbes naturally present in the sewage . This treatment is carried out in two stages . Primary treatment — physical removal These treatment steps basically involve physical removal of particles — large and small — from the sewage through filtration and sedimentation . Secondary treatment — biological treatment The primary effluent is passed into large aeration tanks , where it is constantly agitated mechanically and air is pumped into it. While growing, these microbes consume the major part of the organic matter in the effluent. This significantly reduces the BOD of the effluent. The sewage water is treated till the BOD is reduced. BOD refers to the amount of the oxygen that would be consumed if all the organic matter in one liter of water were oxidised by bacteria . The BOD test measures the rate of uptake of oxygen by micro-organisms in a sample of water. Thus, indirectly, BOD is a measure of the organic matter present in the water. The greater the BOD of waste water, the more is its polluting potential . Physical removal of particles. Filtration removes floating debris; sedimentation removes grit. Settled solids form the primary sludge; the supernatant is the effluent. The effluent still carries most of the organic matter — and a high BOD. ), }, { title: "Secondary treatment", children: ( Biological treatment by aerobic microbes. Microbes grow as flocs in aerated tanks and consume the organic matter. Settled flocs form the activated sludge; part of it is recycled as inoculum. BOD falls significantly, so the effluent can be released into rivers and streams. ), }, ]} /> Microbes treat millions of gallons of waste water every day across the globe, and the methodology has been practised for more than a century in almost all parts of the world. Till date, no man-made technology has been able to rival the microbial treatment of sewage. Increasing urbanisation means sewage is produced in much larger quantities than ever before, while the number of sewage treatment plants has not increased enough to treat it. So untreated sewage is often discharged directly into rivers, leading to their pollution and an increase in water-borne diseases. The Ministry of Environment and Forests has initiated the Ganga Action Plan and the Yamuna Action Plan to save these major rivers from pollution. Under these plans it is proposed to build a large number of sewage treatment plants, so that only treated sewage may be discharged into the rivers. 8.4 Microbes in Production of Biogas Biogas is a mixture of gases (containing predominantly methane) produced by microbial activity and which may be used as fuel. Microbes produce different types of gaseous end-products during growth and metabolism, and the type of gas produced depends upon the microbes and the organic substrates they utilise. In the fermentations met so far — dough, cheese making and production of beverages — the main gas produced was CO₂ . Dough making, cheese making and beverage production. Main gas produced: CO₂ . ), }, { title: "Methanogens", children: ( Certain bacteria that grow anaerobically on cellulosic material. Produce a large amount of methane , along with CO₂ and H₂. Collectively called methanogens; one common bacterium is Methanobacterium . ), }, ]} /> Methanogens are commonly found in the anaerobic sludge during sewage treatment. They are also present in the rumen (a part of the stomach) of cattle. In the rumen they help in the breakdown of cellulose, and play an important role in the nutrition of cattle. The excreta (dung) of cattle, commonly called gobar , is therefore rich in these bacteria. Dung can be used for generation of biogas, commonly called gobar gas . No. Cellulose is broken down by the methanogens that live in the rumen of cattle, not by anything in the human gut, so the cellulosic part of our food passes through undigested. Cattle dung is available in large quantities in rural areas, where cattle are used for a variety of purposes, so biogas plants are more often built in rural areas. The biogas produced is used for cooking and lighting . The technology of biogas production was developed in India mainly due to the efforts of the Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) and the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) . Gas for cooking and lighting out of one outlet; spent slurry as fertiliser out of the other. Nothing is wasted — the fuel and the manure come from the same digestion. 8.5 Microbes as Biocontrol Agents Biocontrol refers to the use of biological methods for controlling plant diseases and pests . Modern farming has answered pests and diseases with chemicals — and paid for it. Insecticides and pesticides are the usual weapon against pests and diseases. Toxic beyond the pest — they harm human beings and animals alike. They travel — into soil and ground water, and into fruits, vegetables and crop plants. Weedicides add to the same load of soil pollution. Biological control of pests and diseases In agriculture there is a method of controlling pests that relies on natural predation rather than introduced chemicals. A key belief of the organic farmer is that biodiversity furthers health. The more variety a landscape has, the more sustainable it is. The organic farmer works to create a system where the insects sometimes called pests are not eradicated , but kept at manageable levels by a complex system of checks and balances within a living and vibrant ecosystem. Conventional farming often uses chemical methods that kill both useful and harmful life forms indiscriminately. Biocontrol is a holistic approach: it seeks to understand the webs of interaction between the many organisms that make up the field fauna and flora. Eradication of pests is not only possible but also undesirable — without them, the beneficial predatory and parasitic insects that depend on them as food or hosts could not survive. Biocontrol measures therefore greatly reduce our dependence on toxic chemicals and pesticides. An important part of biological farming is to know the life forms of the field — predators as well as pests — along with their life cycles, feeding patterns and preferred habitats. Microbial biocontrol agents Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) , "Butterfly caterpillars", "Dried spores sprayed on the crop; the larva eats them and the toxin kills it.", ], }, { cells: [ "Bt-cotton", "Insect pests of cotton", "The same toxin gene is engineered into the plant, so the plant resists the pest.", ], }, { cells: [ Trichoderma , "Several plant pathogens", "Free-living fungi common in root ecosystems; an effective biocontrol of plant disease.", ], }, { cells: [ "Baculoviruses, mostly genus Nucleopolyhedrovirus", "Insects and other arthropods", "Species-specific and narrow spectrum; harmless to plants, mammals, birds, fish and other insects.", ], }, ]} /> Bacillus thuringiensis reaches the field as dried spores in a sachet. Mixed with water, it is sprayed on vulnerable plants — brassicas and fruit trees. Bt-cotton has the same toxin gene built in, and is already cultivated in some states of our country. A narrow spectrum agent is especially desirable when beneficial insects are being conserved to aid in an overall integrated pest management (IPM) programme, or when an ecologically sensitive area is being treated. Biocontrol replaces chemicals with natural predation and microbial pathogens. The aim is not to wipe a pest out, but to hold it at a manageable level while the rest of the ecosystem keeps working. 8.6 Microbes as Biofertilisers Chemical fertilisers met the rising demand for agricultural produce — and became a major source of pollution. Their overuse is now recognised as a problem, so there is a large pressure to switch to organic farming — the use of biofertilisers . Biofertilisers are organisms that enrich the nutrient quality of the soil . The main sources of biofertilisers are bacteria, fungi and cyanobacteria . Plants having mycorrhizal associations show other benefits as well: Resistance to root-borne pathogens. Tolerance to salinity and drought. An overall increase in plant growth and development. The association is a trade, not charity. The fungus gives — it absorbs phosphorus from the soil and passes it to the plant. The plant gives — sugars and other organic food, which the fungus cannot make for itself because it has no chlorophyll. Tightly coiled at metaphase into 46 chromosomes via NHC proteins. 5.2 The Search for Genetic Material 1869: Identification of Nuclein (Miescher). 1926: Core question raised — chemical nature of genetic material? Meischer’s nuclein and Mendel’s factors were simultaneous, but “DNA is the genetic material” took decades. By 1926 chromosomes were narrowed as carriers — but which molecule? 1. Transforming Principle — Frederick Griffith (1928) Organism Used: Streptococcus pneumoniae Bacterial Strains: S strain (Smooth): mucus polysaccharide coat; virulent R strain (Rough): lacks coat; non-virulent Experimental Procedure & Results: Some transforming principle from heat-killed S enabled R to make a smooth coat and become virulent — transfer of genetic material. Biochemical nature not defined yet. 2. Biochemical Characterisation — Avery, MacLeod, McCarty (1933–44) Researchers: Oswald Avery, Colin MacLeod, Maclyn McCarty Objective: Determine chemical nature of transforming principle from Griffith’s experiment. Experimental Setup & Findings: Purified biomolecules (RNA, Protein, DNA) from Heat-Killed S strain and added them to Live R strain: DNA is the polymer (genetic material). DNase is the enzyme that digests DNA. Avery used DNase to prove DNA’s role. 3. Proof That DNA is the Genetic Material — Hershey & Chase (1952) Researchers: Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase Experimental System: Bacteriophages (viruses that infect bacteria) and E. coli Radioactive Isotope Labeling: ³⁵S (Radioactive Sulfur): Labels viral protein coat (Sulfur in protein, absent in DNA) ³²P (Radioactive Phosphorus): Labels viral DNA (Phosphorus in DNA, absent in protein) Experimental Steps: Figure 5.5 — Hershey–Chase experiment (³⁵S protein vs ³²P DNA) DNA is the genetic material passed from virus to bacteria (Figure 5.5). 5.2.2 Properties of Genetic Material (DNA vs RNA) In some viruses (TMV, QB bacteriophage) RNA is the genetic material. Why is DNA predominant while RNA is messenger/adapter? To function as genetic material, a molecule must fulfill four requirements: 1. Replication: It should be able to generate its replica. 2. Stability: It should be structurally and chemically stable. 3. Mutation/Evolution: It should undergo slow changes that lead to evolution. 4. Expression: It should be able to express itself in the form of Mendelian characters. Why DNA is better for storage: 2'-OH in every RNA nucleotide makes RNA labile; RNA is catalytic/reactive; DNA is less reactive, double-stranded, with repair. Thymine (vs uracil) adds stability. DNA for storage , RNA for transmission . RNA is more reactive and mutates faster — hence RNA-genome viruses have short life and evolve fast. 5.3 RNA World RNA was the first genetic material . Essential life processes (metabolism, translation, splicing) evolved around RNA. RNA acted as genetic material + catalyst (important biochemical reactions catalysed by RNA, not protein enzymes). As catalyst, RNA was reactive and unstable → DNA evolved from RNA via chemical modifications for stability. Double-stranded + complementary strand + repair process further resists changes. 5.4 Replication Semiconservative Scheme Each strand separates and acts as a template for a new complementary strand → after replication each DNA has one parental + one new strand → semiconservative (Figure 5.6). Figure 5.6 Watson–Crick model for semiconservative DNA replication Mechanism — three key points DNA replicates semiconservatively. The original double helix separates and each strand acts as a template. Each template builds its complement. Complementary base pairing drives synthesis of a new strand. Result — one old + one new. Every daughter molecule ends with one parental and one newly synthesised strand. 5.4.1 The Experimental Proof — Meselson & Stahl (1958) DNA replicates semiconservatively — shown first in E. coli and later in higher organisms such as plants and human cells. Procedure — three steps Can you recall what centrifugal force is — and why a molecule with higher mass/density sediments faster? On a CsCl gradient: heavy (¹⁵N) DNA → bottom, light (¹⁴N) DNA → top, hybrid → middle. All DNA hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) density , }, { title: "Two generations (40 min)", children: 50% hybrid + 50% light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N) , }, ]} /> 80 min = 4 generations (dividing every 20 min). Start with 2 heavy strands. After n gens: 2 hybrid + (2ⁿ – 2) light. For 80 min (4 gens, 16 strands): 2 hybrid : 14 light = 1:7 . Because after one generation all DNA is hybrid (no heavy, no light), only semiconservative (and dispersive) explain it; conservative replication would show heavy + light with no hybrid. Taylor and Colleagues Experiment (1958) A very similar experiment using radioactive thymidine to detect newly synthesised DNA in chromosomes was performed on Vicia faba (faba beans) by Taylor and colleagues in 1958. Conclusion: DNA in chromosomes also replicates in a semiconservative manner in eukaryotes. 5.4.2 DNA Replication Process and the Machinery Key characteristics Mode: semiconservative. Energy: deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates act as substrates and provide energy (two terminal high-energy phosphates, like ATP). Starting: cannot initiate on its own — needs a definite origin of replication in E. coli DNA. This is why a DNA piece propagated in recombinant procedures needs a vector (vector provides the origin). Mechanism of Replication — the Replicating Fork Long DNA cannot be separated along its whole length (very high energy requirement) — replication occurs in a small opening of the helix called the replication fork (Figure 5.8). Figure 5.8 Replicating Fork Origin of replication: specific site where replication initiates. Unwinding: the fork forms as double-stranded DNA is separated at a small opening. Direction: polymerases synthesise only 5' → 3' — this creates complications at the fork. Template: 3' → 5' Synthesis continuous in 5' → 3' ), }, { title: "Lagging strand — discontinuous", children: ( Template: 5' → 3' Synthesised as small ( Okazaki ) fragments Fragments joined by DNA ligase (Fig 5.8) ), }, ]} /> In eukaryotes replication occurs at S-phase , tightly coordinated with the cell cycle. Failure of replication without division → polyploidy (chromosomal anomaly). Detailed origin structure — higher classes. 5.5 Transcription Copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA . Principle of complementarity — but A pairs with U (not T). Unlike replication (whole DNA duplicated), only one segment + one strand is copied. If both strands as templates → two different RNAs (complementary ≠ identical) → code for two different proteins from one segment → complicates information transfer. Two complementary RNAs made simultaneously would form dsRNA → cannot be translated → transcription becomes futile. 5.5.1 Transcription Unit A transcription unit in DNA is defined by three regions: Promoter: Towards 5' end (upstream) of structural gene (w.r.t. coding strand). Binding site for RNA polymerase; defines template vs coding strands. Structural gene: Region transcribed. Terminator: Towards 3' end (downstream) of coding strand; defines end of transcription. Figure 5.9 Schematic structure of a transcription unit Polymerase also works 5'→3', so the strand with polarity 3'→5' acts as template strand . The other strand (5'→3'), same sequence as RNA (T instead of U), is coding strand (does not code, strange name) — displaced during transcription. Reference point is coding strand. Example: 3'-ATGCATGCATGC-5' Template 5'-TACGTACGTACG-3' Coding RNA transcribed from above template? 5'-UACGUACGUACG-3' (complement of template, same as coding except U). Figure 5.9 schematic. Promoter↔terminator swap would reverse coding/template definitions. Additional regulatory sequences may lie further upstream/downstream — discussed in gene regulation. 5.5.2 Transcription Unit and the Gene Gene = functional unit of inheritance. Difficult to define strictly as DNA sequence. tRNA/rRNA coding DNA also defines a gene . Define cistron as segment coding for polypeptide → structural gene can be monocistronic (mostly eukaryotes) or polycistronic (mostly bacteria/prokaryotes). Eukaryotic monocistronic genes are split : coding exons (appear in mature RNA) interrupted by introns (intervening, removed). Split arrangement complicates gene definition. Promoter/regulatory sequences affect inheritance but don’t code → loosely called regulatory genes . 5.5.3 Types of RNA and the process of Transcription One polymerase for all RNAs σ/ρ factors No processing; coupled transcription-translation ), }, { title: "Eukaryotes — two complexities", children: ( 3 polymerases in nucleus + organellar ones Primary transcripts have exons + introns → splicing + capping + tailing ), }, ]} /> Split genes probably ancient; introns reminiscent of antiquity; splicing represents dominance of RNA world . Translation = nucleotides → amino acids — no complementarity, no theoretical mapping. Yet nucleic acid changes cause amino acid changes → genetic code proposes. Physicist George Gamow argued: 4 bases code for 20 amino acids ⇒ combination. 3-nucleotide code: 4³ = 64 codons (>20, bold proposition).
