Gresham was Robert's employer for 35 years, making the betrayal feel personal. The family argues loyalty should override legal duty, but Robert sees truth as non-negotiable. The title refers to the moment when truth is tested against personal relationships. ), }, { id: "price-of-integrity", title: "The Price of Integrity", content: ( Robert's integrity costs him $100,000 and potentially his friendship with Gresham. Gresham's confession proves that integrity has its own reward — respect from others. ), }, { id: "family-pressure", title: "Family Pressure and Moral Weakness", content: ( Martha, John, and Evie all pressure Robert to accept the bribe, each for different reasons. Famous works include Brothers, Little Shot, and First is Last. The Hour of Truth is from A Question of Morality and Other Plays — a striking psychological study on the corrupting influence of money. Introduction The Hour of Truth is a one-act play by Percival Wilde that explores the conflict between truth and loyalty, integrity and self-interest. Set on a hot Sunday afternoon, the play centres on Robert Baldwin, who must decide whether to testify truthfully against his lifelong friend and employer John Gresham, or accept a $100,000 bribe to lie on the stand. The play examines how the prospect of easy money can corrupt even the closest family bonds, and how true integrity reveals itself when tested. Summary Author : Percival Wilde. Genre: One-act play. Setting: Baldwin cottage, hot Sunday afternoon. Characters : Robert Baldwin (witness), John Gresham (old friend/employer, arrested for bank fraud), Martha (wife), John Jr. (son), Evie (daughter), Mr. Marshall (banker). Conflict : Gresham offers Baldwin $100,000 to say “I don’t remember” on the stand — Baldwin refuses. Family pressure : Son (logic: nobody lost money), wife (emotional: godfather bond), daughter (guilt: you’re the only one). All three want Baldwin to take the money. Resolution : Gresham confesses rather than face Baldwin’s testimony. Baldwin receives a job offer from Mr. Marshall — reward for integrity . Theme : Integrity is revealed when it costs you everything. A clean conscience is worth more than any amount of money. } standard={ The wait : The play opens on a hot Sunday afternoon. The Baldwin family anxiously awaits Robert’s return from meeting John Gresham, his lifelong friend and employer who has been arrested for bank fraud. The family knows Robert is the only witness who can convict Gresham. Robert’s return : Robert arrives and explains: Gresham asked him to forget key details on the stand — just say “I don’t remember.” — which would let Gresham escape punishment. Robert refused. He tells the family he turned down $100,000 , saying those three words would choke him. John Jr.’s argument (logic) : His son argues nobody lost money — it’s just a technicality. Gresham shouldn’t be jailed for something that harmed no one. The argument is rational but morally empty. Martha’s argument (emotion) : Martha reminds Robert that Gresham was their son’s godfather — it would be sad if the name came to grief through him. She appeals to loyalty, history, and family bonds. Evie’s argument (guilt) : Evie cries: Robert would be the only one wanting to punish Gresham. She tries to make him feel isolated — as if his integrity is selfishness. Robert’s explosion : Robert calls his family liars and hypocrites , saying they’ve seen their souls naked and they stink to heaven. The moment is devastating — the family’s true characters are revealed, and Robert has seen them. Mr. Marshall’s arrival : Mr. Marshall arrives with news: Gresham confessed rather than face Baldwin’s testimony. He offers Robert a bank position — the reward for integrity is not money but trust and position . } detailed={ Structure : One-act play, single setting (the Baldwin cottage). The entire conflict unfolds in real time — no scene breaks, no time jumps. The single setting creates claustrophobia: there is nowhere to hide. Every character is trapped in the same room, under the same heat, facing the same moral question. The one-act form forces confrontation — there is no intermission for escape. Moral pressure : Each family member pressures Robert differently: John Jr. (logic: nobody lost money, it’s a technicality), Martha (emotional: the godfather bond, family loyalty), Evie (guilt: you’re the only one who wants to punish him). They represent three forms of moral compromise — rationalisation, sentiment, and emotional manipulation. Together they form a wall of pressure that Robert must break through alone. The bribe : $100,000 is not abstract. Robert has been out of work. The money is real, immediate, life-changing . The temptation is not greed — it’s survival. Wilde makes the bribe large enough to be genuinely tempting, which makes Robert’s refusal genuinely courageous. If the bribe were small, the choice would be easy. At $100,000, it’s a sacrifice. “I don’t remember” : The three words Gresham wants are not a lie — they’re the absence of truth. Robert sees this as worse than lying : it’s erasure. A lie at least acknowledges the truth exists. “I don’t remember” pretends the truth never happened. Robert understands that moral corruption often hides behind technically true statements. Robert’s speech : “You’ve all seen your souls naked, and they stink to heaven.” The family has revealed their true characters — and Robert has seen them. The speech is the play’s turning point. Before it, the family pressures Robert. After it, Robert stands alone, morally clear but personally devastated. He has lost not just Gresham but his family’s respect. Gresham’s confession : Gresham confessed not out of guilt but because he knew Baldwin would never lie. Robert’s integrity changed the outcome without him testifying. The confession is the play’s ironic twist: Robert never had to choose between friendship and truth — Gresham made the choice for him. But the moral test was real, and Robert passed it. Ending : Robert receives a job offer from Mr. Marshall — the reward for integrity is not money but trust and position . The ending is not sentimental: Robert has won, but at great cost. His family exposed their own moral weakness, and his friendship with Gresham is destroyed. The job offer is not a consolation prize — it’s the world recognising someone worth trusting. The poet worries the dentist might get mixed up — the way you do when tying a bow tie in a mirror and forget which side is which. This adds terror to an already terrifying situation. ), }, { question: "Comment on the aptness of the title of the poem.", answer: ( <> The title This Is Going to Hurt Just a Little Bit is very suitable, because going to the dentist is always painful and frightening. It repeats the reassuring words a dentist actually says, and the whole poem measures that “little bit” against what really happens in the chair. Nash uses it ironically : the small hurt the title promises turns out to be demolition with a crowbar. The title also sets the comic tone before a single line is read — we already know the promise is going to be broken. ), }, { question: "The poet compares the mouth to a section of road that is being repaired. Do you feel any exaggeration in it? Find more such instances in the poem.", answer: ( <> Yes, it is an exaggeration. A mouth being drilled is not really a road under repair, but the comparison is deliberately stretched so that the situation seems far worse than it is — and that is exactly what creates the humour. The image also works: stone crushers, concrete mixers, drills and steam rollers describe what the patient thinks he can hear and feel. Other exaggerations in the poem: Teeth that are supposed to be polished seem to be “demolished”. The dentist works with a “crowbar”. The coating he puts on feels like something used to put a shine on a “horse’s hoof”. The jaw is “digging into your chest”. Every nerve in your head is “being irked on”. The patient feels he is one of the “two or three in life most lacking in dignity”. ), }, { question: "What effect does this poetic device (simile) produce in the poem? Find out other similes used in the poem.", answer: ( <> Similes make the poem funnier and help us imagine the discomfort clearly. They give the reader a familiar picture — a road under repair, a horse’s hoof, a bow tie — for an experience that is otherwise hard to describe, so the exaggeration lands instead of merely sounding like complaint. Other similes and comparisons in the poem: “Your mouth is like a section of road that is being worked on.” The coating in the mouth is “something that I suspect is generally used to put a shine on a horse’s hoof.” The dentist’s confusion of left and right is “the way you do when you try to tie a bow tie with the aid of a mirror.” The dentist “may be a bear” — “an ursa,” as the Romans used to say. ), }, { question: "Nash plays with language throughout the poem. Point out his deliberate misspellings and puns, and say what they add to the poem.", answer: ( <> Nash uses deliberate misspellings and puns to keep the tone comic: “hopen” for hoping , “monce” for months , and “ursa” for the Latin word for a bear, which he turns into a joke about a feminine bear. The aside about the Romans is a comic digression: the dentist may be “a bear,” and the Romans, Nash says, used ursa only for a she-bear. It lightens the poem’s tone while the argument — that the whole business is torture — quietly carries on. These small jokes matter because they turn complaint into comedy: the reader laughs at the language itself, not only at the situation. ), }, ]; const DISCUSSION_ITEMS = [ { question: "Ogden Nash's poem is indeed a very strange way of looking at a reality — the painful experience of a dental treatment. Are you convinced of this attitude? Explain.", answer: ( <> Yes, the attitude is convincing. The poet uses humour to deal with fear and pain: by exaggerating the experience until it becomes absurd, he makes it seem funny instead of merely frightening. This way of looking at it helps us realise that sometimes laughing at an uncomfortable situation makes it easier to face. The reader who has sat in a dentist’s chair recognises every detail, and recognition is what turns dread into laughter. Sophia Borger’s idea supports this too — a cheerful, humorous attitude helps us handle difficult realities more wisely. ), }, ]; const DISCOURSES = [ { id: "appreciation", title: "Poem Appreciation", content: ( <> Appreciation of the Poem — by Ogden Nash I. Introduction — Poet, Title, Mood and Theme This Is Going to Hurt Just a Little Bit by Ogden Nash is a humorous poem about a visit to the dentist. The title is the poem’s first joke: the cheerful assurance that it will hurt “just a little bit” is exactly what the patient dreads, and the whole poem measures that little bit against what actually happens in the chair. The mood is light and playful throughout, and the theme is the fear, discomfort and helplessness a person feels during dental treatment — turned into comedy through exaggeration and wit. II. Summary and Central Idea The poet declares that sitting in a dentist’s chair with his mouth wide open is one thing he likes less than most things. Some tortures, he says, are physical and some are mental, but the dental one is both. He cannot stay composed: his jaw digs into his chest, his fingernails make “serious alterations” in his palm lines, and he cannot keep up his usual “cheery benignity” in a position “most lacking in dignity.” The mouth then becomes a section of road being worked on — cluttered with stone crushers, concrete mixers, drills and steam rollers — and every nerve in his head is being irked. The teeth are supposed to be polished but feel as if they are being demolished. Worst of all, it is all done with a mirror, so the dentist — who may be “a bear,” an ursa — holds a crowbar in one hand and a mirror in the other and might confuse left and right, the way one does when tying a bow tie in a mirror. When it is “all over,” he coats the mouth with something the poet suspects is used to put a shine on a horse’s hoof, and says “come back in three monce.” The central idea arrives in the last lines: this is the most vicious circle Fate ever devised — a man must go continually to the dentist to keep his teeth in good condition, when the chief reason he wants them in good condition is so that he will not have to go to the dentist. III. Poetic Devices, Language, Tone and Style The poem runs on hyperbole. A dentist’s drill becomes a steam roller, a probe a crowbar, polishing a demolition, and a mouth a road under repair. The comparisons are what make the terror funny: the mouth is “like a section of road that is being worked on,” the coating is “generally used to put a shine on a horse’s hoof,” and the confusion of the mirror is “like trying to tie a bow tie with the aid of a mirror.” Nash’s irony works from the title downwards — the promise of “just a little bit” against the demolition in the chair, and the closing circle in which the cure is also the cause. The language is colloquial and conversational, with Nash’s deliberate misspellings — “hopen” for hoping, “monce” for months, “sentest” for sent — and comic Latin (“ursa”). The lines are long and loosely rhymed, running on the way a nervous patient’s thoughts run on, and the second person (“your jaw,” “your mouth”) pulls the reader into the chair. The tone is playful and self-mocking: the poet never complains seriously, he laughs at the whole experience. IV. Conclusion — Message, Personal Response and Favourite Lines In conclusion, This Is Going to Hurt Just a Little Bit is a memorable poem because it turns a genuinely painful experience into an entertaining one. Its message — that humour helps us face fear and pain , and that laughing at an uncomfortable situation makes it easier to bear — is as useful as it is funny. My favourite lines are “And your mouth is like a section of road that is being worked on,” because in one image they hold the whole method of the poem: the ordinary mouth, the heavy machinery and the patient’s helplessness at once. Overall, the poem is an effective and enjoyable piece of comic verse that deserves appreciation. ), }, ]; export default function ThisIsGoingToHurtPage() { const [activeTab, setActiveTab] = useState("summary"); return ( {activeTab === "summary" && ( Introduction This Is Going to Hurt Just a Little Bit is a humorous poem by Frederic Ogden Nash , one of America’s best-known light poets. The poem is a graphic, hilarious description of the poet’s experience sitting in a dentist’s chair. Through wild metaphors and escalating exaggeration , Nash transforms a universal dread into comic art. Summary Poet : Ogden Nash — American humorist poet (1902-1971). Subject : The terror and indignity of sitting in a dentist’s chair. Central metaphor : The mouth as a construction site — stone crushers, concrete mixers, drills. Worst element : The dentist uses a mirror — which reverses left and right. Closing : The “most vicious circle” — we keep teeth healthy to avoid the dentist. } standard={ The poet declares that sitting in a dentist’s chair with his mouth open is the thing he likes less than most things . Some tortures are physical, some mental — dental torture is both. He loses all composure: jaw digging into chest, fingernails making “serious alterations” in his palm lines, unable to maintain “cheery benignity.” The position is “one of the two or three in life most lacking in dignity.” The mouth becomes a road under construction — “cluttered up with stone crushers and concrete mixers and drills and steam rollers.” Every nerve is being irked. Teeth are supposed to be polished but feel like they’re being demolished . The worst part is the mirror. The dentist may be a bear (“an ursa”), and how can you be sure he won’t get left and right mixed up — like trying to tie a bow tie in a mirror? After it’s “over,” the dentist says “come back in three monce.” The poet addresses Fate: this is the most vicious circle — we keep teeth healthy so we won’t have to go to the dentist. } detailed={ Opening declaration : The poem opens with a characteristically Nash-like construction: “One thing I like less than most things.” This understatement immediately signals the comic tone. The hope of never having to do it again is itself “against hope hopen” — a deliberate misspelling that establishes the poem’s playful relationship with language. Physical and mental torture : Nash identifies the dual nature of dental anxiety: some tortures are physical, some mental, but dental is both. The jaw digs into the chest. Fingernails make “serious alterations in your life line or love line.” The poet cannot maintain “cheery benignity” — his usual social mask cracks under the indignity. The construction site metaphor : The mouth becomes “a section of road that is being worked on” — cluttered with stone crushers, concrete mixers, drills, and steam rollers. This extended metaphor transforms a medical procedure into industrial demolition . The escalation from “polished” to “demolished” captures the patient’s perception. The mirror and the ursa : The dentist uses a mirror in one hand and a “crowbar” in the other. The poet compares the dentist to a bear (“an ursa”) — with a comic aside that the Romans referred to a feminine bear. The mirror reverses left and right, creating confusion — like trying to tie a bow tie in a mirror. The vicious circle : The poem’s closing is its philosophical peak. Man goes to the dentist to keep teeth healthy so he won’t have to go to the dentist. Nash addresses Fate directly: this is “the most vicious circle that thou ever sentest.” The deliberately archaic “sentest” adds comic gravity to what is essentially a complaint about life’s self-defeating routines. } /> Universal Anxiety The poem captures a shared human experience — the dread of sitting in a dentist’s chair. By describing it in extreme terms, Nash validates the reader’s own fears while simultaneously defusing them through humor. Loss of Control The poet is entirely at the dentist’s mercy. His mouth is “cluttered up” with instruments he cannot see, operated by a man who might “get mixed up.” The powerlessness of the patient — unable to see, speak, or defend himself — is the poem’s emotional core. Vicious Cycles The closing “vicious circle” extends beyond dentistry. We maintain things to avoid maintaining them. We take medicine to avoid taking medicine. The poem uses dental anxiety as a metaphor for life’s self-defeating routines . Nash transforms dental anxiety into comic poetry through hyperbole, wordplay, and escalating imagery . The mouth becomes a construction site, the dentist a bear with a crowbar, and the entire experience a “vicious circle” — we keep our teeth healthy so we won’t have to visit the dentist. The poem reminds us that humor is the best weapon against life’s small torments. Read & Respond )} {activeTab === "creations" && ( {DISCOURSES.map((section) => ( ))} )} ); }
